> **The check against it is simply to ask whether every efficiency in the question has been used — three were given, and a solution that used none of them cannot be right.**

> **A question that supplies data and an answer that ignores it are not compatible, and that observation catches this error and many like it.**

**THE EFFICIENCY CHAIN DESERVES SETTING OUT IN FULL BECAUSE THE THREE GIVEN HERE ARE NOT ALWAYS ALL OF IT:**

| Stage | Typical efficiency |
|---|---|
| **Turbine (Francis or Kaplan at design point)** ← | **0.90 to 0.94** ← |
| **Generator** ← | **0.96 to 0.98** ← |
| **Transformer** ← | **0.98 to 0.995** ← |
| **Speed increaser / gearbox, IF fitted** ← | **0.96 to 0.98 — small units only** ← |
| **Station auxiliaries (own consumption)** ← | **A further 1 to 2 per cent taken off the output** ← |
| **Overall, plant to busbar** ← | **Typically 0.83 to 0.88** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OMITTED AND IT IS NOT AN EFFICIENCY AT ALL BUT A DEDUCTION: the plant consumes some of its own output.**

> **Cooling water pumps, oil pressure units, lighting, ventilation, the drainage and dewatering pumps, and the control systems all draw power continuously.**

> **On a large plant that is 1 to 2 per cent, and on a small one with the same fixed loads it is a larger fraction.**

> **So the energy SOLD is less than the energy generated, and a financial model built on generated energy overstates the revenue by that margin — a small percentage on a large number, which is exactly the kind of error that survives review.**

**AND THE PHRASE 'AT THE DESIGN POINT' IN THE TURBINE ROW CARRIES A WARNING WORTH TAKING:**

> **The efficiencies quoted are peak values, achieved at the design discharge and head.**

> **A turbine running at 40 per cent of design flow may be at 0.75 efficiency or considerably less, depending on its type.**

> **So an annual energy calculation cannot apply the peak efficiency to every flow; it must apply the efficiency appropriate to each flow, read from the turbine's efficiency curve.**

> **Using the peak efficiency throughout overstates the annual energy — by little on a plant that runs near design most of the time, and by a great deal on an ROR plant in a river with a long low-flow season, which is the case where the error is both largest and most likely to be made.**

examTip.trap: **10.0 MW is the water power with NO efficiency applied** — the question gave three efficiencies, so an answer using none of them cannot be right.
examTip.mnemonic: **Station auxiliaries take another 1-2% off the output** — pumps, cooling, lighting. Energy sold is less than energy generated.

questions.stem: A 6 MW plant operates at a capacity factor of 0.55. Its annual energy generation is approximately:
options: 28.9 GWh
52.6 GWh
3.3 GWh
14.5 GWh
questions.solution:
**About 28.9 GWh.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Energy if run flat out all year** | **6 MW × 8760 h = 52,560 MWh = 52.56 GWh** ← |
| **Times the capacity factor** | **52.56 × 0.55 = 28.91 GWh** ← |

> **THE SHORTCUT WORTH CARRYING IS THAT 1 MW FLAT OUT FOR A YEAR IS 8.76 GWh, so 6 MW is 52.56 GWh and the rest is one multiplication.**

> **That single figure — 8.76 GWh per MW-year — turns most annual energy questions into mental arithmetic.**

> **A 50 MW plant at 0.5 capacity factor: 50 × 8.76 × 0.5 = 219 GWh.**

> **A 100 kW micro-hydro at 0.6: 0.1 × 8.76 × 0.6 = 0.53 GWh, or 526,000 units a year.**

**THE DISTRACTORS ARE EACH A NAMED ERROR AND THEY ARE WORTH IDENTIFYING:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **52.6 GWh** | **The energy at 100 per cent capacity factor — the capacity factor was not applied** ← |
| **14.5 GWh** | **Half the correct answer — 6 × 8.76 × 0.55 ÷ 2, or a 3 MW plant** ← |
| **3.3 GWh** | **6 × 0.55 = 3.3 — the multiplication by 8760 omitted, giving megawatts labelled as gigawatt-hours** ← |
| **28.9 GWh** | **Correct** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE ERROR BECAUSE IT IS A UNITS FAILURE RATHER THAN AN ARITHMETIC ONE: 6 × 0.55 = 3.3 is a correct multiplication that produces MEGAWATTS, and the answer required GIGAWATT-HOURS.**

> **Power and energy are different quantities and no multiplication of powers produces an energy without a time.**

> **The habit that catches this is to carry the units through the arithmetic rather than attaching them at the end: MW × dimensionless = MW, and MW × hours = MWh.**

> **Any line whose units do not come out as the answer requires is wrong regardless of the numbers in it, and this check costs nothing and catches a large fraction of all numerical errors.**

**A NOTE ON WHAT A 0.55 CAPACITY FACTOR IMPLIES PHYSICALLY, SINCE THE NUMBER SHOULD MEAN SOMETHING:**

| Interpretation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The plant generated as much as it would running flat out for 55 per cent of the year** ← | **About 4,800 hours** ← |
| **That is NOT the same as running flat out for 4,800 hours and stopping** ← | **It is an equivalent, not a description** ← |
| **In reality an ROR plant runs at full output in the monsoon and part output all year** ← | ← |
| **The same 0.55 could arise from many different patterns** ← | ← |

> **The second row is the interpretive caution and it matters when the figure is used for anything beyond energy: the equivalent full-load hours describe the total, not the profile.**

> **For calculating annual energy, the profile is irrelevant and the capacity factor is sufficient.**

> **For calculating revenue under a time-of-day tariff, or for assessing the plant's contribution to peak supply, the profile is everything and the capacity factor tells you nothing.**

> **So the same statistic is complete for one purpose and useless for another, and knowing which is which is the point of understanding rather than merely computing it.**

examTip.trick: **6 × 8.76 GWh × 0.55 = 28.9 GWh** — carry 8.76 GWh per MW-year and these become mental arithmetic.
examTip.trap: **3.3 is 6 × 0.55 with the hours forgotten** — that is megawatts, not gigawatt-hours. Carry units through every line.
examTip.mnemonic: **0.55 CF means the equivalent of 4,800 full-load hours, not a description of the profile** — sufficient for annual energy, useless for a time-of-day tariff.

questions.stem: In estimating the ANNUAL ENERGY of a run-of-river plant from a flow duration curve, the correct procedure is to:
options: Apply the design flow to all 365 days and multiply by the capacity factor
Use the mean annual flow with the peak turbine efficiency throughout
Divide the curve into intervals
Use only the flow exceeded 50 per cent of the time
questions.solution:
**DIVIDE the curve into intervals, take the flow available in each, CAP it at the design flow, deduct the riparian release, apply the efficiency appropriate to that part-load, and sum the energy of all intervals.**

**The procedure step by step:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Divide the exceedance axis into intervals — 5 or 10 per cent, or better, use the daily series directly** ← | ← |
| **2. For each interval, read the available river flow** ← | ← |
| **3. DEDUCT the riparian release** ← | **Before anything else is done with the flow** ← |
| **4. CAP the remainder at the plant's design flow** ← | **Surplus above design flow is SPILLED and generates nothing** ← |
| **5. Deduct the flow below the plant's MINIMUM operating flow as zero** ← | **A turbine cannot run below roughly 20 to 40 per cent of design flow** ← |
| **6. Compute the net head at that flow** ← | **Head losses fall as flow falls, so net head RISES at part load** ← |
| **7. Read the efficiency at that part-load from the turbine curve** ← | ← |
| **8. Energy for the interval = 9.81 × Q × H × η × hours in the interval** ← | ← |
| **9. Sum over all intervals** ← | ← |

> **STEPS 4 AND 5 ARE THE TWO CAPS AND THEY BOUND THE USEFUL PART OF THE CURVE AT BOTH ENDS: above the design flow the plant cannot use the water, and below the minimum operating flow it cannot run at all.**

> **So the energy comes only from the middle band of the flow duration curve, and the shape of that band is what matters.**

> **A candidate who applies the design flow to the whole year overstates the energy by ignoring the second cap and the whole low-flow tail.**

> **And one who ignores the first cap credits the plant with monsoon flows it physically cannot pass, which on a Nepali river can double the apparent energy.**

> **THE FIFTH STEP IS ROUTINELY FORGOTTEN AND ITS EFFECT IS SUBSTANTIAL ON A SEASONAL RIVER: a Francis turbine will not run below about 40 per cent of design flow and a Pelton will run down to 15 or 20 per cent.**

> **On a river whose dry-season flow falls below that threshold, the plant simply shuts down.**

> **So the machine choice affects the ANNUAL ENERGY and not merely the efficiency — a Pelton or a multi-jet Pelton keeps generating through flows that stop a Francis.**

> **This is one reason multiple smaller units are preferred over a single large one on a highly variable river: two units of half the size let the plant run one unit at its own design point when the flow halves, rather than running one large unit badly or not at all.**

**THE SIXTH STEP IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IS WORTH A SEPARATE NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Head loss varies roughly with the SQUARE of the flow** ← | ← |
| **So at half the design flow, conveyance losses fall to about a QUARTER** ← | ← |
| **The net head therefore RISES as the flow falls** ← | ← |
| **Which partly offsets the loss of power from the reduced flow** ← | **Though only partly — power varies with Q directly and with H's small gain** ← |

> **The offset is modest but it is real, and neglecting it slightly understates part-load energy — which is the opposite direction from the other common errors, and is therefore worth knowing about so the errors are not all assumed to point the same way.**

> **For a plant designed with 6 per cent total losses, running at half flow recovers about 4.5 percentage points of head, which is a 4 to 5 per cent gain in power at that flow.**

> **Over a season spent largely at part load that is not negligible, and the calculation costs nothing once the loss coefficient is known.**
tags: annual energy from a flow duration curve
net head rises at part load

examTip.trick: **Interval by interval: deduct riparian, cap at design flow, zero below minimum operating flow, use part-load efficiency, sum.**
examTip.trap: **Two caps bound the useful band** — spill above design flow, shutdown below minimum flow. Ignoring the upper cap can double the apparent energy on a monsoon river.
examTip.mnemonic: **Net head RISES at part load** — losses go as Q², so half flow means a quarter of the losses. A small real gain that runs opposite to the usual errors.

questions.stem: Where a hydropower site has NO GAUGING RECORD of its own, the standard method of estimating its flows is:
options: Assume a runoff coefficient of 0.5 applied to the rainfall
Use the regional average specific discharge without adjustment
Measure the flow for one year and scale it to the long term by assuming that year was average
Transfer the record from a gauged catchment nearby
questions.solution:
**TRANSFER the record from a gauged catchment nearby** — scaling by CATCHMENT AREA and adjusting for differences in rainfall and elevation — and verify the transfer against whatever short-term measurements the site itself allows.

**The transfer method in its simplest and its better forms:**

| Form | Expression | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple area ratio** | **Q_site = Q_gauged × (A_site / A_gauged)** ← | **Assumes identical yield per unit area** ← |
| **Area and rainfall** | **Q_site = Q_gauged × (A_site/A_gauged) × (P_site/P_gauged)** ← | **Better — corrects for the rainfall difference** ← |
| **With an exponent** | **Q_site = Q_gauged × (A_site/A_gauged)ⁿ** ← | **n slightly less than 1, since large catchments yield a little less per unit area** ← |
| **Regional regression** | **Q = f(area, rainfall, elevation, and other catchment indices)** ← | **The best available where a regional study exists** ← |

> **THE ASSUMPTION IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE ONE THAT FAILS AND KNOWING WHEN IT FAILS IS THE WHOLE SKILL: it holds only if the two catchments are hydrologically similar.**

> **Similar rainfall, similar elevation range, similar geology, similar land cover, and similar snow and glacier contribution.**

> **Two adjacent Nepali catchments can differ radically in all of these — one reaching above the snow line and the other not, one on permeable and one on impermeable rock — and their specific yields then differ by a factor rather than a percentage.**

> **The ELEVATION check is the most important single one in Nepal, because a catchment extending above about 5,000 m has snow and glacier melt sustaining its dry-season flow, and one that does not is rain-fed and nearly dries — and it is exactly the dry-season flow on which the project's firm power depends.**

**THE VERIFICATION STEP DESERVES EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS CHEAP AND IS OFTEN SKIPPED:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Install a staff gauge at the site as early as possible, in the survey license period** ← | **It costs almost nothing and each month of record is valuable** ← |
| **Take current-meter or salt-dilution measurements to build a rating** ← | ← |
| **Compare the site's measured flows with the transferred estimates for the SAME days** ← | ← |
| **And adjust the transfer coefficient to fit** ← | ← |
| **Concentrate the measurements in the DRY season** ← | **That is where the estimate matters most and where the transfer is least reliable** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHERE THE EFFORT SHOULD GO AND IT IS COUNTER TO THE NATURAL INCLINATION: monsoon flows are dramatic and easy to be interested in, and dry-season flows determine the project's value.**

> **A dozen careful dry-season gaugings across two or three years pin down the low-flow end of the curve, which is where the firm power comes from and where the transfer method is most doubtful.**

> **Monsoon flows can be estimated adequately by transfer because the catchments' responses are dominated by rainfall, which is more uniform across a region than the baseflow characteristics are.**

> **So the measurement programme should be designed around the dry season, and a programme that gauges through the monsoon and stops in November has spent its money on the part of the curve it needed least.**

> **THE THIRD DISTRACTOR — ONE YEAR ASSUMED AVERAGE — IS A REAL AND SERIOUS ERROR RATHER THAN AN INVENTED ONE, and it is worth naming: a single year's record establishes nothing about the long-term distribution.**

> **A wet year overstates the resource and a dry year understates it, and there is no way to know which the year was without a long-term reference — which is precisely what the transfer method supplies.**

> **So the correct use of a single year's site record is not as a resource estimate but as a CALIBRATION of the transfer from a long-record station, and the distinction between those two uses is the difference between a defensible hydrology and an indefensible one.**
tags: snow contribution and dry season flow
one year is a calibration not an estimate

examTip.trick: **Transfer from a gauged neighbour, scaled by area and adjusted for rainfall** — then verify against short measurements at the site.
examTip.trap: **Check whether the donor catchment reaches the SNOW LINE** — snowmelt sustains dry-season flow, and dry-season flow is what firm power depends on.
examTip.mnemonic: **Gauge the DRY season, not the monsoon** — that is where the value lies and where the transfer is least reliable. A single year calibrates; it never estimates.

questions.stem: The RESERVOIR MASS CURVE (Rippl diagram) is used to determine the storage required to meet a given demand. On the diagram, the required storage is:
options: The maximum vertical distance between a demand line drawn tangent to a peak of the cumulative inflow curve and the curve itself
The total volume under the inflow curve
The horizontal distance between successive tangent points
The slope of the steepest part of the mass curve
questions.solution:
**The MAXIMUM VERTICAL DISTANCE between a demand line drawn tangent to a peak of the cumulative inflow curve and the curve itself, before the two meet again.**

**How the construction works:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Plot CUMULATIVE inflow volume against time — this is the mass curve** ← | **It always rises, steeply in the wet season and gently in the dry** ← |
| **2. Draw the DEMAND line, whose slope is the constant demand rate** ← | **Since cumulative demand rises at a steady rate** ← |
| **3. Draw demand lines TANGENT to each PEAK of the mass curve** ← | **A peak is the end of a wet period, when the reservoir would be full** ← |
| **4. Measure the maximum VERTICAL gap between each tangent and the curve below it** ← | **That is the deficit accumulating through the dry period** ← |
| **5. The LARGEST of those gaps over the whole record is the required storage** ← | ← |

> **THE VERTICAL AXIS IS VOLUME AND THAT IS WHY THE VERTICAL GAP IS THE ANSWER — a point worth fixing, because the temptation is to measure something along the time axis.**

> **The demand line's height at any moment is the cumulative water demanded; the curve's height is the cumulative water supplied.**

> **The gap between them is the cumulative shortfall, which is exactly the volume the reservoir must have held.**

> **So the maximum gap is the maximum draw on storage, and the reservoir must be at least that large.**

**WHAT THE CONSTRUCTION ASSUMES, WHICH BOUNDS ITS VALIDITY:**

| Assumption | Consequence if it fails |
|---|---|
| **The reservoir is FULL at each tangent point** ← | **If it was not, the storage computed is insufficient** ← |
| **The demand is CONSTANT — a straight demand line** ← | **A varying demand needs a demand mass curve, not a straight line** ← |
| **Evaporation and seepage are ignored, or added to the demand** ← | **They must be included, and on a large hot-climate reservoir they are large** ← |
| **The historical record will repeat** ← | **The critical drought may not be in the record at all** ← |
| **The reservoir refills between critical periods** ← | **Two consecutive dry years may combine into one longer critical period** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE CONSTRUCTION'S MOST IMPORTANT SUBTLETY AND IT IS WHY THE WHOLE RECORD MUST BE EXAMINED RATHER THAN THE WORST SINGLE YEAR: the critical period is not necessarily one dry season.**

> **A dry year followed by a poor wet season and then another dry year forms a critical period spanning two or three years, and the storage needed is the deficit accumulated across the whole of it.**

> **Taking the worst individual dry season and sizing for that gives a reservoir that empties in the second year of a run.**

> **So the tangent must be drawn from the last peak at which the reservoir was genuinely full, and if that peak is two years before the trough, the critical period is two years long — which the graphical construction handles automatically, provided the analyst draws the tangent from the right peak and does not assume it is the most recent one.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW CARRIES A CAUTION THAT NO GRAPHICAL METHOD CAN ANSWER AND IT IS WORTH STATING: sizing to the historical record's worst drought guarantees performance only against a repeat of that drought.**

> **A longer or deeper drought will empty the reservoir, and there is nothing in the record to say one cannot occur.**

> **The modern treatment is stochastic — generate many synthetic flow sequences with the same statistical properties as the record, size the reservoir for a chosen reliability, and state that reliability explicitly.**

> **That produces an answer of the form 'this storage meets the demand in 95 per cent of years', which is honest about the residual risk in a way that 'sized for the worst recorded drought' is not.**
tags: maximum vertical gap is the storage

examTip.trick: **Maximum VERTICAL gap between a tangent demand line and the mass curve** — the axis is volume, so the vertical gap is the accumulated deficit.
examTip.trap: **The critical period may span two or three years** — draw the tangent from the last peak at which the reservoir was genuinely FULL, not the most recent peak.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sizing to the worst recorded drought guarantees only against a repeat of it** — state a reliability instead, from synthetic sequences.

questions.stem: In sizing the INSTALLED CAPACITY of an ROR plant, choosing a larger design discharge than the optimum results in:
options: More firm power but less total annual energy
A higher capacity factor and lower capital cost
Machines that are more efficient throughout the year
More total annual energy but a lower capacity factor and a higher cost per unit of energy
questions.solution:
**More total annual energy but a LOWER capacity factor and a higher cost per unit of energy** — because the extra capacity is used only during the brief high flows and stands idle the rest of the year.

**What happens as the design discharge is increased:**

| Quantity | Direction |
|---|---|
| **Installed capacity** | **RISES, in proportion to the design flow** ← |
| **Annual energy** | **RISES, but by less and less for each increment** ← |
| **Capacity factor** | **FALLS** ← |
| **Capital cost** | **RISES** ← |
| **Cost per unit of energy** | **Falls at first, reaches a minimum, then RISES** ← |
| **FIRM power** | **UNCHANGED — it depends on the low flows, which the larger machine does not affect** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE ONE THAT SURPRISES AND IT IS THE POINT OF DISTRACTOR (a): enlarging the plant does nothing whatever for firm power.**

> **Firm power is set by the flow available almost all the time, and that flow is small.**

> **A larger turbine passes more water when more water is there, which is in the monsoon, and the monsoon has nothing to do with the dry-season minimum.**

> **So a developer seeking to raise firm power must add STORAGE or pondage, and adding machine capacity is precisely the wrong intervention — an important distinction because the two are easily conflated as 'making the plant bigger'.**

**WHY THE COST PER UNIT HAS A MINIMUM, WHICH IS THE OPTIMISATION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Each increment of capacity costs roughly the same per MW** ← | **Turbine, generator, penstock enlargement, powerhouse** ← |
| **But each increment earns LESS energy than the one before** ← | **Because it captures a thinner slice of the flow duration curve** ← |
| **So cost per unit of energy falls while the slices are thick and rises once they are thin** ← | ← |
| **The minimum is the economic design flow** ← | ← |
| **Which for a Nepali ROR scheme commonly lands around Q40 to Q50** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE DIMINISHING RETURN AND ITS SHAPE COMES DIRECTLY FROM THE FLOW DURATION CURVE'S SHAPE, so the optimum moves with the river: a flat curve, with well-sustained flows, justifies a larger plant than a steep flashy one.**

> **On a snowfed river with a long sustained melt season the slices stay thick well to the left, and the optimum design flow is a higher exceedance percentile.**

> **On a flashy monsoon river the flows collapse quickly and the optimum is a smaller plant.**

> **So there is no universal design percentile, and Q40 is a starting point for a calculation rather than a rule to apply.**

**AND THE OPTIMISATION IS NOT PURELY TECHNICAL, WHICH DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE:**

| Factor | Effect on the optimum size |
|---|---|
| **A tariff paying more for DRY-season energy** ← | **Pushes toward a SMALLER plant, since the extra monsoon energy is worth less** ← |
| **A tariff paying a CAPACITY charge as well as energy** ← | **Pushes toward a LARGER plant** ← |
| **A grid that cannot absorb the monsoon output** ← | **Pushes toward smaller — surplus energy is curtailed and earns nothing** ← |
| **An export market for surplus monsoon energy** ← | **Pushes toward larger** ← |

> **The third row is a real and frequently binding constraint in Nepal and it is worth recognising as an economic rather than an engineering limit: capacity that generates energy nobody will take is worthless however cheaply it was built.**

> **A plant sized on the flow duration curve alone, in a system already spilling monsoon energy, is oversized regardless of what the hydrology says.**

> **So the sizing calculation must include the market as one of its inputs, and the engineer who optimises against the river alone will produce a plant that is optimal for a system that does not exist.**
tags: firm power unaffected by machine size
optimum depends on the curve shape

examTip.trick: **More energy, lower capacity factor, higher cost per unit** — the extra capacity works only during brief high flows.
examTip.trap: **FIRM power is unchanged by a bigger machine** — it depends on the low flows. To raise firm power you add storage, not capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Q40-Q50 is a starting point, not a rule** — a sustained snowfed river justifies a larger plant than a flashy one, and a grid that cannot absorb the output shrinks it again.

questions.stem: The DESIGN FLOOD for the diversion works and spillway of a hydropower project is selected on the basis of:
options: The mean annual flood in every case
The largest flood in the available record, regardless of its return period
The consequence of failure
A uniform 100-year return period for all hydropower structures
questions.solution:
**The CONSEQUENCE of failure** — with a higher return period, up to the probable maximum flood, adopted where failure would endanger life or destroy the works, and a lower one where the consequence is limited.

**Typical design flood standards by structure and consequence:**

| Structure or situation | Design flood |
|---|---|
| **Temporary works — cofferdams, diversion during construction** ← | **10 to 25-year, accepting some risk over a short exposure** ← |
| **Intake and diversion weir of a small ROR scheme** ← | **50 to 100-year** ← |
| **Spillway of a small or medium dam** ← | **100 to 1,000-year** ← |
| **Spillway of a large dam whose failure would be catastrophic** ← | **PROBABLE MAXIMUM FLOOD (PMF), or a 10,000-year flood** ← |
| **Check flood, for stability rather than freeboard** ← | **A larger event the structure must survive with reduced freeboard** ← |

> **THE PRINCIPLE UNDERLYING THE WHOLE TABLE IS THAT RISK IS PROBABILITY TIMES CONSEQUENCE, AND ONLY THE PROBABILITY IS BEING CHOSEN HERE: the consequence is a property of the site and cannot be adjusted.**

> **A dam above an inhabited valley has a catastrophic failure consequence, and the only way to keep the risk tolerable is to make the probability very small.**

> **A small weir in an uninhabited gorge has a modest consequence, and a higher failure probability is acceptable because the product remains small.**

> **So the same engineer, applying the same principle, correctly designs one structure to the PMF and another to a 50-year flood — and a code that prescribed a single return period for all would be wrong for most of them.**

**THE FIRST ROW DESERVES A SEPARATE NOTE BECAUSE ITS LOGIC DIFFERS FROM THE REST:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Temporary works are exposed for a SHORT time** ← | **One or two dry seasons** ← |
| **So the probability of encountering a given flood is correspondingly smaller** ← | ← |
| **The risk of a 25-year flood in a 2-year exposure is about 8 per cent** ← | **1 − (1 − 1/25)² = 0.078** ← |
| **Which may be an acceptable commercial risk for a cofferdam** ← | **If its failure floods an excavation rather than killing anyone** ← |
| **But NOT if its failure would drown a workforce in a tunnel** ← | ← |

> **THE FORMULA IN THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE TO KNOW FOR THIS CLASS OF QUESTION: the risk of at least one exceedance in n years of exposure is R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ.**

> **It converts a return period into the thing that actually matters, which is the chance of the event happening during the period of interest.**

> **A 100-year flood has a 26 per cent chance of occurring at least once in 30 years, which people find startling and which is simply what the definition means.**

> **And over a 50-year project life the same flood is 39 per cent likely — so designing a permanent structure to a 100-year flood accepts a better-than-one-in-three chance of exceedance during its life, which is a decision that should be made consciously rather than inherited from a standard.**

> **THE LAST ROW OF THE TEMPORARY-WORKS TABLE IS THE OVERRIDE AND IT IS ABSOLUTE: where failure endangers life, the commercial risk calculation does not apply.**

> **A cofferdam protecting an excavation may be designed to an economically optimal return period, weighing the cost of a higher dam against the expected cost of flooding the works.**

> **A cofferdam whose overtopping would trap workers underground may not, and its design flood is set by safety rather than by economics — with an evacuation procedure and flood warning as additional layers rather than as substitutes.**

examTip.trick: **Consequence of failure sets the return period** — PMF where failure is catastrophic, 50-100 year for a small weir, 10-25 year for temporary works.
examTip.trap: **R = 1 − (1 − 1/T)ⁿ** — a 100-year flood is 26% likely in 30 years and 39% likely in 50. That is what the return period means.
examTip.mnemonic: **Risk = probability × consequence, and only the probability is yours to choose** — the consequence belongs to the site. Life safety overrides the economics entirely.

questions.stem: A GLOF (Glacial Lake Outburst Flood) presents a design problem distinct from an ordinary flood for a Himalayan hydropower project chiefly because it:
options: Occurs only during the monsoon, when the plant is already shut down
Produces a flood of very high peak and enormous sediment and debris load that is not represented in the gauged flood record at all
Is always smaller than the design flood and can be neglected
Affects only the transmission line and not the waterway
questions.solution:
**It produces a flood of very high peak and enormous SEDIMENT and DEBRIS load that is not represented in the gauged flood record at all** — so it cannot be estimated by frequency analysis of the river's flows.

**Why a GLOF defeats ordinary flood analysis:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is not a RAINFALL-driven event, so it bears no relation to the rainfall record** ← | ← |
| **It arises from the sudden failure of a moraine dam impounding a glacial lake** ← | **Often triggered by an ice avalanche or a rise in lake level** ← |
| **The peak can exceed the largest recorded monsoon flood many times over** ← | ← |
| **It carries an extraordinary load of boulders, debris and moraine material** ← | **A debris flow rather than a water flood** ← |
| **And gauged records are short and may contain no GLOF at all** ← | ← |
| **So frequency analysis of the gauged series cannot produce it** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE METHODOLOGICAL FAILURE AND IT IS THE POINT WORTH GRASPING: extreme value analysis extrapolates the distribution of the events in the record.**

> **A GLOF is not a large member of that distribution — it is a member of a DIFFERENT distribution, generated by a different physical process.**

> **Fitting a Gumbel or a log-Pearson curve to fifty years of monsoon peaks and reading off the 1,000-year value gives the 1,000-year MONSOON flood, and says nothing about GLOFs.**

> **So a GLOF must be assessed separately, by identifying the lakes upstream, estimating their volumes, assessing their moraine dams' stability, and routing a hypothetical breach down to the site — which is a deterministic study, not a statistical one.**

> **This is a general lesson worth carrying beyond GLOFs: where two distinct physical processes can produce the same kind of loading, they must be analysed separately and the results combined, because no single statistical fit represents both.**

**WHAT CAN BE DONE ABOUT IT, WHICH IS LESS THAN ONE WOULD WISH:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **INVENTORY the glacial lakes in the catchment and assess their hazard** ← | **ICIMOD's inventories are the standard reference for Nepal** ← |
| **Route a credible breach hydrograph to the site** ← | **And design the structures to survive it, or accept and plan for the damage** ← |
| **EARLY WARNING systems on the lakes and along the valley** ← | **Which protect life even where they cannot protect works** ← |
| **LOWER the lake artificially, by siphon or a controlled outlet channel** ← | **Done at Tsho Rolpa, at considerable cost** ← |
| **Design the intake and powerhouse to be REPAIRABLE rather than indestructible** ← | ← |
| **Locate critical works — the powerhouse especially — OUT of the flood path** ← | **An underground powerhouse away from the river is far less exposed** ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS ARE THE PRAGMATIC RESPONSES AND THEY DESERVE EMPHASIS BECAUSE THE FIRST FOUR ARE EXPENSIVE OR UNCERTAIN: it is generally not feasible to build a headworks that survives a large GLOF undamaged.**

> **The energies involved are enormous and the boulders are metres across.**

> **So the realistic strategy accepts that the diversion works may be destroyed, and concentrates on protecting the expensive and slow-to-replace elements — the powerhouse, the turbines, the transformers, the tunnel.**

> **A weir that is rebuilt in a season is a tolerable loss; a powerhouse filled with debris is a multi-year outage and may be the end of the project.**

> **So the design philosophy is one of GRADED protection — sacrificial elements at the river and hardened, remote or underground elements for everything whose loss cannot be borne — which is a mature way to handle a hazard that cannot be excluded.**

> **The financial counterpart of that philosophy is insurance and a contingency reserve for the sacrificial elements, and a project in a GLOF-exposed catchment that has neither has not completed its risk treatment however good its engineering.**

examTip.trick: **A different physical process, absent from the flow record** — so no frequency analysis produces it. Assess it deterministically, by routing a breach.
examTip.trap: **Fitting Gumbel to 50 years of monsoon peaks gives the 1000-year MONSOON flood, not a GLOF** — two distributions, analysed separately.
examTip.mnemonic: **Graded protection** — accept a sacrificial weir, harden or bury the powerhouse. A weir rebuilds in a season; a debris-filled powerhouse may end the project.

questions.stem: Two hydropower plants on the same river system are said to have COMPLEMENTARY flows when:
options: Their catchments have high flows at different times of year
They are owned by the same developer
They share a common transmission line
One is a storage plant and the other run-of-river
questions.solution:
**Their catchments have HIGH FLOWS at DIFFERENT times of year** — so their combined output is steadier than either alone, and the firm power of the pair exceeds the sum of their individual firm powers.

**Why the combination is worth more than its parts:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Firm power is set by the MINIMUM of the output, not the average** ← | ← |
| **If two plants have their minima at the SAME time, the combined minimum is the sum of the minima** ← | **No gain** ← |
| **If they have their minima at DIFFERENT times, one is producing well when the other is low** ← | ← |
| **So the combined output never falls as far as either individually would suggest** ← | ← |
| **And the pair's firm power exceeds the sum of the individual firm powers** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS A GENUINE SUPERADDITIVITY AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHY IT IS NOT A TRICK: firm power is a minimum, and the minimum of a sum is greater than or equal to the sum of the minima.**

> **The two are equal only when the minima coincide.**

> **So any lack of correlation between the two flow series produces a gain, and negative correlation produces a large one.**

> **This is the same mathematics as portfolio diversification in finance and it has the same practical consequence: combining imperfectly correlated sources reduces the variability of the whole without reducing its expectation.**

**WHERE COMPLEMENTARITY COMES FROM IN NEPAL:**

| Source | Note |
|---|---|
| **SNOWFED versus RAIN-FED catchments** ← | **Snowmelt peaks in spring, monsoon rain in summer — genuinely offset** ← |
| **EASTERN versus WESTERN Nepal** ← | **The monsoon arrives in the east first and withdraws from the west last** ← |
| **High-altitude versus low-altitude catchments** ← | ← |
| **HYDRO versus SOLAR** ← | **Solar output is highest in the clear dry season, exactly when hydro is lowest** ← |
| **HYDRO versus WIND** ← | **Wind in Nepal's valleys is often strongest in the dry pre-monsoon** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST PROMISING COMPLEMENTARITY AVAILABLE TO NEPAL AND IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT PLAINLY: solar and run-of-river hydro are close to ideally anti-correlated in this climate.**

> **The monsoon brings water and cloud; the dry season brings sunshine and low flows.**

> **So a portfolio of ROR hydro and solar has a much flatter combined output than either alone, and the solar generates precisely in the season when the hydro deficit occurs.**

> **It does not solve the problem completely — solar produces nothing in the evening peak, which is when the winter deficit is sharpest — but combined with even modest storage or pondage it addresses a large part of it.**

> **That combination is considerably cheaper than the equivalent storage hydro and can be built far faster, which makes it the most practical near-term response to the seasonal mismatch even though storage remains the complete answer.**

**AND A CAUTION ABOUT MEASURING COMPLEMENTARITY, SINCE IT IS EASILY OVERSTATED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Complementarity must be measured on CONCURRENT records** ← | **Two series from different periods say nothing about their correlation** ← |
| **Monthly averages can hide daily coincidence** ← | **Two plants may look complementary monthly and both fail in the same week** ← |
| **And a regional drought affects everything at once** ← | **Correlation rises sharply in extreme events, which is when it matters most** ← |

> **The third row is the diversification argument's standard failure mode and it is exactly the one that finance rediscovers in every crisis: correlations that are low in normal conditions approach one in extreme ones.**

> **A regional drought reduces every catchment in Nepal at the same time, and the portfolio benefit largely evaporates in precisely the event it was meant to protect against.**

> **So complementarity should be relied on for ordinary seasonal smoothing and not counted on as protection against a system-wide extreme — for which the answer is storage, reserve capacity, or an interconnection to a genuinely different climate region.**

examTip.trick: **High flows at different times, so the combined minimum beats the sum of the minima** — firm power is superadditive whenever the flows are uncorrelated.
examTip.trap: **Hydro and solar are near-ideally anti-correlated in Nepal** — monsoon brings water and cloud, the dry season sunshine and low flows.
examTip.mnemonic: **Correlations approach one in extremes** — a regional drought hits every catchment together, so diversification fails exactly when it is needed.

questions.stem: A reservoir has a live storage of 90 million m³ and serves a plant with an average net head of 120 m and an overall efficiency of 0.85. The energy stored in the reservoir is approximately:
options: 25 GWh
9 GWh
250 GWh
2.5 GWh
questions.solution:
**About 25 GWh.**

**The computation, using energy rather than power:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Potential energy of the stored water** | **E = ρ g V H = 1000 × 9.81 × 90 × 10⁶ × 120 joules** ← |
| ** ** | **= 9.81 × 90 × 10⁶ × 120 × 10³ = 1.0595 × 10¹⁴ J** ← |
| **Convert to kWh** | **1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J** ← |
| ** ** | **1.0595 × 10¹⁴ ÷ 3.6 × 10⁶ = 2.943 × 10⁷ kWh = 29.43 GWh** ← |
| **Apply the efficiency** | **29.43 × 0.85 = 25.0 GWh** ← |

> **THE SHORTCUT FOR THIS CLASS OF PROBLEM IS WORTH LEARNING BECAUSE IT REMOVES THE JOULE CONVERSION ENTIRELY: E (kWh) = 0.002725 × η × V × H, with V in m³ and H in metres.**

> **The constant is 9.81 ÷ 3600 ÷ 1000 = 0.002725, and it packages the gravity, the joule-to-kWh conversion and the watt-to-kilowatt step into one number.**

> **Checking: 0.002725 × 0.85 × 90 × 10⁶ × 120 = 0.002725 × 0.85 × 1.08 × 10¹⁰ = 2.50 × 10⁷ kWh = 25.0 GWh.**

> **The same relation in more memorable form: one million cubic metres falling 100 m yields about 272 MWh of electricity at 100 per cent efficiency, or about 230 MWh at 85 per cent.**

**WHAT THE ANSWER TELLS YOU ABOUT STORAGE, WHICH IS THE POINT WORTH TAKING AWAY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **90 million m³ is a substantial reservoir** ← | **A dam of real size, with real inundation and real displacement** ← |
| **And it stores 25 GWh** ← | ← |
| **Nepal's annual consumption is of the order of 10,000 GWh** ← | ← |
| **So this reservoir holds under a day of the country's electricity** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS SOBERING AND IT IS WHY SEASONAL STORAGE REQUIRES SUCH ENORMOUS RESERVOIRS: water is a very dilute energy store.**

> **Storing a month of a country's electricity in water requires either a vast volume or a very great head, and preferably both.**

> **This is exactly why high-head storage sites are so valuable — the energy stored goes directly with the head, so a reservoir 400 m above its powerhouse stores three times what the same volume stores at 120 m.**

> **And it is why pumped storage schemes are sited for head above all else: a small upper reservoir at great height beats a large one at modest height, and it inundates far less land in the process.**

**A CROSS-CHECK WORTH DOING ON ANY SUCH ANSWER:**

| Check | Working |
|---|---|
| **What plant capacity could this reservoir run, and for how long?** | ← |
| **A 100 MW plant drawing on 25 GWh** | **25,000 MWh ÷ 100 MW = 250 hours ≈ 10 days of continuous full output** ← |
| **Or, at 4 peak hours a day** | **250 ÷ 4 ≈ 62 days of peaking operation** ← |

> **The second row is the useful interpretation and it converts an abstract figure into an operating reality: this reservoir gives a 100 MW plant about two months of evening peaking, or ten days of emergency full output.**

> **That is a meaningful capability and it is what a storage reservoir is actually for.**

> **Expressing storage in DAYS OF OPERATION rather than in cubic metres or gigawatt-hours is the form in which it can be judged, and it is the form in which an operator thinks about it — so converting to it is a habit worth acquiring.**
tags: water is a dilute energy store
express storage in days of operation

examTip.trick: **E (kWh) = 0.002725 × η × V × H** with V in m³ and H in m — the constant packages g, the joule conversion and the kilo step.
examTip.trap: **One million m³ falling 100 m is only about 272 MWh** — water is a dilute store, which is why seasonal storage needs vast reservoirs.
examTip.mnemonic: **Convert storage to DAYS OF OPERATION** — 25 GWh is ten days of a 100 MW plant flat out, or two months of evening peaking. That is how an operator judges it.

questions.stem: The DEAD STORAGE of a reservoir is provided principally to:
options: Accommodate the sediment expected to deposit over the project's design life
Meet the demand during the most severe drought on record
Provide the head required by the turbines
Hold the flood inflow temporarily during the passage of a flood
questions.solution:
**To accommodate the SEDIMENT expected to deposit over the project's design life**, so that the live storage above it remains available throughout that life.

**The zones once more, with dead storage in its place:**

| Zone | Function |
|---|---|
| **Surcharge, above FRL** ← | **Temporary flood passage** ← |
| **Flood control storage** ← | **Kept empty in the flood season** ← |
| **LIVE (conservation) storage** ← | **The usable water — between the minimum drawdown level and full reservoir level** ← |
| **DEAD storage, below the lowest outlet** ← | **Sediment accumulation over the design life** ← |

> **THE PHRASE 'BELOW THE LOWEST OUTLET' IS THE DEFINING FEATURE AND IT EXPLAINS THE NAME: water in the dead storage cannot be drawn out, because there is no opening low enough to release it.**

> **It is dead in the sense of being permanently out of use, not in the sense of being useless.**

> **And its allocation to sediment is a planning device rather than a physical partition — nothing prevents sediment depositing above the dead storage level, and in general it does.**

> **The design assumes that the volume BELOW the minimum drawdown level equals the sediment volume expected over the life, and the assumption is only as good as the sediment estimate and the deposition pattern behind it.**

**THAT LAST QUALIFICATION MATTERS AND IS WORTH DEVELOPING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sediment does NOT deposit uniformly or fill from the bottom up** ← | ← |
| **COARSE material drops at the reservoir's head, forming a DELTA** ← | **Which advances downstream over the years** ← |
| **FINE material carries further, and the finest may pass the dam** ← | ← |
| **So the delta occupies LIVE storage at the upstream end while dead storage remains partly empty** ← | ← |
| **And the useful life is shorter than a simple volume calculation predicts** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE FLAW IN THE SIMPLE DESIGN ASSUMPTION AND IT IS WHY MEASURED RESERVOIRS LOSE LIVE CAPACITY FASTER THAN PREDICTED: the sediment does not politely fill the space reserved for it.**

> **The delta forms where the river enters and grows downstream, taking live storage from the top of the reservoir first.**

> **Meanwhile the deepest part near the dam, which is the dead storage, receives only the fine fraction and fills slowly.**

> **So a reservoir may lose a third of its live storage while its dead storage is half empty, and the design life computed from total volume is optimistic.**

> **A proper assessment uses a deposition pattern — an empirical area-reduction method, or a numerical sediment model — and estimates the loss of LIVE storage specifically, which is the quantity that matters.**

**AND ONE FURTHER FUNCTION OF DEAD STORAGE DESERVES MENTION SINCE IT IS SOMETIMES THE GOVERNING ONE:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sediment accommodation** ← | **The principal reason, as above** ← |
| **Maintaining a MINIMUM HEAD on the turbines** ← | **The plant cannot operate below a certain level, whatever water remains** ← |
| **Keeping the intake SUBMERGED** ← | **To prevent vortex formation and air entrainment** ← |
| **Fisheries and ecological minimum pool** ← | **Sometimes required by the environmental approval** ← |

> **The second and third rows mean that the minimum drawdown level is often set by the PLANT rather than by the sediment allowance, and where that is so the dead storage is larger than the sediment alone would require.**

> **The intake submergence condition is a hydraulic one: draw the level too low and an air-entraining vortex forms above the intake, which reduces efficiency, causes vibration and can force a shutdown.**

> **So the minimum operating level is the highest of the several requirements — sediment allowance, turbine head, intake submergence and any ecological pool — and identifying which one governs is part of the design rather than an afterthought.**
tags: delta deposition takes live storage first

examTip.trick: **Space reserved for the design life's sediment, below the lowest outlet** — dead because it cannot be drawn, not because it is useless.
examTip.trap: **Sediment forms a DELTA at the reservoir head and eats LIVE storage first** — so live capacity is lost faster than a total-volume calculation predicts.
examTip.mnemonic: **The minimum drawdown level is the highest of sediment, turbine head, intake submergence and ecological pool** — work out which governs.

questions.stem: The TRAP EFFICIENCY of a reservoir — the proportion of incoming sediment it retains — depends principally on:
options: The sediment's chemical composition
The height of the dam alone
The ratio of the reservoir's capacity to the annual inflow
The type of spillway provided
questions.solution:
**The RATIO of the reservoir's CAPACITY to the annual INFLOW** — a large reservoir on a small river detains water long enough to settle nearly everything, while a small reservoir on a large river passes most of it.

**Why the capacity-inflow ratio governs:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Settling requires TIME — a particle must fall through the depth before the water leaves** ← | ← |
| **The time available is the DETENTION TIME = capacity ÷ inflow rate** ← | ← |
| **So the capacity-to-annual-inflow ratio is a direct measure of detention time** ← | ← |
| **A ratio of 1.0 means a year's inflow is detained — nearly everything settles** ← | **Trap efficiency approaching 100 per cent** ← |
| **A ratio of 0.01 means a few days' detention — only the coarsest settles** ← | **Trap efficiency perhaps 30 to 50 per cent** ← |

> **THE BROWN AND THE BRUNE CURVES ARE THE STANDARD EMPIRICAL RELATIONS FOR THIS, and both plot trap efficiency against the capacity-inflow ratio on a logarithmic scale.**

> **The curve rises steeply at small ratios and flattens toward 100 per cent above a ratio of about 0.5.**

> **So the first increment of storage traps a great deal of sediment and further increments add little, which is a relationship with an uncomfortable consequence.**

> **The uncomfortable consequence is that even a SMALL pondage reservoir on a sediment-laden river traps a large share of the coarse load — so an ROR scheme with a modest daily pond is not exempt from sedimentation, and it will fill far faster than a large reservoir precisely because it is small relative to the flow.**

**THE SAME RELATION READ THE OTHER WAY GIVES THE RESERVOIR'S LIFE, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL USE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Annual sediment inflow, in tonnes, from measurement or a regional estimate** ← | ← |
| **Divided by the deposited BULK DENSITY to get a volume** ← | **Typically 1.1 to 1.6 t/m³, and it increases with age as the deposit consolidates** ← |
| **Times the trap efficiency to get the volume retained each year** ← | ← |
| **Reservoir volume divided by that gives a first estimate of the life** ← | ← |
| **But the trap efficiency FALLS as the reservoir fills** ← | **So the life is longer than the simple division suggests** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A GENUINE AND SLIGHTLY CONSOLING FEEDBACK AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: as the reservoir loses capacity, its capacity-inflow ratio falls, so its trap efficiency falls, so it retains a smaller fraction of what arrives.**

> **The filling therefore decelerates, and the reservoir approaches a much-reduced equilibrium capacity rather than filling completely and stopping.**

> **A simple calculation dividing volume by annual deposition gives a 'life' that is really the time to fill at the initial rate, and the true time to reach the same condition is considerably longer.**

> **But the consolation is limited, because most of the USEFUL capacity is lost long before the reservoir is full — a reservoir at 40 per cent of its original live storage may still be technically operating and may no longer be economically worth operating.**

> **So 'reservoir life' should be defined as the time to fall below a useful capacity threshold, not the time to fill, and the two differ by decades.**

**AND NEPAL'S POSITION ON THIS DESERVES A CLOSING WORD BECAUSE IT IS EXTREME:**

> **Himalayan rivers carry among the highest sediment loads in the world — the young, rapidly uplifting and heavily fractured geology of the Chure and the High Himalaya sheds enormous quantities.**

> **Specific sediment yields of 2,000 to 5,000 tonnes per km² per year are recorded, against perhaps 100 to 500 in a temperate catchment.**

> **So a reservoir in Nepal fills perhaps ten times faster than the same reservoir in Europe would, and design lives that are comfortable elsewhere are not comfortable here.**

> **This single fact does more to shape Nepali hydropower design than any other, and it is why sediment handling — settling basins, flushing arrangements, sacrificial capacity, drawdown flushing gates in the dam — is a first-order design concern rather than a detail.**
tags: trap efficiency falls as it fills

examTip.trick: **Capacity ÷ annual inflow** — it is detention time in disguise, and the Brune curve turns it into trap efficiency.
examTip.trap: **Even a small pondage traps most of the coarse load** — and fills fastest, because it is small relative to the flow. ROR is not exempt from sedimentation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Define life as the time to fall below a USEFUL capacity, not the time to fill** — trap efficiency falls as it fills, so those two differ by decades.

questions.stem: A plant's PEAKING CAPABILITY is measured by the pondage it holds. A plant with a design discharge of 8 m³/s that must generate at full output for 4 hours of peak using stored water requires a pondage of at least:
questions.solution:
**115,200 m³.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Volume required** | **Q × time** ← |
| **Time in seconds** | **4 hours × 3600 = 14,400 s** ← |
| **Volume** | **8 × 14,400 = 115,200 m³** ← |

> **THE ONLY TRAP HERE IS THE UNIT OF TIME AND IT CATCHES A GREAT MANY PEOPLE: the discharge is per SECOND and the duration is in HOURS.**

> **8 × 4 = 32 gives option (a) as 32,000 m³, which is the answer to a question nobody asked — cubic metres per second multiplied by hours, a quantity with no meaning.**

> **The habit that prevents it is the one already recommended: write the units alongside the numbers, and m³/s × h will not reduce to m³ without the 3600.**

> **A rough check also helps: 8 m³/s is 8,000 litres a second, which is around 29,000 m³ an hour and about 115,000 m³ in four hours — reached by a different route and agreeing.**

**WHAT THE ANSWER IMPLIES PHYSICALLY, WHICH IS THE ENGINEERING CONTENT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **115,200 m³ is a pond roughly 150 m × 80 m × 10 m deep** ← | ← |
| **Which is a substantial structure but by no means a dam and reservoir** ← | ← |
| **It can often be formed by widening and deepening the headrace, or by a separate pond beside the forebay** ← | ← |
| **And it must be located where the water can be released to the turbines by gravity** ← | ← |
| **So it sits between the headworks and the powerhouse, not at the intake** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS AN IMPORTANT LAYOUT POINT AND IT IS SOMETIMES GOT WRONG: the pond must be downstream of the settling basin and upstream of the penstock.**

> **Placed at the intake it would fill with sediment, since the water there has not yet been settled.**

> **Placed below the penstock it would be useless, since the water has already been through the turbines.**

> **So the peaking pond is normally at or adjacent to the FOREBAY, receiving settled water from the headrace and feeding the penstock — which also makes it the surge-absorbing element of the system, and lets one structure serve two purposes.**

**AND THE REQUIREMENT MUST BE CHECKED AGAINST THE RIVER'S FLOW, WHICH IS THE STEP THE ARITHMETIC OMITS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The pond must REFILL during the 20 off-peak hours** ← | ← |
| **Refilling 115,200 m³ in 20 hours needs 115,200 ÷ 72,000 = 1.6 m³/s of surplus inflow** ← | **20 h = 72,000 s** ← |
| **So the river must supply at least 1.6 m³/s more than the plant uses off-peak** ← | ← |
| **If the plant shuts down entirely off-peak, the river need only supply 1.6 m³/s** ← | ← |
| **But if the plant runs at part load off-peak, the river must supply that plus 1.6** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CHECK THAT MAKES THE POND USABLE RATHER THAN MERELY LARGE AND IT IS THE HALF OF THE PROBLEM THAT THE VOLUME CALCULATION HIDES: a pond that cannot refill is a pond that works once.**

> **In the dry season, when peaking is most valuable, the river's flow may be barely enough to refill it — which is exactly when the plant most wants to peak.**

> **So the peaking capability is not a fixed property of the plant; it varies through the year with the flow, and it is least in the season when it is worth most.**

> **A peaking study must therefore be done month by month against the flow record, not once against the design flow, and stating a plant's peaking capability as a single number without naming the season overstates what it can do in December.**

examTip.trick: **8 m³/s × 4 h × 3600 = 115,200 m³.** The discharge is per second and the duration in hours.
examTip.trap: **32,000 is 8 × 4 × 1000 — m³/s times hours, a quantity with no meaning.** Write the units beside the numbers.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the REFILL** — 115,200 m³ in 20 off-peak hours needs 1.6 m³/s of surplus, and in the dry season the river may not have it.

questions.stem: In a POWER PURCHASE AGREEMENT for a Nepali ROR plant, the tariff is typically structured with a HIGHER rate for DRY-SEASON energy than for wet-season energy because:
options: Dry-season generation is more expensive to produce
The transmission losses are greater in the dry season
Dry-season energy is scarce and therefore more valuable to the system
Water rights are more costly to acquire in the dry season
questions.solution:
**Dry-season energy is SCARCE and therefore more valuable to the system** — so the tariff signal encourages developers to build plants and adopt designs that deliver in the dry season.

**How the seasonal tariff works and what it is trying to achieve:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **The year is divided into a WET and a DRY season by defined months** ← | **Commonly the dry season is mid-December to mid-April** ← |
| **Dry-season energy is paid at a HIGHER rate** ← | **Historically around 1.2 times the wet-season rate** ← |
| **So a plant delivering a larger share of its energy in the dry season earns more per unit overall** ← | ← |
| **Which rewards designs that sustain dry-season output** ← | **Pondage, a smaller design flow, a machine with good part-load performance** ← |
| **And rewards SITES with a better sustained flow** ← | **Snowfed catchments over rain-fed ones** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE TARIFF'S REAL WORK AND IT IS WORTH SEEING IT AS A DESIGN INSTRUMENT RATHER THAN A PRICE: the tariff structure changes what gets built.**

> **A flat tariff pays the same for a monsoon kilowatt-hour that the system will spill and a January kilowatt-hour it desperately needs, so it rewards maximising total energy.**

> **A seasonally differentiated tariff makes the January unit worth more, so it rewards a different design.**

> **So the tariff is a lever on the shape of the country's generation fleet, applied years in advance, and setting it badly produces a fleet of plants optimised for the wrong thing — which is a slow and expensive error to correct because plants last fifty years.**

**WHETHER THE SIGNAL IS STRONG ENOUGH IS A FAIR QUESTION AND IT DESERVES AN HONEST ANSWER:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The actual VALUE difference between dry and wet season energy is very large** ← | **Dry-season shortfall is met by imports at a high price, or by load shedding** ← |
| **A 1.2 ratio understates that difference considerably** ← | ← |
| **So the signal points the right way but is too weak to change many decisions** ← | ← |
| **A larger differential would attract more storage and more pondage** ← | ← |
| **But it also raises the average tariff, which is politically constrained** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS DESCRIBE THE REAL CONSTRAINT AND IT IS NOT A TECHNICAL ONE: a tariff that properly reflected dry-season scarcity would raise the price paid to generators, and that cost passes to consumers.**

> **The differential could in principle be widened without raising the average — by lowering the wet-season rate as the dry-season rate rises — which sharpens the signal at no net cost.**

> **That is the economically clean solution and it is resisted because it reduces the revenue of plants already built and financed on the existing structure.**

> **So the tariff tends to be adjusted upward in the dry season without a corresponding reduction in the wet, or not adjusted at all, and the signal stays weaker than the underlying economics warrant.**

> **A CLOSING OBSERVATION ON WHAT THIS MEANS FOR A DEVELOPER'S CALCULATION: the seasonal split must be modelled explicitly, month by month, and not by applying an average tariff to the annual energy.**

> **Two plants with identical annual energy can differ by 10 per cent or more in revenue purely through their seasonal distribution.**

> **So the energy calculation described earlier — interval by interval down the flow duration curve — is not sufficient by itself for the financial model, because the flow duration curve has no seasons in it.**

> **A chronological or at least a monthly simulation is required, which is the same conclusion reached from the load duration curve's limitations, arrived at from the revenue side instead.**

examTip.trick: **Dry-season energy is scarce and worth more** — so the tariff pays more for it and steers what gets built.
examTip.trap: **The tariff is a DESIGN instrument, not just a price** — a flat tariff rewards total energy, and the fleet it produces lasts fifty years.
examTip.mnemonic: **Model the seasons explicitly** — the flow duration curve has no seasons in it, so it cannot produce the revenue figure on its own.

questions.stem: The ECONOMIC LIFE assumed for the civil works of a hydropower project is typically much longer than that assumed for the electromechanical equipment because:
options: Civil works are subject to lower quality standards and therefore fail more gradually
Dams, tunnels and intakes are largely passive structures subject to slow deterioration
Electromechanical equipment is not depreciated in project accounts
Civil works can be replaced more cheaply
questions.solution:
**Dams, tunnels and intakes are largely passive structures subject to slow deterioration, while turbines, generators and control systems have moving and wearing parts and are also overtaken by technological obsolescence.**

**Typical design lives:**

| Component | Life assumed |
|---|---|
| **Dam, intake, tunnel, powerhouse structure** ← | **50 to 100 years, and often much longer in practice** ← |
| **Penstock (steel)** ← | **40 to 50 years, depending on corrosion protection** ← |
| **Turbine runner** ← | **20 to 30 years — LESS on a sediment-laden river** ← |
| **Generator** ← | **30 to 40 years, with rewinding at intervals** ← |
| **Control, protection and SCADA systems** ← | **10 to 20 years, limited by obsolescence rather than wear** ← |
| **Transformers** ← | **30 to 40 years** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW BUT ONE IS INTERESTING BECAUSE ITS LIMIT IS NOT PHYSICAL AND IT CATCHES OWNERS OUT: a control system fails economically when its spares are no longer made and nobody can maintain its software, not when it wears out.**

> **A twenty-year-old control system may be functioning perfectly and be unmaintainable, because the manufacturer has moved on three generations and the engineers who understood it have retired.**

> **So its replacement is forced by the supply chain rather than by its condition, on a timescale nobody controls.**

> **The defence is to specify open standards and documented interfaces at procurement, and to keep the documentation — which is cheap at the time and is very often not done, because the benefit falls fifteen years later on somebody else's watch.**

**THE CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FINANCIAL MODEL, WHICH IS THE PRACTICAL POINT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A 50-year appraisal must include REPLACEMENT of the electromechanical plant partway through** ← | ← |
| **Typically a major refurbishment or runner replacement at 25 to 30 years** ← | ← |
| **And a control system replacement at 15 and again at 30** ← | ← |
| **Those costs are large and are frequently omitted from the model** ← | ← |
| **Which makes the LCOE look better than it is** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A COMMON AND MATERIAL OMISSION AND IT IS EASY TO MAKE HONESTLY: the replacements fall far beyond the debt tenor and beyond most people's planning horizon, so a model built around the financing period simply does not reach them.**

> **A twenty-year financial model of a fifty-year asset never encounters the refurbishment, and its LCOE is therefore computed on capital costs that are incomplete.**

> **The correct treatment is to model the full economic life with all replacements, and to state the financing period separately.**

> **Conflating the two — using the financing period as the economic life — understates the cost per unit and also, incidentally, understates the project's value, because it discards thirty years of nearly cost-free generation after the debt is repaid.**

> **So the error runs in both directions and the reason to avoid it is accuracy rather than conservatism.**

**AND THE LONG CIVIL LIFE IS HYDROPOWER'S QUIET ADVANTAGE, WHICH DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD:**

> **A well-built dam and tunnel may serve for a century or more, and many nineteenth-century schemes are still generating.**

> **Once the debt is repaid, such a plant produces electricity at close to its operating cost alone, which is very low.**

> **So a hydropower plant's later decades are extraordinarily valuable, and a country that builds one is buying an asset that will still be earning long after everyone involved in it has gone.**

> **That is a poor fit with a commercial discount rate, which values year eighty at almost nothing, and an excellent fit with a national interest that extends that far — which is the same divergence noted in the LCOE discussion, and it is the strongest argument for public participation in storage hydropower specifically.**
tags: financing period is not economic life
long civil life as an advantage

examTip.trick: **Passive structures deteriorate slowly; machines wear and become obsolete** — 50-100 years civil against 20-30 for a runner.
examTip.trap: **Control systems die of OBSOLESCENCE, not wear** — perfectly functional and unmaintainable at twenty. Specify open standards and keep the documentation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Model the full life with replacements; state the financing period separately** — conflating them understates both the cost and the value.

questions.stem: In a hydropower financial appraisal, the DEBT SERVICE COVERAGE RATIO (DSCR) is:
options: The ratio of total debt to total equity in the project
The number of years required to repay the loan
The ratio of the interest paid to the principal repaid
The ratio of the cash available for debt service in a period to the debt service due in that period
questions.solution:
**The ratio of the CASH AVAILABLE FOR DEBT SERVICE in a period to the DEBT SERVICE due in that period** — a lender's test of whether the project can pay, typically required to be at least 1.2 to 1.3.

**Stated as a formula and explained:**

| Element | Expression |
|---|---|
| **DSCR** | **= Cash available for debt service ÷ (interest + principal due)** ← |
| **Cash available (CFADS)** | **= Revenue − operating costs − taxes − any required reserve contributions** ← |
| **Debt service** | **= interest + scheduled principal repayment in the period** ← |
| **A DSCR of 1.0** | **The project exactly covers its obligation, with nothing spare** ← |
| **A DSCR of 1.3** | **30 per cent headroom before default** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW EXPLAINS WHY LENDERS DEMAND MORE THAN 1.0 AND IT IS A STRAIGHTFORWARD POINT ABOUT RISK: a project at exactly 1.0 defaults on the first bad year.**

> **A dry year, an outage, a delayed payment from the offtaker, a repair — any of them turns 1.0 into less than 1.0, and the loan is in default.**

> **The margin above 1.0 is the buffer against that, and its size reflects how variable the lender expects the cash flow to be.**

> **So a hydropower project with a firm power purchase agreement and a creditworthy offtaker may be lent at 1.2, while one with hydrological risk and a weaker offtaker is asked for 1.4 — and the required ratio is the lender's summary of everything they fear about the project.**

**HOW THE DSCR SHAPES THE PROJECT, WHICH IS ITS REAL SIGNIFICANCE FOR AN ENGINEER:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The DSCR requirement determines how much DEBT the project can carry** ← | ← |
| **Which determines the required EQUITY** ← | ← |
| **Which is usually the scarce resource** ← | ← |
| **So a design change that raises dry-year revenue raises the DSCR in the worst year** ← | ← |
| **Which permits more debt, less equity, and a project that can actually be financed** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE ENGINEERING CONNECTION AND THEY ARE WORTH DWELLING ON BECAUSE THEY ARE NOT OBVIOUS: the binding constraint is the DSCR in the WORST year, not the average.**

> **A lender sizes the debt so that even in a poor hydrological year the ratio holds.**

> **So the project's financeable debt is set by its worst-year cash flow, and any measure that lifts the worst year — pondage, a more conservative design flow, a firmer contract, hydrological insurance — increases the debt capacity disproportionately.**

> **A design change that raises average energy by 5 per cent may do nothing for financeability, and one that raises the dry-year minimum by 5 per cent may transform it.**

> **That is a direct and frequently unrecognised link between hydraulic design decisions and whether the project can be built at all, and it is a good reason for the engineer and the financial analyst to work the model together rather than in sequence.**

**A CLOSING NOTE ON TWO RELATED RATIOS THAT APPEAR ALONGSIDE IT:**

| Ratio | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **DSCR** ← | **Period by period — can it pay this year?** ← |
| **LLCR (Loan Life Coverage Ratio)** ← | **PV of cash flow over the loan's life ÷ debt outstanding — can it pay over the whole loan?** ← |
| **PLCR (Project Life Coverage Ratio)** ← | **The same over the whole project life — a longer and more generous view** ← |

> **The three answer the same question over three horizons, and a project can pass one and fail another.**

> **A project with weak early years and strong later ones passes the LLCR and fails the DSCR in year three, which is exactly the profile of a hydropower plant whose tariff escalates or whose debt amortises unevenly.**

> **The remedy in that case is not more equity but a differently SHAPED repayment schedule — sculpted amortisation, matching the principal repayments to the cash flow rather than to a flat annuity — which is a standard project finance technique and one worth knowing exists, because it can rescue a project that appears unfinanceable under a conventional loan structure.**

examTip.trick: **Cash available for debt service ÷ debt service due** — lenders want 1.2 to 1.3, because 1.0 defaults on the first bad year.
examTip.trap: **The binding constraint is the WORST year, not the average** — so lifting the dry-year minimum raises debt capacity far more than raising average energy does.
examTip.mnemonic: **DSCR yearly, LLCR over the loan, PLCR over the project** — a project can pass one and fail another, and sculpted amortisation is the fix.

questions.stem: In assessing a small hydropower scheme for RURAL ELECTRIFICATION as against grid connection, the decisive consideration is usually:
options: The scheme's installed capacity in kilowatts
The turbine type available locally
The head available at the site
The distance and terrain to the nearest grid
questions.solution:
**The DISTANCE and TERRAIN to the nearest grid, since the cost of a transmission line through mountainous country can exceed the cost of the generation itself** — making an isolated mini-grid cheaper than a connection for a remote settlement.

**The comparison set out:**

| Option | Costs | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **GRID EXTENSION** ← | **Line cost per km, which is high in the hills; plus the energy tariff** ← | **Settlements near the grid, or with a large load** ← |
| **ISOLATED MINI-GRID (micro-hydro)** ← | **The scheme's full capital cost, plus a small local distribution network** ← | **Remote settlements with a suitable stream** ← |
| **SOLAR HOME SYSTEMS** ← | **Per household, no network at all** ← | **Scattered households with small loads** ← |

> **THE ECONOMIC CROSSOVER BETWEEN THE FIRST TWO IS A DISTANCE AND IT IS THE CALCULATION THAT DECIDES THE QUESTION: at what distance does the line cost exceed the mini-grid cost?**

> **A medium-voltage line through Nepali hill terrain may cost several million rupees per kilometre, with the towers, the access, the wayleave and the difficulty of construction.**

> **A 50 kW micro-hydro scheme serving a village may cost a few tens of millions in total.**

> **So the crossover falls at a distance of a few kilometres to a few tens of kilometres depending on the load — and beyond it the isolated scheme is genuinely cheaper, not merely a second best.**

**THE FACTORS THAT SHIFT THE CROSSOVER, WHICH IS WHERE THE JUDGEMENT LIES:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **A LARGER load** ← | **Favours the grid — the line's cost is spread over more energy** ← |
| **A load that will GROW** ← | **Favours the grid, which has no capacity limit** ← |
| **DIFFICULT terrain** ← | **Favours the isolated scheme — line cost rises steeply** ← |
| **A good local STREAM with head** ← | **Favours the isolated scheme, obviously** ← |
| **A need for RELIABILITY** ← | **Favours the grid — a single micro-hydro has no backup** ← |
| **Local capacity to OPERATE and maintain** ← | **Essential for the isolated scheme; irrelevant for the grid** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CONSIDERATION MOST OFTEN UNDERWEIGHTED AND IT HAS PRODUCED A GREAT MANY STRANDED MICRO-HYDRO SCHEMES: the load grows, and a fixed 50 kW scheme cannot.**

> **A village electrified at 50 kW acquires mills, refrigeration, small workshops and more households, and within a decade wants 200 kW.**

> **The micro-hydro cannot supply it, so the grid arrives after all — and the micro-hydro scheme is then redundant, having been built and operated for a decade at considerable cost.**

> **The mitigation is to design the scheme so it can be GRID-CONNECTED when the grid arrives, feeding its output into the network rather than being abandoned — which requires synchronous rather than induction generation, appropriate protection, and a tariff arrangement agreed in advance.**

> **That foresight costs a modest amount at construction and preserves the asset's value entirely, and it should be a standard requirement for any publicly funded scheme rather than the exception it currently is.**

> **THE LAST ROW DESERVES THE FINAL WORD BECAUSE IT DETERMINES WHETHER THE SCHEME SURVIVES: an isolated scheme needs someone competent and paid to run it, for as long as it operates.**

> **The technical failure of rural micro-hydro is rare; the institutional failure is common — a scheme built by a donor, handed to a committee, and unmaintained after the first serious fault because no one has the skill, the spares or the money.**

> **So the tariff collection arrangement, the operator's training and pay, and the spares supply chain are as much part of the design as the turbine selection.**

> **A scheme delivered without them is a capital gift that becomes scrap in five years, and the engineering that went into it is wasted along with the money.**

examTip.trick: **Distance and terrain to the grid** — a hill transmission line can cost more than the generation, so isolated is genuinely cheaper beyond the crossover.
examTip.trap: **Load GROWTH strands micro-hydro** — a village electrified at 50 kW wants 200 kW in a decade. Design it to be grid-connectable when the grid arrives.
examTip.mnemonic: **Micro-hydro fails institutionally, not technically** — no operator, no spares, no tariff collection. Those are part of the design, not an afterthought.

questions.stem: A GRAVITY DAM resists the water thrust principally by:
options: Arch action transferring the load to the abutments
Its own weight, which generates the friction and the stabilising moment needed to resist sliding and overturning
The tensile strength of the concrete on the upstream face
The passive resistance of the downstream foundation soil
questions.solution:
**ITS OWN WEIGHT, which generates the friction and the stabilising moment needed to resist sliding and overturning.**

**The forces on a gravity dam and how weight answers them:**

| Force | Resisted by |
|---|---|
| **WATER PRESSURE, horizontal, acting on the upstream face** ← | **Friction at the base, which is proportional to the WEIGHT** ← |
| **The OVERTURNING MOMENT of that thrust about the toe** ← | **The restoring moment of the weight acting through the centroid** ← |
| **UPLIFT pressure under the base** ← | **Reduces the effective weight and therefore both resistances** ← |
| **SILT pressure against the upstream face** ← | **The same mechanisms, with a larger horizontal force** ← |
| **EARTHQUAKE inertia and hydrodynamic pressure** ← | **The same, with a dynamic increment** ← |
| **Ice and wave forces where they apply** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE THAT TRANSFORMED GRAVITY DAM DESIGN AND IT IS THE HISTORICALLY IMPORTANT POINT: UPLIFT was not understood in the earliest dams and it is what caused several of them to fail.**

> **Water enters the foundation and the concrete's pores, and it acts upward over the whole base area.**

> **That uplift directly reduces the effective weight — the dam is partly floated — and since the weight is the source of BOTH the friction and the restoring moment, uplift attacks both stability mechanisms at once.**

> **So a dam that appears amply stable on its dry weight can be marginal or unstable once uplift is included, and the difference is not a small correction but a large one, commonly a third of the base pressure.**

**HOW UPLIFT IS CONTROLLED, WHICH IS A DEFINING FEATURE OF MODERN GRAVITY DAM DESIGN:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **A GROUT CURTAIN near the upstream heel** ← | **Reduces the seepage entering the foundation** ← |
| **A line of DRAINAGE HOLES just downstream of the curtain** ← | **Relieves the pressure by giving the water an escape** ← |
| **A gallery inside the dam collecting that drainage** ← | **Which also permits inspection and measurement** ← |
| **Together these reduce the uplift at the drain line to a small fraction of the reservoir head** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW DOES MORE WORK THAN THE FIRST AND THE ORDER OF IMPORTANCE SURPRISES PEOPLE: the drains matter more than the curtain.**

> **A grout curtain reduces the flow but cannot be relied on to be continuous or permanent — grouting a fractured rock mass is an imperfect operation and the curtain can crack or be bypassed.**

> **The drains relieve the pressure regardless of how much water arrives, because they provide a path to atmosphere at a defined location.**

> **So the design should not depend on the curtain performing, and the drains must be maintained and their flows monitored for the dam's whole life — a blocked drainage system silently restores the full uplift that the design assumed away, and it is one of the more insidious deterioration mechanisms in an ageing dam.**

**AND THE CHARACTERISTIC GEOMETRY FOLLOWS FROM ALL OF THIS:**

| Feature | Reason |
|---|---|
| **A near-VERTICAL upstream face** ← | **Keeps the water load simple and the heel from opening** ← |
