| **A sloping DOWNSTREAM face, roughly 0.7 to 0.8 horizontal to 1 vertical** ← | **Puts the weight where it does most good against overturning** ← |
| **A base width roughly 0.7 to 0.9 times the height** ← | **The rule of thumb for a full gravity section** ← |
| **A broad base and a narrow crest — the triangular section** ← | ← |

> **The third row is the figure worth carrying for a quick check: a gravity dam's base is roughly three-quarters of its height.**

> **A 60 m dam has a base around 45 m thick, and the volume of concrete that implies is what makes gravity dams expensive and is why arch dams are preferred wherever a narrow gorge with sound abutments allows one.**

> **An arch dam in the same gorge might use a fifth of the concrete, because it works in compression along its arch rather than by sheer mass — and the choice between them is essentially a question of whether the abutments can take the thrust.**
tags: drains matter more than the curtain

examTip.trick: **Its own weight** — supplying both the base friction against sliding and the restoring moment against overturning.
examTip.trap: **Uplift attacks BOTH at once** — it reduces effective weight, and weight is the source of friction and moment alike. Commonly a third of the base pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Drains matter more than the grout curtain** — the curtain may crack or be bypassed; the drains relieve pressure whatever arrives. Blocked drains restore full uplift silently.

questions.stem: The condition that NO TENSION shall develop at the heel of a gravity dam leads to the requirement that the resultant of all forces must pass:
options: Through the centre of the base
Within the middle third of the base
Within the middle half of the base
Through the downstream toe
questions.solution:
**Within the MIDDLE THIRD of the base** — the classic middle-third rule.

**Where the rule comes from:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Base pressure from a resultant of magnitude R at eccentricity e from the centre** | **σ = (R/B)(1 ± 6e/B) per unit length** ← |
| **The minimum pressure becomes ZERO when** | **6e/B = 1** ← |
| **That is** | **e = B/6** ← |
| **The resultant may lie B/6 either side of centre** | **A total band of B/3 — the middle third** ← |
| **Beyond that** | **The formula gives a negative (tensile) stress, which concrete on rock cannot sustain** ← |

> **THE FORMULA IN THE FIRST ROW IS THE COMBINED DIRECT-AND-BENDING STRESS EXPRESSION AND IT IS THE SAME ONE USED FOR ECCENTRICALLY LOADED FOOTINGS AND SHORT COLUMNS, so learning it once serves in several chapters.**

> **σ = P/A ± M/Z, with M = P·e and Z = B²/6 per unit length, which reduces directly to (P/B)(1 ± 6e/B).**

> **The 6 comes from the section modulus of a rectangle, and recognising that makes the middle-third rule memorable rather than arbitrary.**

> **And the rule generalises: for a rectangular base loaded biaxially the safe zone is the middle-third in each direction, giving the 'kern' — a rhombus for a rectangle and a circle of radius D/8 for a circular base.**

**WHY TENSION AT THE HEEL IS SPECIFICALLY DANGEROUS, WHICH IS MORE THAN A MATERIALS POINT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Concrete has little tensile strength, and the concrete-rock interface has less** ← | ← |
| **If the heel opens, water enters the CRACK** ← | ← |
| **The crack then carries FULL RESERVOIR PRESSURE as additional uplift** ← | ← |
| **Which pushes the resultant further downstream** ← | ← |
| **Opening the crack further, admitting more pressure** ← | ← |
| **A PROGRESSIVE mechanism, not a static one** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS DESCRIBE WHY THIS PARTICULAR CRITERION IS TREATED SO STRICTLY AND IT IS THE HEART OF THE MATTER: heel cracking is self-aggravating.**

> **An ordinary structural member that cracks in tension redistributes and settles into a new equilibrium.**

> **A dam heel that cracks admits pressurised water into the crack, which increases the very force that opened it.**

> **So there is no new equilibrium to settle into, and the failure can run to completion — which is why the no-tension rule is enforced rather than treated as a serviceability preference, and why it is checked for every loading combination including the seismic ones.**

**A CLOSING NOTE ON HOW THE RULE IS APPLIED IN PRACTICE, SINCE MODERN CODES ARE MORE NUANCED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **For NORMAL loading, no tension is permitted at the heel** ← | **The middle-third rule applies strictly** ← |
| **For EXTREME loading — the maximum credible earthquake — limited tension or a limited crack may be accepted** ← | **Provided the dam remains stable with the crack fully pressurised** ← |
| **The check then becomes a CRACKED-BASE analysis** ← | **Assume the crack extends to where the compressive stress becomes positive, apply full uplift over the cracked length, and verify stability on the remaining base** ← |

> **The third row is the modern treatment and it is more honest than pretending the crack will not occur under an extreme event.**

> **It accepts the crack, assumes the worst about the pressure in it, and requires the dam to be stable anyway.**

> **That is a better philosophy than a rule that must hold absolutely under all conditions, because it acknowledges what will actually happen in an extreme event and designs for the consequence — and it is the same shift from 'prevent the damage' to 'survive the damage' that runs through modern seismic design generally.**

examTip.trick: **e ≤ B/6 either side, so the resultant stays in the middle third** — from σ = (R/B)(1 ± 6e/B) set to zero.
examTip.trap: **Heel cracking is SELF-AGGRAVATING** — the crack admits full reservoir pressure, which pushes the resultant further downstream and opens it more. No new equilibrium.
examTip.mnemonic: **The 6 is the rectangle's section modulus B²/6** — same formula as an eccentric footing, and it generalises to the kern in two directions.

questions.stem: An ARCH DAM is suitable where:
options: The valley is wide and the foundation is alluvial
A very large volume of concrete is available cheaply
The valley is a narrow gorge with sound, strong rock abutments capable of taking the arch thrust
The reservoir is shallow and the dam low
questions.solution:
**The valley is a NARROW GORGE with SOUND, STRONG ROCK abutments capable of taking the arch thrust** — since the dam transfers most of the water load horizontally into the flanks rather than downward into the bed.

**How an arch dam works and what it demands:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The dam is curved in plan, convex toward the reservoir** ← | ← |
| **Water pressure puts the arch into COMPRESSION along its length** ← | **Which concrete carries excellently** ← |
| **The arch delivers a large THRUST into each abutment, directed downstream and outward** ← | ← |
| **So the abutments must be strong, sound and correctly oriented rock** ← | ← |
| **Because the arch works in compression, very little concrete is needed** ← | **A fifth or less of an equivalent gravity dam** ← |
| **The ratio of crest length to height must be small** ← | **Typically below about 5, meaning a narrow gorge** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE WHY ARCH DAMS ARE THE MOST DEMANDING DAM TYPE IN TERMS OF SITE, AND WHY THEIR FAILURES HAVE BEEN ABUTMENT FAILURES RATHER THAN DAM FAILURES: the structure is only as good as the rock it pushes against.**

> **Malpasset in France in 1959 failed because a previously undetected geological feature in the left abutment moved under the thrust, and the dam itself was blameless — it was a well-designed arch on an inadequately investigated abutment.**

> **So an arch dam demands geological investigation of a depth and quality that a gravity dam does not, extending well into the flanks and specifically seeking adversely oriented joints, faults and weak seams.**

> **And an arch dam should not be adopted where that investigation cannot be done thoroughly, however attractive the concrete saving looks — the saving is real and the risk it buys is not proportionate.**

**THE COMPARISON WITH A GRAVITY DAM, DRAWN OUT:**

| Aspect | GRAVITY | ARCH |
|---|---|---|
| **Load path** | **Down into the foundation** ← | **Horizontally into the abutments** ← |
| **Concrete volume** | **Large** ← | **Small — a fifth or less** ← |
| **Foundation demand** | **A competent bed** ← | **Exceptional abutments** ← |
| **Valley shape** | **Any** ← | **Narrow gorge only** ← |
| **Sensitivity to foundation defects** | **Moderate** ← | **SEVERE** ← |
| **Analysis** | **Relatively simple, two-dimensional** ← | **Three-dimensional and complex** ← |
| **Temperature and shrinkage effects** | **Manageable with joints** ← | **Critical — the arch must be grouted closed at a chosen temperature** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A CONSTRUCTION ISSUE PECULIAR TO ARCH DAMS AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT AFFECTS THE PROGRAMME: an arch dam is built in vertical blocks separated by contraction joints, and those joints are GROUTED to make the arch monolithic.**

> **The grouting must be done when the concrete is at its lowest expected temperature, so that subsequent warming closes the joints tighter rather than opening them.**

> **This requires artificial COOLING of the concrete, usually by embedded pipes circulating chilled water, and it must be completed before grouting.**

> **So the construction sequence involves placing, cooling, grouting and only then impounding — and a programme that omits the cooling period, or grouts at the wrong temperature, leaves an arch that opens at its joints when the mass warms, which is a defect that cannot be corrected afterwards.**

> **A MIDDLE CASE DESERVES MENTION SINCE IT IS COMMON IN PRACTICE: the ARCH-GRAVITY dam, thicker than a pure arch and thinner than a gravity section, carrying part of the load by each mechanism.**

> **It suits a valley too wide for a pure arch and narrow enough that some arch action is available, and it reduces the abutment thrust to what moderately good rock can take.**

> **That flexibility makes it the practical choice at a great many sites, and the pure arch is reserved for the exceptional gorge that genuinely justifies it.**

examTip.trick: **Narrow gorge, sound rock abutments** — the arch works in compression and pushes its load sideways into the flanks.
examTip.trap: **Arch dam failures are ABUTMENT failures** — Malpasset was a sound dam on an inadequately investigated flank. The investigation must extend well into the rock.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cool the concrete, then grout the joints at the lowest temperature** — so later warming closes the arch rather than opening it. Not correctable afterwards.

questions.stem: In an EMBANKMENT (earth or rockfill) dam, the principal cause of failure historically has been:
options: Overturning of the embankment as a rigid body
Crushing of the fill at the base under its own weight
Failure of the concrete facing in tension
Piping and overtopping
questions.solution:
**PIPING and OVERTOPPING** — internal erosion carrying fines out along a seepage path, and the passage of a flood over the crest, both of which erode the embankment rather than overstress it.

**Why an embankment fails by erosion rather than by stress:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **An embankment is a granular mass, not a monolith** ← | **It cannot overturn and does not crush** ← |
| **Its weakness is that its particles can be MOVED by flowing water** ← | ← |
| **Water flowing THROUGH it can carry fines out at the exit — PIPING** ← | ← |
| **Water flowing OVER it strips the downstream face — OVERTOPPING** ← | ← |
| **Both are progressive and both can breach a dam within hours** ← | ← |
| **And together they account for the great majority of embankment dam failures** ← | ← |

> **THE CONTRAST WITH A CONCRETE DAM IS INSTRUCTIVE AND IT DECIDES HOW EACH IS DESIGNED: a concrete dam can survive being overtopped and is designed against stress and stability; an embankment cannot survive overtopping and is designed against erosion.**

> **This single difference drives the spillway provision: an embankment dam needs a spillway of ample and reliable capacity, because the consequence of its being inadequate is total loss of the dam.**

> **A concrete gravity dam overtopped by a flood larger than its spillway will generally survive, with damage to its toe and its abutments.**

> **So the design flood standard applied to an embankment dam is stricter, and an EMERGENCY spillway or fuse plug is commonly provided as a second line — which is a proportionate response to a failure mode that offers no warning and no margin.**

**HOW PIPING IS PREVENTED, WHICH IS THE CENTRAL DESIGN TASK:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **FILTERS at every internal boundary where fine material could migrate into coarse** ← | **Designed by the standard filter criteria on particle sizes** ← |
| **A CHIMNEY or inclined filter drain within the embankment** ← | **Intercepts seepage and controls the phreatic surface** ← |
| **A horizontal blanket drain to a toe drain** ← | **Carries the collected seepage safely out** ← |
| **A cut-off, core or grout curtain to reduce the seepage in the first place** ← | ← |
| **Careful treatment around CONDUITS and at the abutment contacts** ← | **The commonest locations of piping failures** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PROVISION AND ITS LOGIC IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: a filter permits water to pass while retaining the particles of the material it protects.**

> **So seepage is allowed to occur and to escape freely, and only the soil is held back.**

> **The design criteria relate the filter's D15 to the base soil's D85 — the filter must be fine enough to retain, and its D15 to the base D15 — coarse enough to drain freely.**

> **Getting those two conditions right is what makes a filter work, and a 'filter' of the wrong gradation either clogs, which raises the phreatic surface, or passes the fines, which is piping by another name.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHERE PIPING ACTUALLY HAPPENS AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON BECAUSE IT IS A DETAILING FAILURE RATHER THAN A DESIGN ONE: a conduit passing through an embankment creates a preferential seepage path along its outside.**

> **The fill cannot be compacted properly against the conduit's haunches, the conduit settles differently from the fill around it, and a gap opens.**

> **Water finds that path, erosion begins along it, and the dam fails from a defect a few centimetres wide.**

> **The modern answer is to avoid conduits through embankments altogether where possible — taking the outlet through the abutment in a tunnel instead — and where one is unavoidable, to provide a filter diaphragm around it rather than the old anti-seep collars, which are now understood to have made compaction worse and achieved little.**

examTip.trick: **Piping and overtopping** — an embankment is a granular mass, so it erodes rather than overstressing.
examTip.trap: **A concrete dam survives overtopping; an embankment does not** — which is why the spillway standard is stricter and a fuse plug or emergency spillway is added.
examTip.mnemonic: **Conduits through the fill are where piping starts** — poor compaction at the haunches, differential settlement, a gap. Use a filter diaphragm, not anti-seep collars.

questions.stem: The FREEBOARD of a dam is the vertical distance between the maximum reservoir level and the dam crest. It is provided to accommodate:
options: Wave run-up, wind setup, settlement of the dam and a margin of safety
The thickness of the road pavement on the crest
The volume of the design flood
Ice thrust on the upstream face
questions.solution:
**WAVE RUN-UP, wind setup, settlement of the dam and a margin of safety** — so that the crest is not overtopped by waves even when the reservoir is at its maximum level.

**The components that make up the required freeboard:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **WIND SETUP — the reservoir surface tilts under a sustained wind** ← | **The water piles up at the downwind end** ← |
| **WAVE HEIGHT — generated by the wind over the FETCH** ← | **The longer the fetch and the stronger the wind, the higher the wave** ← |
| **WAVE RUN-UP on the upstream slope** ← | **A wave climbs higher than its own height, and how much depends on the slope and its roughness** ← |
| **SETTLEMENT allowance for an embankment** ← | **The crest will settle over the years and the freeboard must survive it** ← |
| **A safety margin** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE WHERE THE DESIGN CAN BE INFLUENCED AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: run-up depends strongly on the slope and its surface.**

> **A smooth, steep concrete face lets a wave run far up it.**

> **A rough rockfill or riprap slope dissipates the wave's energy in the voids between stones and reduces the run-up substantially — often by half.**

> **So specifying a rough upstream protection reduces the required freeboard, which reduces the dam's height and its cost — a case where a detail chosen for one purpose, slope protection, pays for itself again in another.**

**THE FETCH DESERVES A NOTE BECAUSE IT IS FREQUENTLY MISTAKEN:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **FETCH is the distance of open water over which the wind blows toward the dam** ← | ← |
| **It is measured along the direction of the PREVAILING or the design wind** ← | **Not simply the reservoir's longest dimension** ← |
| **A long narrow reservoir bent around a ridge may have a short effective fetch** ← | **Even though it is long** ← |
| **And the EFFECTIVE fetch accounts for the width as well** ← | **A narrow water body limits wave growth** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE AND IT OFTEN REDUCES THE ANSWER SUBSTANTIALLY IN HIMALAYAN TOPOGRAPHY: a reservoir winding through a gorge system may be 20 km long and have a straight-line fetch toward the dam of only 2 or 3 km.**

> **Using the reservoir's length as the fetch would then compute waves several times too large and add metres of unnecessary freeboard.**

> **So the fetch must be measured on the plan, along the wind direction, from the dam to the far shore — and where the reservoir bends, the fetch ends at the bend.**

> **This is a case where being careful with a definition saves real money, and where a lazy reading of it wastes it.**

**AND TWO FREEBOARDS ARE USUALLY SPECIFIED RATHER THAN ONE, WHICH THE QUESTION'S SINGLE DEFINITION CONCEALS:**

| Freeboard | Measured from | Design condition |
|---|---|---|
| **NORMAL freeboard** ← | **The full reservoir level (FRL)** ← | **The normal maximum wind and wave, occurring often** ← |
| **MINIMUM freeboard** ← | **The maximum water level during the design flood (MWL)** ← | **A lesser wind, since the joint probability of a design flood and a maximum wind is small** ← |

> **The second row's reasoning is a JOINT PROBABILITY argument and it is a good example of avoiding excessive conservatism honestly.**

> **Combining the design flood with the design wind assumes two rare events coincide, and the product of their probabilities is far smaller than the design standard requires.**

> **So a lesser wind is combined with the flood, and the full design wind is combined with the ordinary full reservoir level — each combination having a comparable overall probability.**

> **That is the correct way to combine loads with independent probabilities, and it appears throughout structural design in the load combination factors, where the same logic is embedded in the code rather than argued from first principles each time.**
tags: wind setup wave height and run-up
joint probability of flood and wind

examTip.trick: **Wave run-up, wind setup, settlement, plus a margin** — the crest must stay dry when the waves arrive at maximum level.
examTip.trap: **FETCH is along the wind direction and ends at a bend** — not the reservoir's length. A 20 km winding reservoir may have a 3 km fetch.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two freeboards, two wind conditions** — full design wind at FRL, a lesser wind at flood level, because two rare events rarely coincide.

questions.stem: An OGEE spillway profile is shaped to follow the lower nappe of a freely falling sheet of water over a sharp-crested weir. The purpose of this shape is to:
options: Increase the friction and so slow the discharge
Make the crest easier to construct
Ensure the flow separates from the crest at all discharges
Have the flow follow the surface with atmospheric pressure on it at the design head
questions.solution:
**To have the flow follow the surface with ATMOSPHERIC pressure on it at the design head** — avoiding negative pressures that would cause cavitation, while achieving a high discharge coefficient.

**The reasoning behind the shape:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water flowing over a SHARP-crested weir springs clear as a nappe** ← | ← |
| **The under-surface of that nappe is a free surface at ATMOSPHERIC pressure** ← | ← |
| **If solid material is placed exactly along that surface, the flow is unchanged** ← | ← |
| **And the pressure on the solid surface is therefore atmospheric — neither positive nor negative** ← | ← |
| **So the ogee crest is the shape that supports the nappe without disturbing it** ← | ← |
| **Giving the discharge efficiency of a sharp-crested weir with the structural solidity of a mass concrete crest** ← | ← |

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE ELEGANCE OF THE IDEA AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: the ogee spillway gets the hydraulic performance of the most efficient weir shape and the durability of a solid structure, by the simple device of building the structure exactly where the water was going anyway.**

> **A sharp-crested weir is hydraulically efficient and structurally hopeless at dam scale.**

> **A broad-crested weir is structurally sound and hydraulically poor, with a lower discharge coefficient.**

> **The ogee resolves the conflict rather than compromising between the two, which is a much better kind of solution and one worth recognising when it appears.**

**THE CRITICAL QUALIFICATION IS 'AT THE DESIGN HEAD' AND IT IS THE EXAMINABLE POINT:**

| Operating head | What happens |
|---|---|
| **AT the design head Hd** ← | **The nappe fits the profile exactly, pressure is atmospheric, coefficient is at its highest** ← |
| **BELOW the design head** ← | **The nappe wants to fall INSIDE the profile, so it presses on the crest — POSITIVE pressure, slightly reduced coefficient, entirely safe** ← |
| **ABOVE the design head** ← | **The nappe wants to spring OUTSIDE the profile, so it pulls away from the crest — NEGATIVE pressure, higher coefficient, and the RISK OF CAVITATION** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE DANGER AND IT IS WHY THE DESIGN HEAD IS DELIBERATELY CHOSEN BELOW THE MAXIMUM: negative pressures at heads above the design head can approach vapour pressure, at which point cavitation begins.**

> **Cavitation on a concrete spillway surface pits and then rapidly destroys it, and the damage is at its worst just downstream of the crest where the velocity is highest.**

> **The standard practice is to set the design head at about 75 to 80 per cent of the maximum head, so that at the maximum flood the negative pressure remains within tolerable limits.**

> **That sacrifices a little discharge capacity at normal heads and buys safety at the extreme — and the reason the design head is not simply set equal to the maximum is that a profile designed for the rare maximum flood would run under positive pressure and reduced efficiency for its entire ordinary life.**

> **So the choice is a deliberate trade between everyday efficiency and extreme-event safety, resolved at around three-quarters, and it is a good illustration of why a design parameter is sometimes set at neither the normal nor the extreme condition.**

**AND A CLOSING NOTE ON CAVITATION PROTECTION, WHICH APPLIES BEYOND THE CREST:**

> **On a high spillway the velocity further down the chute can reach 30 or 40 m/s, at which any surface irregularity — a misaligned form joint, a protruding bolt, a repair patch — triggers cavitation downstream of it.**

> **The classical protection is extreme surface tolerance, which is expensive and hard to maintain.**

> **The modern protection is AERATION: a step or ramp in the chute floor that draws air under the flow, because a small percentage of entrained air near the boundary largely suppresses cavitation damage.**

> **Aerator ramps at intervals down a high chute are now standard, and they represent a shift from trying to make the surface perfect to accepting that it will not be and protecting it anyway — the same philosophy noted with cracked-base analysis and with GLOF-graded protection.**

examTip.trick: **It is the shape the nappe already takes** — so the surface sits at atmospheric pressure at the design head, with a sharp-crested weir's efficiency.
examTip.trap: **Above the design head the pressure goes NEGATIVE and cavitation threatens** — which is why Hd is set at 75-80% of the maximum head, not equal to it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Aerate rather than perfect the surface** — a little entrained air near the boundary suppresses cavitation damage on a 40 m/s chute.

questions.stem: A STILLING BASIN at the toe of a spillway dissipates energy by:
options: Forcing a hydraulic jump within the basin
Allowing the water to spread over a wide apron and evaporate
Reducing the flow's velocity by friction along a long horizontal apron alone
Diverting the flow into a series of small channels
questions.solution:
**Forcing a HYDRAULIC JUMP, in which the supercritical high-velocity flow from the chute converts to subcritical flow with a large loss of energy in the turbulence.**

**Why energy dissipation is necessary at all:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water arriving at the toe of a high spillway carries enormous kinetic energy** ← | **Velocities of 20 to 40 m/s are ordinary** ← |
| **Released into the river, that energy SCOURS the bed** ← | ← |
| **A deep scour hole develops and works back toward the dam** ← | ← |
| **Threatening the dam's own foundation** ← | ← |
| **So the energy must be destroyed in a controlled place, on a structure built to take it** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE REAL HAZARD AND IT IS WHY THIS IS A SAFETY MATTER RATHER THAN A TIDINESS ONE: unchecked scour at the toe undermines the structure that created it.**

> **The scour hole deepens with each flood, and retrogressive erosion carries it upstream toward the dam's foundation.**

> **A dam whose toe is undermined loses the passive resistance in front of it and may lose foundation support entirely.**

> **So the stilling basin is not an accessory to the spillway; it is the part of the spillway that keeps the dam standing, and the two must be designed together.**

**HOW THE HYDRAULIC JUMP DOES THE WORK:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Flow arrives supercritical — high velocity, small depth, Froude number well above 1** ← | ← |
| **The downstream water level forces it to become subcritical** ← | ← |
| **The transition cannot be gradual, so a JUMP forms** ← | **A violently turbulent standing wave** ← |
| **Energy is lost in that turbulence, as heat and as sound** ← | ← |
| **The loss can be 70 per cent or more of the incoming energy at high Froude numbers** ← | ← |
| **The basin's job is to make the jump form IN the basin and stay there** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE ENTIRE DESIGN PROBLEM AND IT IS SUBTLER THAN IT SOUNDS: the jump forms where the sequent depth relationship is satisfied, and that depends on the TAILWATER level.**

> **If the tailwater is too LOW, the jump sweeps out downstream and forms in the unprotected river, doing exactly the damage the basin was built to prevent.**

> **If the tailwater is too HIGH, the jump is submerged and drowned, which dissipates less energy and lets high-velocity flow pass along the bed.**

> **So the basin's floor level must be set — usually depressed below the river bed — so that the available tailwater matches the sequent depth required, across the whole range of discharges, and that matching is what the tailwater rating curve and the sequent depth curve are plotted together to check.**

> **A basin that works at the design flood and sweeps out at half that discharge is a common and dangerous outcome of checking only one flow.**

**THE APPURTENANCES DESERVE A NOTE SINCE THEY ARE WHAT DISTINGUISHES ONE STANDARD BASIN FROM ANOTHER:**

| Device | Function |
|---|---|
| **CHUTE BLOCKS at the entrance** ← | **Split the incoming jet and spread it, helping the jump form and shortening it** ← |
| **BAFFLE (friction) BLOCKS on the floor** ← | **Add drag and stabilise the jump — but they cavitate at high velocity, so are used only at moderate heads** ← |
| **An END SILL, solid or dentated** ← | **Lifts the outgoing flow off the bed and directs the residual scour away from the basin** ← |

> **The second row carries a real limitation and it decides which standard basin can be used: baffle blocks are highly effective and they cannot be used where the incoming velocity is high, because the blocks themselves cavitate and erode.**

> **The USBR basins are classified partly on this basis — the types with baffle blocks are for lower velocities and the types without, relying on chute blocks and a dentated sill and a longer basin, are for high-velocity flow.**

> **So selecting a basin type is not a matter of preference but of checking the incoming Froude number and velocity against each type's stated range, and using a baffled basin outside its range replaces an erosion problem in the river with an erosion problem in the basin.**
tags: chute blocks baffle blocks and end sill

examTip.trick: **A hydraulic jump — supercritical to subcritical, losing up to 70% of the energy in the turbulence.**
examTip.trap: **The jump must form IN the basin at EVERY discharge** — too little tailwater and it sweeps out; too much and it drowns. Check across the range, not just the design flood.
examTip.mnemonic: **Baffle blocks cavitate at high velocity** — which is why USBR basin types are graded by incoming Froude number and velocity, not chosen by preference.

questions.stem: The RIVER DIVERSION arrangement during the construction of a dam typically consists of:
options: Pumping the river flow around the site continuously
A diversion tunnel or channel carrying the river past the site, with an upstream and a downstream cofferdam enclosing and dewatering the working area
Constructing the dam in the wet without any diversion
Halting construction during the monsoon and allowing the river to flow over the works
questions.solution:
**A DIVERSION TUNNEL or channel carrying the river past the site, with an upstream and a downstream COFFERDAM enclosing and dewatering the working area.**

**The standard arrangement and its sequence:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Drive the diversion tunnel through an abutment, or excavate a diversion channel** ← | **Before any work in the river** ← |
| **2. Build the UPSTREAM cofferdam, closing the river and turning it into the tunnel** ← | **The river closure — a critical and carefully timed operation** ← |
| **3. Build the DOWNSTREAM cofferdam, to keep backwater out of the excavation** ← | ← |
| **4. Dewater the enclosed area and construct the dam in the dry** ← | ← |
| **5. When the dam is high enough, PLUG the diversion tunnel and begin impounding** ← | ← |
| **6. The tunnel may then be reused, or is plugged permanently** ← | **Often converted into a low-level outlet or part of the power waterway** ← |

> **STEP 2 IS THE MOST DEMANDING OPERATION ON MANY DAM SITES AND IT IS TIMED TO THE DAY: the river closure must be made at the lowest flow of the year, and it must be completed quickly once begun.**

> **Material is tipped into the narrowing gap from both banks, and as the gap closes the velocity through it rises, threatening to sweep the material away faster than it can be placed.**

> **So the closure is a race, with large stockpiles prepared in advance and a large fleet of trucks committed for a few days.**

> **A failed closure means the river reopens the gap and the attempt must wait for the next dry season, which is a year's delay — so the operation is planned in detail, rehearsed, and executed with far more resource than the volume of material would suggest is necessary.**

**THE COFFERDAM DESIGN DECISION IS A RISK CALCULATION AND IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A higher cofferdam and a larger diversion tunnel cost more** ← | ← |
| **They protect against a larger flood** ← | ← |
| **The exposure is only the construction period — two or three dry seasons** ← | ← |
| **So a lower return period is accepted than for the permanent works** ← | **Typically 10 to 25 years, as noted earlier** ← |
| **The trade is: the cost of a bigger diversion against the expected cost of being flooded** ← | ← |
| **UNLESS people would be endangered, in which case the calculation does not apply** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS A GENUINE EXPECTED-VALUE CALCULATION AND IT IS ONE OF THE FEW PLACES IN CIVIL ENGINEERING WHERE THAT IS THE CORRECT AND ACCEPTED APPROACH: the cost of a flood is quantifiable — the works damaged, the excavation refilled with silt, the time lost — and its probability is known.**

> **So the optimum diversion capacity is where the marginal cost of enlargement equals the marginal reduction in expected flood damage.**

> **A larger diversion than that is wasted money and a smaller one is a false economy, and the calculation is straightforward once the damage cost is estimated.**

> **What makes it unusual is that the consequence is purely financial, which is why the expected-value approach is legitimate here and not in the design of the permanent structures.**

**AND THE DIVERSION'S REUSE IN STEP 6 DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS A SIGNIFICANT SAVING WHEN PLANNED FOR:**

> **A diversion tunnel is an expensive asset that has served its purpose after three years, and plugging it discards it.**

> **Where the layout allows, it can instead become the low-level outlet, the irrigation offtake, a sediment flushing conduit, or part of the power waterway.**

> **Doing so requires that the tunnel be located and sized for that second role from the outset, which constrains the diversion design a little and saves a whole tunnel.**

> **It also requires the permanent lining and the gate arrangements to be built during or after the diversion period, which complicates the programme — so the saving is real and is not free, and the decision belongs at the layout stage where the tunnel's alignment is still open.**

examTip.trick: **Diversion tunnel or channel, plus upstream and downstream cofferdams** — then build the dam in the dry.
examTip.trap: **The river closure is a race against rising gap velocity** — attempted at the lowest flow, with stockpiles ready. A failed closure costs a full year.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cofferdam sizing is a legitimate expected-value calculation** — the consequence is purely financial. That is why it works here and not for the permanent works.

questions.stem: A LOW-LEVEL OUTLET (bottom outlet) is provided in a storage dam principally to:
options: Increase the total spillway discharge capacity during floods
Provide additional head for the power turbines
Permit the reservoir to be drawn down or emptied
Supply water to the fish ladder
questions.solution:
**To permit the reservoir to be DRAWN DOWN or emptied** — for flushing accumulated sediment, for inspection and repair of the dam, and as an emergency measure if the dam is found to be in distress.

**The functions of a bottom outlet, in order of importance:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **EMERGENCY DRAWDOWN** ← | **If the dam shows distress — excessive seepage, movement, a developing crack — lowering the reservoir reduces the load and buys time** ← |
| **SEDIMENT FLUSHING** ← | **Drawing the level down and opening the outlet scours deposited sediment through** ← |
| **Emptying for INSPECTION and repair of the upstream face and the outlet works** ← | ← |
| **Riparian and downstream RELEASES independent of the power plant** ← | ← |
| **Passing flows during the first filling, under control** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE SAFETY FUNCTION AND IT IS WHY A BOTTOM OUTLET IS ESSENTIALLY MANDATORY ON A LARGE DAM: the ability to reduce the reservoir load quickly is the single most valuable emergency measure available.**

> **A dam showing signs of distress under full reservoir is in a race between the deterioration and the response, and the only response that acts on the CAUSE is to remove the load.**

> **Every other measure — grouting, buttressing, filters at the seepage exit — takes time that may not be available.**

> **So the outlet's capacity should be set by how fast the reservoir must be lowered in an emergency, not merely by the flushing requirement, and a common criterion is the ability to lower the level by a specified amount within a specified number of days.**

**SEDIMENT FLUSHING THROUGH A BOTTOM OUTLET IS THE FUNCTION MOST RELEVANT TO NEPAL AND IT DESERVES ITS OWN TREATMENT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **DRAWDOWN FLUSHING lowers the reservoir until a river channel re-forms through the deposits** ← | ← |
| **The flowing river then scours a channel and carries sediment out through the outlet** ← | ← |
| **It is effective only if the level is drawn LOW ENOUGH for riverine flow to establish** ← | **Partial drawdown achieves very little** ← |
| **It works best in narrow reservoirs where the scoured channel occupies most of the width** ← | ← |
| **It requires abundant water, so it is done at the start or end of the monsoon** ← | ← |
| **And it costs the stored water and the energy that water would have generated** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHY FLUSHING SO OFTEN DISAPPOINTS AND IT IS A CONDITION THAT MUST BE DESIGNED FOR RATHER THAN HOPED FOR: the outlet must be low enough and large enough to draw the reservoir down to near the original river bed.**

> **An outlet placed part-way up the dam permits partial drawdown, and partial drawdown scours a channel through the upper deposits only, leaving the bulk in place.**

> **So the outlet's INVERT LEVEL determines whether flushing is possible at all, and it is fixed at the design stage and cannot be changed afterwards.**

> **A dam built without a sufficiently low outlet has forfeited the flushing option permanently, and its reservoir will silt up on the schedule the sediment inflow dictates.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE COST THAT MAKES OPERATORS RELUCTANT AND IT SHOULD BE ACKNOWLEDGED HONESTLY: flushing empties the reservoir, which means forgoing the energy that water represented and accepting a period of reduced or no generation.**

> **There is also a downstream environmental cost, since a flushing release carries a very high sediment concentration that can kill aquatic life for a considerable distance.**

> **So flushing is deferred, and deferred again, and the reservoir fills.**

> **The answer is to make flushing a scheduled and budgeted operation with its cost recognised in the financial model from the outset — because a reservoir's capacity is an asset that requires maintenance expenditure like any other, and treating that expenditure as an avoidable loss guarantees that the asset is consumed.**

examTip.trick: **Drawdown and emptying** — for flushing, for inspection, and above all as the emergency measure that removes the load from a distressed dam.
examTip.trap: **Flushing needs near-full drawdown to re-establish riverine flow** — partial drawdown scours only the top. The outlet's INVERT LEVEL decides this, permanently.
examTip.mnemonic: **Budget flushing as maintenance, not as lost generation** — a reservoir's capacity is an asset needing upkeep. Treat the cost as a loss and the asset gets consumed.

questions.stem: A gravity dam 45 m high has a base width of 34 m. Taking the density of concrete as 2400 kg/m³ and neglecting uplift, the ratio of the resisting moment about the toe to the overturning moment of the water thrust at full reservoir is approximately (assume a triangular section with a vertical upstream face):
questions.solution:
**About 2.6.**

**Working per metre length of dam:**

| Quantity | Working |
|---|---|
| **Water thrust** | **P = ½ γw H² = ½ × 9.81 × 45² = ½ × 9.81 × 2025 = 9,932.6 kN** ← |
| **Its lever arm above the base** | **H/3 = 45/3 = 15 m** ← |
| **Overturning moment** | **M_o = 9,932.6 × 15 = 148,989 kN·m** ← |
| **Weight of the triangular section** | **W = ½ × B × H × γc = ½ × 34 × 45 × 23.54** ← |
| ** ** | **γc = 2400 × 9.81 ÷ 1000 = 23.54 kN/m³** ← |
| ** ** | **½ × 34 × 45 = 765 m², so W = 765 × 23.54 = 18,008 kN** ← |
| **Its centroid from the toe** | **For a triangle with the vertical face upstream, the centroid is B/3 from the vertical face, so 34 − 34/3 = 22.67 m from the toe** ← |
| **Resisting moment** | **M_r = 18,008 × 22.67 = 408,241 kN·m** ← |
| **Ratio** | **408,241 ÷ 148,989 = 2.74 ≈ 2.6 to 2.7** ← |

> **THE CENTROID POSITION IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG AND IT IS WORTH BEING DELIBERATE ABOUT: a triangle's centroid lies one-third of the base from the side where the area is concentrated.**

> **With a vertical upstream face and a sloping downstream face, the mass is concentrated near the upstream side, so the centroid is B/3 = 11.33 m from the heel, which is 22.67 m from the toe.**

> **Taking it as B/3 from the TOE instead gives 11.33 m and halves the resisting moment, producing a ratio of about 1.37 — which is option (a), and is the single commonest error in this calculation.**

> **The check is a physical one: the dam's mass is obviously toward the upstream side of a triangle whose vertical face is upstream, so its centroid must be FAR from the toe, not near it.**

**A SANITY CHECK ON THE ANSWER, WHICH CONFIRMS THE SECTION IS SENSIBLE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A factor of safety against overturning of 2 to 3 is the expected range for a gravity dam neglecting uplift** ← | ← |
| **2.7 sits comfortably in it** ← | ← |
| **The base width of 34 m on 45 m height is B/H = 0.76** ← | **Which matches the 0.7 to 0.9 rule of thumb** ← |
| **So the section is a normal gravity profile and the answer should be a normal factor** ← | ← |

> **THAT KIND OF CHECK — DOES THE ANSWER LIE WHERE ANSWERS OF THIS KIND USUALLY LIE — IS WORTH BUILDING INTO EVERY CALCULATION, and it catches the halved-moment error immediately.**

> **A ratio of 1.37 for a dam of standard proportions would mean that standard proportions were marginal, which they are not.**

> **And a ratio of 3.5 would mean they were extravagant.**

> **So both the plausible-looking wrong answers can be rejected on proportions alone, before the arithmetic is examined.**

**AND THE PHRASE 'NEGLECTING UPLIFT' CARRIES THE REAL LESSON OF THIS QUESTION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **With full uplift assumed varying linearly from full head at the heel to zero at the toe** ← | ← |
| **U = ½ × 9.81 × 45 × 34 = 7,505 kN, acting at B/3 from the heel** ← | ← |
| **Its moment about the toe is 7,505 × 22.67 = 170,138 kN·m, and it is DESTABILISING** ← | ← |
| **So the ratio becomes 408,241 ÷ (148,989 + 170,138) = 1.28** ← | ← |
| **Which is barely adequate and would require a wider base** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW SHOWS UPLIFT'S TRUE MAGNITUDE AND IT IS STARTLING: including it more than halves the factor of safety, taking a comfortable 2.7 to a marginal 1.28.**

> **That is why the drainage provision described earlier matters so much — with drains reducing the uplift at the drain line to a third of the head, the effective uplift force falls by around half and the factor recovers to roughly 1.8.**

> **So the drainage system is not a refinement; it is what makes the standard gravity profile viable.**

> **A dam designed to that profile with a blocked drainage gallery is operating at a factor of safety it was never designed for, which is the practical reason the drain flows must be measured and recorded for the dam's whole life.**
tags: uplift more than halves the factor

examTip.trick: **P = ½γH² at H/3; W = ½BH γc with its centroid B/3 from the VERTICAL face** — so 2B/3 from the toe. Ratio ≈ 2.7.
examTip.trap: **Putting the centroid B/3 from the TOE halves the resisting moment and gives 1.4** — the commonest error. The mass is on the upstream side.
examTip.mnemonic: **Uplift takes 2.7 down to 1.28** — more than halving it. The drainage gallery is what makes a standard gravity profile work at all.

questions.stem: In the stability analysis of a gravity dam, the SLIDING FACTOR (or shear-friction factor of safety) is checked because:
options: Concrete may crush at the toe under the vertical load
The dam may slide horizontally along its base or along a weak plane in the foundation
The dam may float when the reservoir is full
The abutments may spread apart
questions.solution:
**The dam may slide HORIZONTALLY along its base or along a weak plane in the foundation**, resisted by friction and by the cohesion or shear strength of the contact.

**The two forms of the check:**

| Form | Expression | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| **Simple SLIDING FACTOR** | **F = μ (ΣV − U) ÷ ΣH** ← | **Friction only — conservative, ignores any cohesion** ← |
| **SHEAR-FRICTION FACTOR** | **F = [μ(ΣV − U) + c·A] ÷ ΣH** ← | **Includes the cohesion or bond of the contact over area A** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO IS WHETHER COHESION IS CREDITED AND IT MATTERS ENORMOUSLY TO THE ANSWER: the simple sliding factor typically requires F ≥ 1.0, and the shear-friction factor requires F ≥ 3 to 4 because it counts a resistance that may not be reliably present.**

> **The different required values are not inconsistent — they reflect the different confidence in what is being counted.**

> **Friction at a rough concrete-rock contact is dependable; cohesion depends on the bond having been achieved everywhere, on the rock not being fractured along that surface, and on nothing having debonded over the years.**

> **So the higher required factor on the cohesive form is a discount for uncertainty rather than an inconsistency, and quoting a shear-friction factor of 1.5 as 'satisfactory' by the sliding factor's standard is a serious misreading.**

**THE PHRASE 'OR ALONG A WEAK PLANE IN THE FOUNDATION' IS THE MORE IMPORTANT HALF OF THE ANSWER AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The critical sliding surface is not necessarily the dam's own base** ← | ← |
| **A bedding plane, a clay seam, a sheared fault or a set of joints dipping downstream may be weaker** ← | ← |
| **In that case the dam and a wedge of foundation rock slide together** ← | ← |
| **So the analysis must examine surfaces WITHIN the foundation, not merely the contact** ← | ← |
| **Which requires the geology to be known in three dimensions** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW NAMES THE FEATURE THAT MATTERS MOST — A PLANE DIPPING DOWNSTREAM — AND THE ORIENTATION IS THE WHOLE POINT: a weak plane dipping UPSTREAM is harmless, because sliding along it would require the dam to move upward against its own weight.**

> **The same plane dipping DOWNSTREAM is dangerous, because sliding along it moves the dam down as well as along, and gravity assists.**

> **So two identical seams of identical weakness, differing only in dip direction, present entirely different hazards.**

> **This is why a geological map showing the strike and dip of every discontinuity is essential to a dam foundation assessment, and why 'the rock is sound' is not an adequate description of a foundation — a strong rock with an adversely oriented weak seam is a worse foundation than a uniformly moderate one.**

**AND THE MEASURES AVAILABLE WHEN THE CHECK FAILS DESERVE LISTING, SINCE THEY ARE THE DESIGN RESPONSE:**

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **WIDEN the base** ← | **More weight, more friction, more cohesive area** ← |
| **Slope the base into the hill — an upstream-dipping base** ← | **Sliding must then climb, which gravity resists** ← |
| **Provide a SHEAR KEY into the foundation** ← | **Forces the sliding surface through intact rock** ← |
| **Anchor the dam with post-tensioned CABLES into the foundation** ← | **Adds vertical force directly, and is the standard remedy for an existing dam** ← |
| **Excavate and replace the weak seam with concrete — dental treatment** ← | **Removes the weakness rather than compensating for it** ← |
| **Improve the DRAINAGE to reduce uplift** ← | **Raises the effective weight, helping both friction and cohesion terms** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE ONE USED WHEN A DAM IS FOUND DEFICIENT IN SERVICE AND IT IS REMARKABLY EFFECTIVE: post-tensioned anchors drilled through the dam and grouted deep into the foundation add a large vertical prestress.**

> **That prestress increases the frictional resistance directly and it acts on the existing structure without any need to enlarge it.**

> **Many older dams worldwide have been brought up to modern seismic standards this way, at a small fraction of what buttressing would cost.**

> **The caution is that the anchors must be corrosion-protected and monitorable, because an anchor that has lost its prestress silently is providing the safety margin only on paper — which is the same theme as the blocked drains, and it recurs because these are all provisions whose failure is invisible from outside.**

examTip.trick: **F = μ(ΣV − U) ÷ ΣH, or with c·A added** — friction alone needs F ≥ 1, with cohesion counted it needs 3 to 4.
examTip.trap: **A weak plane dipping DOWNSTREAM is dangerous; the same plane dipping upstream is harmless** — sliding would have to climb. Dip direction is everything.
examTip.mnemonic: **Post-tensioned anchors are the retrofit** — vertical prestress on an existing dam. But a de-tensioned anchor, like a blocked drain, fails invisibly.

questions.stem: A CHUTE (trough) spillway is generally preferred over an ogee overflow spillway on the dam itself when:
options: The dam is a concrete gravity dam of great height
The design flood is very small
The spillway must discharge into a stilling basin
The dam is an embankment, which cannot be overtopped
questions.solution:
**The dam is an EMBANKMENT, which cannot be overtopped** — so the spillway is placed in a separate excavated channel on an abutment or a saddle, clear of the embankment.

**Why the dam type dictates the spillway arrangement:**

| Dam type | Spillway arrangement |
|---|---|
| **CONCRETE gravity or arch** ← | **An OGEE overflow section built into the dam itself — the water falls down the dam's own face** ← |
| **EMBANKMENT (earth or rockfill)** ← | **A SEPARATE spillway — chute, side channel, shaft or tunnel — placed away from the fill** ← |

> **THE REASON IS THE EROSION VULNERABILITY ESTABLISHED EARLIER AND IT ADMITS OF NO EXCEPTION: an embankment cannot have water flowing over or against it.**

> **So the spillway must be somewhere the flowing water touches only rock or concrete.**

> **The natural place is a saddle, a low col in the reservoir rim, or an abutment where a channel can be excavated in rock.**

> **The consequence is that an embankment dam's spillway is a separate and often very expensive structure — sometimes a third of the project's cost — whereas a concrete dam's spillway is largely part of the dam it is built into.**

> **That cost difference partly offsets the embankment's cheaper dam, and it is why the dam-type comparison must be made on the TOTAL cost of dam plus spillway plus diversion, not on the dam alone.**

**THE MAIN SPILLWAY TYPES AND WHERE EACH SUITS:**

| Type | Description | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **OGEE / overflow** ← | **Over the dam crest, down the dam face** ← | **Concrete dams** ← |
| **CHUTE (trough)** ← | **A control structure then a steep open channel down the hillside** ← | **Embankment dams with a suitable saddle or abutment** ← |
| **SIDE CHANNEL** ← | **Crest parallel to the channel, flow turns 90° into a trough alongside** ← | **Narrow gorges where there is no room for a wide crest at right angles** ← |
| **SHAFT / MORNING GLORY** ← | **A circular crest dropping into a vertical shaft and a tunnel** ← | **Sites with no room for a surface spillway — often reusing the diversion tunnel** ← |
| **SIPHON** ← | **Self-priming, operating automatically at a fixed level** ← | **Small schemes needing automatic operation with no gates** ← |
| **LABYRINTH** ← | **A zigzag crest giving a long crest length in a short width** ← | **Where capacity must be increased without widening — often a retrofit** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW HAS A CHARACTERISTIC AND DANGEROUS BEHAVIOUR THAT DESERVES NAMING: a shaft spillway's discharge is limited once the shaft runs FULL.**

> **Below that point it behaves as a weir and its discharge grows rapidly with head, which is the desired behaviour.**

> **Once the shaft primes and flows full it behaves as a pipe, and its discharge then grows only as the square root of the head — so a large increase in reservoir level produces very little extra discharge.**

> **That makes a shaft spillway unsuitable as the sole spillway for a dam where a flood much larger than the design flood is credible, because it cannot pass the excess, and it is normally paired with an auxiliary or emergency spillway.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE COMMON MODERN RETROFIT AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING WHY IT WORKS: weir discharge is proportional to crest LENGTH, and a labyrinth folds a long crest into a short opening.**

> **A zigzag crest three or four times the width of the opening passes correspondingly more water at the same head.**

> **So a dam whose spillway is found inadequate — because the design flood estimate has been revised upward, which happens regularly as records lengthen — can often be upgraded by replacing a straight crest with a labyrinth, without widening the opening or raising the dam.**

> **That is a great deal cheaper than the alternatives, and it is why labyrinth and piano-key weirs have become common on rehabilitation projects worldwide.**
tags: total cost comparison of dam types

examTip.trick: **An embankment cannot be overtopped** — so the spillway goes in a separate excavated channel on a saddle or abutment.
examTip.trap: **Compare dam types on dam PLUS spillway PLUS diversion** — an embankment's separate spillway can be a third of the project cost, offsetting the cheaper dam.
examTip.mnemonic: **A shaft spillway chokes once it primes** — weir flow becomes pipe flow, and discharge then grows only as √H. Never the sole spillway for a credible larger flood.

questions.stem: GATED spillways are provided in preference to ungated (free overflow) spillways chiefly because they:
options: Allow the reservoir to be stored above the spillway crest level
Cannot fail to operate during a flood
Are cheaper to build and require no mechanical equipment
Reduce the design flood that must be passed
questions.solution:
**They allow the reservoir to be stored ABOVE the spillway crest level — gaining storage and head — while retaining the ability to pass the design flood by opening the gates.**

**The trade between gated and ungated:**

| Aspect | UNGATED (free overflow) | GATED |
|---|---|---|
| **Storage** | **Limited to the crest level** ← | **Extends above the crest, to the top of the gates** ← |
| **Cost** | **Lower — no gates, hoists, power or piers** ← | **Higher, and it includes lifetime maintenance** ← |
| **Reliability** | **ABSOLUTE — it works because water flows downhill** ← | **Depends on gates opening when required** ← |
| **Operation** | **None required** ← | **Requires operators, procedures and power** ← |
| **Flood routing** | **Passive, and it begins as soon as the level exceeds the crest** ← | **Controllable — releases can be shaped and pre-released** ← |
| **Failure mode** | **None of consequence** ← | **A gate that will not open, or one that will not close** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE UNGATED SPILLWAY'S DECISIVE ADVANTAGE AND IT SHOULD NOT BE UNDERVALUED: it cannot fail to operate.**

> **There is no mechanism, no power supply, no operator decision and no procedure.**

> **A great many dam incidents worldwide have involved gates that failed to open — power lost in the storm that caused the flood, a hoist seized through lack of maintenance, an operator absent or hesitating, or debris jamming the gate.**

> **So the choice for a gated spillway must be justified by the storage it gains, and the justification must include the cost of ensuring, for the dam's whole life, that the gates will open — standby power, regular exercising of every gate, trained operators and a rehearsed procedure.**

> **A gated spillway without that regime has traded a certain benefit for an uncertain safety.**

**THE STORAGE GAIN THAT JUSTIFIES GATES IS OFTEN LARGE AND THAT DESERVES QUANTIFYING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Gates 8 m high on a reservoir whose surface area is 10 km² hold an extra 80 million m³** ← | ← |
| **Which on a 100 m head is worth roughly 0.002725 × 0.85 × 80×10⁶ × 100 ≈ 18.5 GWh of stored energy** ← | ← |
| **And the 8 m of extra head raises the output of every cubic metre passing the plant** ← | ← |
| **Achieved without raising the dam at all** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE ECONOMIC ARGUMENT IN ITS SHARPEST FORM AND IT IS WHY LARGE STORAGE DAMS ARE ALMOST ALWAYS GATED: eight metres of gates cost a fraction of eight metres of dam.**

> **The dam must be raised over its whole length and its whole section to gain that height, and the gates occupy only the spillway opening.**

> **So gates buy storage and head at perhaps a tenth of the cost of the equivalent dam raising, and the inundation footprint is identical either way.**

> **The counterweight is the operational burden and the failure mode, which is why the decision is made deliberately and why very small dams, which cannot support an operating organisation, are usually left ungated even at some cost in storage.**

**A CLOSING NOTE ON GATE TYPES, SINCE THE RADIAL GATE'S DOMINANCE HAS A CLEAR REASON:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **RADIAL (Tainter) gate** ← | **A curved skin plate on radial arms pivoting at a trunnion — the water thrust passes THROUGH the pivot, so the hoisting force is small** ← |
| **VERTICAL LIFT gate** ← | **Must be lifted against the full friction of the water load on its seals — a much larger hoist** ← |
| **DRUM and FLAP gates** ← | **Hinged at the bottom and lowered by water pressure or buoyancy — suit small heads and automatic operation** ← |

> **The first row explains why the radial gate is standard on large spillways and it is a genuinely elegant piece of mechanics: because the skin plate is a circular arc centred on the trunnion, every element of water pressure acts along a radius and therefore passes through the pivot.**

> **So the water load exerts no moment about the trunnion at all, and the hoist must overcome only the gate's own weight and the seal friction.**

> **A vertical lift gate of the same size needs a hoist several times larger.**

> **The geometry does the work that machinery would otherwise have to do, which is the mark of a good design and is why the arrangement has been standard for over a century.**
tags: gates cheaper than raising the dam

examTip.trick: **Storage above the crest, released by opening gates** — gaining volume and head without raising the dam.
examTip.trap: **An ungated spillway CANNOT fail to operate** — many incidents involve gates that would not open. Gates require standby power, exercising and rehearsed procedures for life.
examTip.mnemonic: **A radial gate's thrust passes through the trunnion** — a circular arc centred on the pivot exerts no moment, so the hoist lifts only the gate's weight.

questions.stem: FLOOD ROUTING through a reservoir shows that the outflow peak is smaller than the inflow peak and occurs later. The peak outflow occurs at the moment when:
options: The inflow hydrograph reaches its own peak
The reservoir reaches its full supply level
The inflow equals the outflow
The inflow has fallen to zero
questions.solution:
**When the inflow EQUALS the outflow** — that is, when the storage stops increasing and the reservoir level is at its maximum.

**Why this must be so:**

| Step | Reasoning |
|---|---|
| **Continuity: I − O = dS/dt** ← | **Inflow minus outflow equals the rate of change of storage** ← |
| **While I > O, storage INCREASES and the level RISES** ← | ← |
| **A higher level means a greater head on the spillway, so O increases** ← | ← |
| **When I = O, dS/dt = 0 and the level stops rising — it is at its MAXIMUM** ← | ← |
| **Since outflow is a function of level, the outflow is also at its maximum at that instant** ← | ← |
| **Thereafter I < O, the level falls and the outflow falls with it** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE LINK THAT MAKES THE ANSWER INEVITABLE AND IT DEPENDS ON ONE CONDITION WORTH NAMING: the outflow must be a single-valued function of the reservoir level.**

> **That holds for an UNGATED spillway, where discharge depends only on the head over the crest.**

> **It does NOT hold for a gated spillway, where the outflow depends on the gate opening as well as the level, and the operator can therefore make the peak outflow occur whenever they choose.**

> **So the classic result — peak outflow at the intersection of the two hydrographs — is a property of uncontrolled reservoirs, and a gated reservoir's routing depends on the operating rule rather than on hydraulics alone.**

**THE GRAPHICAL CONSEQUENCE IS WORTH PICTURING BECAUSE IT IS FREQUENTLY EXAMINED:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **The outflow hydrograph crosses the RECESSION limb of the inflow hydrograph at its own peak** ← | ← |
| **The peak outflow is therefore always LATER than the peak inflow** ← | ← |
| **And always SMALLER, for an uncontrolled reservoir** ← | ← |
| **The area between the curves before the crossing is the storage GAINED** ← | ← |
| **The area after it is the storage RELEASED, and the two are equal** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A USEFUL CHECK ON ANY ROUTING CALCULATION AND IT IS SIMPLY CONTINUITY EXPRESSED GRAPHICALLY: whatever went into storage must come out.**

> **So the two areas between the hydrographs must balance, and a routed hydrograph in which they do not has an arithmetic error in it.**

> **This is a quick and complete check that can be done by eye on a plotted result, and it catches the commonest routing mistakes — a wrong time step, a misread storage-elevation curve, an inconsistent discharge relation.**

**AND THE ATTENUATION'S MAGNITUDE DEPENDS ON WHAT THE RESERVOIR OFFERS, WHICH IS THE DESIGN-RELEVANT PART:**

| Factor | Effect on attenuation |
|---|---|
| **A large SURFACE AREA at spillway level** ← | **More storage per metre of rise, so more attenuation** ← |
| **A SMALL spillway** ← | **The level must rise further to pass the flow, storing more — more attenuation, but a higher dam** ← |
| **A sharp, brief inflow peak** ← | **More attenuation — there is less volume to absorb** ← |
| **A long, flat inflow flood** ← | **Little attenuation — the reservoir fills and then passes what arrives** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS A GENUINE DESIGN TRADE AND IT IS THE ONE FLOOD ROUTING EXISTS TO RESOLVE: a smaller spillway attenuates the flood more, which sounds attractive, but it does so by letting the reservoir rise higher — which requires more freeboard and a taller dam.**

> **So the spillway size and the dam height trade directly against each other, and routing is how the trade is evaluated.**

> **The optimum balances the cost of spillway capacity against the cost of dam height, and it differs between a concrete dam, where extra height is expensive, and an embankment, where extra spillway is expensive.**

> **The fourth row is the caution that limits the whole device: a reservoir attenuates a SHARP flood well and a LONG one hardly at all, so a scheme relying on routing for its flood safety must be tested against a long-duration flood as well as a peaky one — and the critical duration is not necessarily the one that gives the largest peak.**
tags: peak outflow at I equals O
spillway size trades against dam height

examTip.trick: **When I = O the storage stops growing, so the level and the outflow are both at maximum** — it crosses the inflow's recession limb.
examTip.trap: **Only true for an UNGATED spillway** — with gates the outflow depends on the opening too, so the operator decides when the peak occurs.
examTip.mnemonic: **Equal areas either side of the crossing** — continuity drawn out, and a free check on any routed hydrograph.

questions.stem: The INSTRUMENTATION installed in a large dam — piezometers, inclinometers, extensometers, seepage weirs and survey monuments — is of value only if:
options: It is installed after the dam has been in service for some years
The readings are taken from the day of first filling
The instruments are read once a year by an external consultant
The instruments are of the most expensive type available
questions.solution:
**The readings are taken from the day of first filling, recorded consistently, and compared against PREDICTED behaviour and previous readings** — since a single reading means nothing and only the TREND against expectation reveals distress.

**What each instrument watches and what change would signify:**

| Instrument | Measures | A worrying change |
|---|---|---|
| **PIEZOMETERS in the foundation and the fill** ← | **Pore pressure and uplift** ← | **A rise not explained by the reservoir level — suggests a blocked drain or a new seepage path** ← |
| **SEEPAGE MEASURING WEIRS** ← | **Total leakage flow, and its CLARITY** ← | **Increasing flow at constant reservoir level; or any TURBIDITY, which means material is moving** ← |
| **INCLINOMETERS** ← | **Lateral movement with depth** ← | **A developing shear at one depth** ← |
| **EXTENSOMETERS and joint meters** ← | **Opening of joints and cracks** ← | **Progressive opening rather than seasonal cycling** ← |
| **SURVEY MONUMENTS** ← | **Crest and face displacement** ← | **Movement that does not reverse with the reservoir cycle** ← |
| **PENDULUMS in a concrete dam** ← | **Deflection of the dam body** ← | **A drift in the annual cycle's mean position** ← |

> **THE SEEPAGE WEIR'S SECOND MEASUREMENT — CLARITY — IS THE SINGLE MOST IMPORTANT OBSERVATION MADE AT A DAM AND IT REQUIRES NO INSTRUMENT AT ALL: clear seepage is normal and expected; CLOUDY seepage means soil particles are being carried out.**

> **That is piping in progress, and it is the beginning of the failure mode that has destroyed more embankment dams than any other.**

> **The observation costs nothing, requires no calibration, and can be made by anyone who walks the toe.**

> **So a dam surveillance regime that collects elaborate piezometric data and does not have someone looking at the seepage every day has its priorities inverted, and the daily walk along the downstream toe by an observant person remains the most valuable single element of dam safety monitoring.**

**WHY THE COMPARISON MUST BE AGAINST PREDICTION AND NOT MERELY AGAINST HISTORY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Every reading varies with the reservoir level, the season and the temperature** ← | ← |
| **So 'higher than last month' may be entirely normal** ← | ← |
| **The design should PREDICT what each instrument will read at each reservoir level** ← | ← |
| **And the reading is then compared with that prediction** ← | ← |
| **A deviation from prediction is meaningful; a change from last month often is not** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN OMITTED AND IT IS WHAT SEPARATES MONITORING FROM MERE DATA COLLECTION: the designer should state, before first filling, what each instrument is expected to read and what value would constitute a threshold requiring action.**

> **Without those thresholds, the readings accumulate in a file and nobody knows whether they are acceptable.**

> **With them, a reading that crosses a threshold triggers a defined response — increased frequency, investigation, notification, or drawdown.**

> **So the instrumentation's value is created at the DESIGN stage, when the predictions and thresholds are set, and a dam instrumented without them has bought the hardware and not the capability.**

> **A CLOSING POINT ON FIRST FILLING, WHICH IS THE MOST CRITICAL PERIOD IN A DAM'S LIFE: the great majority of dam failures occur during or shortly after first filling, when the structure and its foundation experience full load for the first time.**

> **So first filling should be STAGED — raised in increments, held at each level while the instruments are read and the behaviour assessed, and continued only when the readings are satisfactory.**

> **Filling fast, because the reservoir is wanted, forgoes the only opportunity to observe the dam's response in stages while the load is still partial and the reservoir can still be lowered easily.**

> **A staged first filling with a proper hold at each stage costs a few months of generation and is the cheapest insurance a dam owner will ever buy.**
tags: seepage clarity is the key observation
first filling is the critical period

examTip.trick: **Read from first filling, compared against PREDICTED behaviour** — a single reading means nothing; only the trend against expectation does.
examTip.trap: **Cloudy seepage means particles are moving — piping in progress.** It needs no instrument, costs nothing, and is the most valuable observation at any dam.
examTip.mnemonic: **Set the thresholds at DESIGN stage, before first filling** — instrumentation without predicted values is data collection, not monitoring.

questions.stem: In the seismic design of a dam, the OPERATING BASIS EARTHQUAKE (OBE) and the MAXIMUM CREDIBLE EARTHQUAKE (MCE) differ in that:
options: The OBE applies to concrete dams and the MCE to embankment dams
The two are the same event described by different agencies
The MCE is used only for dams above 100 m in height
The dam must remain operational with only minor repairable damage under the OBE
questions.solution:
**The dam must remain OPERATIONAL with only minor repairable damage under the OBE, whereas under the MCE it need only avoid CATASTROPHIC RELEASE of the reservoir** — damage, even severe damage, being acceptable.

**The two levels and their performance requirements:**

| Level | Definition | Required performance |
|---|---|---|
| **OBE (Operating Basis Earthquake)** ← | **An event with a reasonable probability of occurring in the dam's life — often a 145-year return period** ← | **Remain operational; damage minor and repairable without emptying the reservoir** ← |
| **MCE (Maximum Credible Earthquake)** ← | **The largest event the regional geology and seismology can plausibly produce** ← | **No UNCONTROLLED RELEASE of the reservoir. The dam may be severely damaged and may need replacing** ← |

> **THE TWO-LEVEL APPROACH IS THE HEART OF MODERN SEISMIC DESIGN AND IT APPLIES FAR BEYOND DAMS, so it is worth understanding as a philosophy: design for FUNCTION under the event you expect, and for SURVIVAL under the event you cannot exclude.**

> **Requiring a dam to remain fully operational after the maximum credible earthquake would make it impossibly expensive, and would buy a level of performance nobody needs — after such an event the dam's continued generation is not the priority.**

> **Requiring it merely to avoid catastrophic release under a moderate earthquake would be far too lax, since such an earthquake will probably occur and the dam should keep working through it.**

> **So two events, two requirements, each proportionate — and the same structure is checked twice, against different criteria.**

> **The parallel in building codes is exact: a building must be undamaged in a frequent earthquake, repairable in a design earthquake and standing but perhaps unusable in the maximum considered one.**

**THE MCE'S DEFINITION DESERVES CAREFUL ATTENTION BECAUSE IT IS NOT A PROBABILISTIC ONE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The MCE is DETERMINISTIC — it is the largest event the known faults could produce** ← | ← |
| **Established by identifying the seismic sources, their maximum magnitudes and their distances** ← | ← |
| **Not by extrapolating a recurrence curve to a very long return period** ← | ← |
| **Though a probabilistic assessment is usually done in parallel and the more onerous adopted** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE SAME METHODOLOGICAL POINT MADE EARLIER ABOUT GLOFS AND IT RECURS FOR THE SAME REASON: an extreme governed by a physical limit should be assessed against that limit, not by statistical extrapolation.**

> **A fault of a given length and character can produce an earthquake of a certain maximum magnitude and no larger, because there is only so much rock to rupture.**

> **So the maximum credible event is bounded by geology, and identifying that bound is a more reliable procedure than extending a Gutenberg-Richter relation out to a ten-thousand-year return period.**

> **Nepal's setting makes this concrete: the Main Himalayan Thrust is capable of a magnitude 8 or greater event, and any dam in the country must be assessed against that possibility regardless of what the instrumental record of the last century contains.**

**AND THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES FOR DESIGN DESERVE THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Embankment dams need generous FREEBOARD against seismic settlement** ← | **The fill settles during shaking, and the crest can drop by a metre or more** ← |
| **And a wide, well-filtered core, so a crack that forms cannot pipe** ← | **CRACK-STOPPING filters are the key seismic detail for an embankment** ← |
| **Liquefiable foundation materials must be removed or treated** ← | **A liquefiable layer beneath a dam is not acceptable at any level of shaking** ← |
| **Concrete dams need the cracked-base analysis noted earlier** ← | ← |
| **And appurtenances — gates, hoists, power supply, access roads — must survive too** ← | **A dam that survives while its gates cannot be opened is not safe** ← |

> **The second row is the most important embankment detail and it is worth remembering as the seismic counterpart of the ordinary filter: a wide chimney filter of properly graded sand will heal a transverse crack that opens through the core during shaking.**

> **Water flowing into the crack meets the filter, the filter's sand washes into the crack and plugs it, and the erosion stops.**

> **That is a self-healing mechanism designed in deliberately, and it is the reason a well-detailed modern embankment can survive severe shaking that would breach an older homogeneous one.**

> **The last row is the one most often forgotten in practice, and it fails whole schemes: the dam is designed to survive the MCE and the access road, the substation and the gate hoists are not — so the dam stands and cannot be operated, which under a full reservoir after a major earthquake is precisely the situation in which operation matters most.**

examTip.trick: **OBE: stay operational. MCE: no uncontrolled release, damage acceptable** — function under the expected event, survival under the unexcludable one.
examTip.trap: **The MCE is DETERMINISTIC, bounded by what the faults can rupture** — not a very long return period read off a recurrence curve.
examTip.mnemonic: **A crack-stopping filter heals a seismic crack** — its sand washes in and plugs the crack. And the gates, hoists and access must survive too, or the dam cannot be operated.

questions.stem: An EMERGENCY PREPAREDNESS (or Emergency Action) PLAN for a large dam is required principally because:
options: No dam can be made absolutely safe
It is a condition of obtaining construction insurance
It replaces the need for regular dam safety inspections
It transfers legal liability for a failure from the owner to the authorities
questions.solution:
**No dam can be made absolutely safe, so the residual risk must be managed** — by ensuring that a developing failure is DETECTED, that the downstream population is WARNED in time, and that everyone knows in advance what they are to do.

**What the plan must contain:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **DAM BREAK ANALYSIS and inundation mapping** ← | **Where the water goes, how deep, and how soon — the technical foundation of everything else** ← |
| **Defined EMERGENCY LEVELS with triggering conditions** ← | **Linked to instrument thresholds, reservoir levels and observed conditions** ← |
| **NOTIFICATION flowchart — who calls whom, in what order, with what message** ← | **Names and numbers, kept current** ← |
| **WARNING system to the population at risk** ← | **Sirens, mobile alerts, and a means that works when power and network fail** ← |
| **EVACUATION routes and assembly areas** ← | **Marked on the ground, not merely on a map** ← |
| **Responsibilities of the owner, the police, the local authority and the district administration** ← | ← |
| **A programme of DRILLS and annual review** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS WHERE THE ENGINEERING SITS AND IT IS THE PART WITHOUT WHICH THE REST IS GUESSWORK: a dam break analysis routes the outflow from a hypothetical breach down the valley and maps the resulting flood.**

> **It gives the arrival time and the depth at every settlement, and it is from those arrival times that the warning system's required speed is determined.**

> **A village 40 minutes downstream needs a warning within minutes to have any chance; one four hours downstream can be reached by telephone and vehicle.**

> **So the analysis defines what the warning system has to achieve, and designing the warning system without it is designing to an unknown requirement.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHERE MOST PLANS FAIL AND IT IS A FAILURE OF UPKEEP RATHER THAN OF DESIGN: a plan written once, filed and never exercised will not work.**

> **The telephone numbers change, the officials are transferred, the siren is not maintained, the population turns over, and nobody has ever practised.**

> **In the emergency, the plan is found, and it names people who left five years ago.**

> **So the annual drill and review are not administrative overhead — they are what keeps the plan real, and a plan without them is a document rather than a capability.**

**AND THE PHRASE 'NO DAM CAN BE MADE ABSOLUTELY SAFE' DESERVES DEFENDING BECAUSE IT SOUNDS DEFEATIST AND IS NOT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Every design uses estimated loads, assumed material properties and imperfect knowledge of the foundation** ← | ← |
| **Construction introduces defects that are not all detected** ← | ← |
| **Deterioration occurs over decades** ← | ← |
| **And events larger than those designed for remain possible** ← | ← |
| **So the probability of failure is small and it is NOT zero** ← | ← |
| **Managing a small non-zero probability of a catastrophic outcome is exactly what an emergency plan is for** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE THE MATURE POSITION AND IT IS WORTH ADOPTING EXPLICITLY: acknowledging residual risk is not an admission of poor engineering.**

> **It is a recognition that engineering reduces risk and does not eliminate it, and that the remaining risk deserves its own treatment.**

> **The alternative posture — that the dam is safe and therefore no plan is needed — leaves the population with no protection precisely in the circumstance the whole enterprise was meant to guard against.**

> **And it is worth noting that the emergency plan is by far the cheapest element of dam safety: the dam costs billions, and the plan costs a few million and saves the lives that the billions could not guarantee.**

> **Option (d)'s suggestion about liability is worth rejecting explicitly, since it inverts the position: preparing a plan does not transfer liability, and failing to prepare one where it is required is itself a source of liability — so the plan protects the population first and the owner second, and never at the population's expense.**
