The residual risk must be managed by ensuring that a developing failure is DETECTED, that the downstream population is WARNED in time, and that everyone knows in advance what they are to do.
tags: dam break analysis and inundation mapping

examTip.trick: **Detect, warn, and have everyone know their part** — because engineering reduces risk without eliminating it.
examTip.trap: **The dam break analysis defines the warning system's requirement** — arrival times set how fast the warning must be. Without it you design to an unknown target.
examTip.mnemonic: **Drills keep the plan real** — an unexercised plan names people who left five years ago. And the plan is the cheapest element of dam safety by far.

questions.stem: A SIDE INTAKE on a run-of-river scheme is normally located on the OUTER bank of a river bend because:
options: The outer bank is where the river is shallowest
Secondary (helicoidal) flow at a bend carries the surface water
The outer bank requires less excavation
Floods do not reach the outer bank
questions.solution:
**SECONDARY (helicoidal) FLOW at a bend carries the surface water — which is relatively sediment-free — toward the outer bank and sweeps the bed load along the bed toward the INNER bank**, so an outer-bank intake draws the cleanest available water.

**The mechanism, which is worth understanding rather than memorising:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water rounding a bend requires a centripetal force, supplied by a transverse water-surface slope** ← | **The surface is higher at the outer bank** ← |
| **That pressure gradient is uniform with depth, but the VELOCITY is not — it is greater near the surface** ← | ← |
| **So the fast surface water has more inertia than the pressure gradient can turn, and it moves OUTWARD** ← | ← |
| **The slow near-bed water is over-turned by the same gradient, and it moves INWARD** ← | ← |
| **The result is a spiral: outward at the surface, downward at the outer bank, inward along the bed** ← | ← |
| **And the bed load, which travels along the bed, is carried toward the INNER bank** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE AND IT IS THE WHOLE REASON FOR THE SITING RULE: the sediment sorts itself, and the engineer merely has to take water from the side where it is not.**

> **This is the same mechanism that builds a POINT BAR on the inner bank of every meander and scours a deep pool against the outer bank.**

> **So the river itself demonstrates where the sediment goes — the inner bank has a shoal of sand and the outer bank has deep clear water.**

> **Reading that from the river's own form, on a site visit or an aerial image, is a quicker and more reliable guide than any calculation, and it is available before any survey is done.**

**THE FULL SET OF ADVANTAGES OF AN OUTER-BANK LOCATION:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cleanest water, by the mechanism above** ← | ← |
| **DEEP water at the intake, so submergence is maintained at low flow** ← | **The outer bank is where the scour pool is** ← |
| **The river is unlikely to shift AWAY from the outer bank** ← | **A meander migrates outward, so the intake stays in the flow** ← |
| **A deeper channel means less risk of the intake being stranded by a shifting braid** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS AN OFTEN-DECISIVE ADVANTAGE ON A BRAIDED HIMALAYAN RIVER AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS: the commonest failure of an intake on such a river is that the river MOVES and leaves the intake dry.**

> **A braided river in the Terai can shift its main channel by hundreds of metres in a single monsoon.**

> **An intake placed on a straight braided reach has no assurance that the water will still be in front of it next year.**

> **An intake on the outer bank of a well-developed bend, preferably where the bend is anchored by a rock outcrop, is far more secure — which is why the search for an intake site on such a river is largely a search for a stable bend with a hard bank.**

> **THE QUALIFICATION 'RELATIVELY SEDIMENT-FREE' IN THE ANSWER DESERVES HONESTY: the mechanism separates the BED LOAD effectively and the SUSPENDED load hardly at all.**

> **Fine suspended silt is distributed fairly uniformly through the depth and it does not sort across the section.**

> **So an outer-bank intake excludes gravel and sand moving along the bed, and it still admits the fine suspended fraction — which is precisely the fraction that damages turbines at high head.**

> **The bend therefore solves part of the problem and the settling basin must solve the rest, and a scheme that relies on its intake siting alone and provides a token settling basin has misjudged which fraction does the damage.**
tags: bed load to the inner bank
bend excludes bed load not silt

examTip.trick: **Spiral flow at a bend sweeps bed load to the INNER bank** — so the outer bank has deep, comparatively clean water.
examTip.trap: **It separates BED load, not suspended silt** — and fine silt is what destroys high-head runners. The settling basin still has to do its job.
examTip.mnemonic: **The river shows you: point bar inside, scour pool outside** — and an outer-bank intake on an anchored bend also survives a braided river's wandering.

questions.stem: A TYROLEAN (or trench / bottom rack) INTAKE differs from a conventional side intake in that it:
options: Takes water from a reservoir rather than from a flowing river
Requires a tall diversion weir across the river
Uses no screen of any kind
Takes water through a horizontal or gently sloping bar rack set in the river bed, over which the flow passes
questions.solution:
**It takes water through a horizontal or gently sloping BAR RACK set in the river BED, over which the flow passes** — the water falling between the bars into a collection trench while coarse material is carried on over the rack.

**Why it suits steep mountain streams:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **No tall weir is needed — the structure sits IN the bed** ← | **So there is little to be damaged by a flood** ← |
| **Boulders and debris pass OVER the rack and continue downstream** ← | **Rather than accumulating against a weir** ← |
| **It works over a wide range of flows** ← | **Taking its design flow and letting the excess pass over** ← |
| **It is compact and cheap** ← | ← |
| **And it is well suited to steep, boulder-strewn torrents** ← | **Where a conventional weir and side intake would be destroyed** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE KEY VIRTUE ON A HIMALAYAN TORRENT AND IT IS WHY THE TYPE IS SO WIDELY USED IN NEPAL'S SMALL SCHEMES: such streams carry boulders, and boulders destroy structures that try to stop them.**

> **A Tyrolean intake does not try — it is a low structure aligned with the bed, and the boulders roll over it.**

> **The rack bars take a battering and are replaceable; the structure beneath survives.**

> **That is the sacrificial-element philosophy again, applied at small scale, and it is why a Tyrolean intake in a torrent outlasts a more substantial-looking weir.**

**THE BAR DETAILING IS WHERE THESE INTAKES SUCCEED OR FAIL AND IT REPAYS ATTENTION:**

| Detail | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bars run PARALLEL to the flow** ← | **So material slides along them rather than lodging across them** ← |
| **Clear spacing typically 10 to 30 mm** ← | **Set by the size of particle the settling basin can handle** ← |
| **Bars are wider at the top than the bottom — a TRAPEZOIDAL or teardrop section** ← | **So anything that passes the top gap cannot jam lower down** ← |
| **The rack slopes downstream at about 1 in 5 to 1 in 10** ← | **Helping material self-clear** ← |
| **The collection trench beneath is sized to carry the design flow without surcharging** ← | **If it backs up, water rises through the rack and the intake stops working** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A PIECE OF DETAILING THAT SOLVES A REAL AND OTHERWISE INTRACTABLE PROBLEM AND IT IS WORTH REMEMBERING AS A GENERAL PRINCIPLE: a gap that narrows downward jams; a gap that widens downward cannot.**

> **With parallel-sided bars, a stone that just enters the gap at the top wedges partway down and stays there, and each such stone reduces the intake's capacity permanently until someone prises it out.**

> **With bars tapering so the gap widens downward, any stone that enters passes straight through into the trench, where it is dealt with by the flushing arrangement.**

> **The same principle appears in crusher jaws, in hopper outlets and in trash rack design generally — make the passage widen in the direction of travel, and blockage becomes impossible rather than merely unlikely.**

**AND THE TYPE'S LIMITATIONS DESERVE STATING, SINCE IT IS NOT UNIVERSALLY APPLICABLE:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **The rack CLOGS with leaves, twigs and fine debris** ← | **Requiring frequent manual raking — the type's main operating burden** ← |
| **It admits SAND and fine material freely** ← | **Only coarse material is excluded, so a settling basin is essential** ← |
| **Its capacity is limited by the rack's plan area** ← | **Large flows need long racks, and the arrangement becomes unwieldy** ← |
| **It suits STEEP streams and works poorly on flat ones** ← | **Self-cleaning depends on the flow's energy** ← |

> **The first row is the reason these intakes need an attentive operator and it is the commonest cause of their disappointing in service: a rack blanketed with leaves after an autumn storm passes almost no water.**

> **Nothing in the design prevents this, and the remedy is a person with a rake.**

> **So the type trades capital cost and flood robustness for an operating burden — an excellent trade for a scheme with a resident operator and a poor one for a scheme intended to run unattended, which is a distinction worth making before the type is selected.**

examTip.trick: **A bar rack in the bed; water falls through, boulders roll over** — no tall weir for a flood to destroy.
examTip.trap: **Bars must taper so the gap WIDENS downward** — a parallel gap wedges stones permanently. Same principle as crusher jaws and hoppers.
examTip.mnemonic: **It excludes boulders, not sand** — a settling basin is still essential, and someone must rake the leaves off after every storm.

questions.stem: The GRAVEL TRAP placed immediately downstream of an ROR intake, before the settling basin, is provided to:
options: Remove the coarse fraction
Remove dissolved salts from the water
Store gravel for use as construction aggregate
Increase the water's velocity before it enters the settling basin
questions.solution:
**To remove the COARSE fraction — gravel and coarse sand that the intake has admitted — close to the river**, where it can be flushed straight back with a short sluice and a steep gradient.

**Why a separate gravel trap is provided rather than leaving the work to the settling basin:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Coarse material settles almost at once and would fill the settling basin's head end** ← | **Wasting its length on material that needed no length at all** ← |
| **Gravel is ABRASIVE and would damage the basin's floor and gates** ← | ← |
| **A gravel trap can be flushed FREQUENTLY and cheaply** ← | **Being close to the river with a short, steep flushing channel** ← |
| **Whereas flushing a settling basin is a larger operation** ← | ← |
| **So separating the duties lets each structure be optimised for its own fraction** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE DESIGN PRINCIPLE AND IT RUNS THROUGH THE WHOLE HEADWORKS: the sediment is removed in STAGES, coarsest first, each stage using the cheapest method that works on its fraction.**

> **The intake excludes boulders, the gravel trap takes gravel and coarse sand, the settling basin takes medium and fine sand, and the finest silt is allowed through because removing it would be uneconomic.**

> **Each stage handles material the previous one passed and protects the next from material it cannot handle efficiently.**

> **Trying to do the whole job in one structure produces a structure that is too large for the coarse fraction and too small for the fine one, and does neither well.**

**THE FLUSHING ARRANGEMENT IS WHAT MAKES OR BREAKS A GRAVEL TRAP AND IT HAS SPECIFIC REQUIREMENTS:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **A flushing SLUICE discharging back to the river** ← | ← |
| **Enough HEAD DIFFERENCE between the trap and the river to generate scouring velocity** ← | **This is the critical dimension and it must be checked at HIGH river stage, not low** ← |
| **A steep flushing channel with a smooth, abrasion-resistant invert** ← | ← |
| **Sufficient WATER to flush with — which is water diverted from generation** ← | ← |
| **And an arrangement permitting flushing WITHOUT shutting the plant down, where possible** ← | **A duplicated trap, or a continuous flushing slot** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE COMMONEST DESIGN FAILURE AND IT IS A CONSEQUENCE OF CHECKING THE WRONG CONDITION: during a monsoon flood the river level rises, and the head available for flushing falls.**

> **That is precisely when the sediment load is greatest and flushing is most needed.**

> **A trap designed on the dry-season head difference may have almost no head at flood stage, and it silts up solid exactly when it has most work to do.**

> **So the flushing check must be made at the HIGH river stage coincident with high sediment load, and the trap's invert set accordingly — which usually means setting it higher than the minimum, and accepting a smaller trap that can actually be cleared.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS WORTH PROVIDING WHEREVER IT CAN BE AFFORDED AND ITS VALUE IS EASILY UNDERSTATED: a trap that requires the plant to stop will be flushed less often than it should be.**

> **The operator weighs lost generation against a gradually filling trap, and defers.**

> **A duplicated trap — two compartments, either one isolatable for flushing while the other passes the flow — removes the conflict entirely, and it costs perhaps 60 per cent more than a single trap of the same total capacity.**

> **Given that the alternative is a trap that is habitually not flushed and therefore does not work, the duplication is usually money well spent, and the same argument applies with even more force to the settling basin behind it.**
tags: flushing head must be checked at high stage

examTip.trick: **Takes gravel and coarse sand right at the river**, with a short steep sluice back to it.
examTip.trap: **Check the flushing head at HIGH river stage** — that is when sediment is heaviest and available head is least. Designing on dry-season head guarantees failure.
examTip.mnemonic: **Remove sediment in stages, coarsest first** — intake, gravel trap, settling basin, and let the finest silt through. One structure cannot do all of it.

questions.stem: In designing a SETTLING BASIN, the required LENGTH is governed by the relationship between the flow-through time and the time a particle takes to fall to the floor. For a particle of settling velocity w in a basin of depth D carrying a mean velocity V, the minimum length is:
options: L = V D w
L = V w / D
L = V D / w
L = D / (V w)
questions.solution:
**L = V D / w.**

**The derivation, which is a single idea:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Time for a particle at the surface to reach the floor** | **t_fall = D / w** ← |
| **Time for the water to travel the basin's length** | **t_flow = L / V** ← |
| **For the particle to be caught, it must reach the floor before the water leaves** | **t_flow ≥ t_fall** ← |
| **So** | **L / V ≥ D / w** ← |
| **Giving** | **L ≥ V D / w** ← |

> **A DIMENSIONAL CHECK SETTLES THE CHOICE AMONG THE OPTIONS WITHOUT ANY DERIVATION AT ALL, and it is worth doing as a matter of course: L must come out in metres.**

> **V D / w has units (m/s)(m)/(m/s) = m. Correct.**

> **V D w gives (m/s)(m)(m/s) = m³/s². Wrong.**

> **V w / D gives (m/s)(m/s)/m = 1/s. Wrong. And D/(Vw) gives m/(m²/s²) = s²/m. Wrong.**

> **So three of the four options are eliminated on units alone, which takes about ten seconds and requires no understanding of settling at all — a technique worth applying to every formula-selection question before any thought is given to the physics.**

**WHAT THE RELATIONSHIP TELLS THE DESIGNER, WHICH IS MORE INTERESTING THAN THE FORMULA:**

| Observation | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **L is proportional to V** ← | **A slower basin can be shorter — hence basins are made WIDE and slow** ← |
| **L is proportional to D** ← | **A SHALLOWER basin can be shorter, since particles have less distance to fall** ← |
| **L is inversely proportional to w** ← | **Removing finer particles (small w) requires a disproportionately longer basin** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IT LEADS SOMEWHERE USEFUL: making a settling basin SHALLOWER makes it more effective for its length, not less.**

> **The particle has less far to fall, so it is caught sooner.**

> **Taken to its conclusion this gives the TUBE or PLATE SETTLER — a stack of closely spaced inclined plates within the basin, each acting as a very shallow settling zone.**

> **A basin fitted with plates at 50 mm spacing achieves in a short length what an open basin would need many times the length to achieve, because each particle need only fall 50 mm.**

> **The catch is that the settled material must slide down the inclined plates and be collected, and in a sediment-heavy Himalayan river the plates foul and the arrangement becomes a maintenance liability — which is why plate settlers are common in water treatment and rare in hydropower headworks.**

> **THE THIRD ROW EXPLAINS WHY A DESIGN PARTICLE SIZE MUST BE CHOSEN AND WHY THAT CHOICE DOMINATES THE COST: settling velocity falls roughly with the SQUARE of particle diameter in the fine range, by Stokes' law.**

> **So halving the design particle size quadruples the required basin length.**

> **Designing to remove 0.2 mm particles gives a basin of reasonable size; designing to remove 0.1 mm gives one four times as long, and 0.05 mm is out of the question.**

> **The design particle size is therefore chosen from the TURBINE's tolerance — which depends on the head, since abrasion goes with velocity — and it is the single parameter that determines whether the basin is a modest structure or the dominant cost of the headworks.**

examTip.trick: **L = V D / w** — the water must take longer to cross than the particle takes to fall.
examTip.trap: **Check the UNITS and three options die instantly** — only VD/w gives metres. Ten seconds, no physics needed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Halving the design particle size roughly quadruples the length** — settling velocity goes with diameter squared. That one choice sets the headworks cost.

questions.stem: A DIVERSION WEIR across a river for an ROR scheme differs from a storage dam principally in that the weir:
options: Creates no significant storage
Is always constructed of earthfill
Must be higher than a storage dam for the same river
Requires no foundation treatment
questions.solution:
**It creates NO SIGNIFICANT STORAGE — it raises the water level just enough to command the intake**, and passes the flood over its crest.

**The weir's purpose and what follows from it:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Its only job is to raise the water surface to the intake's sill level** ← | ← |
| **So it is low — typically a few metres** ← | ← |
| **The pool behind it is small and fills with sediment quickly** ← | **And this is accepted** ← |
| **Floods pass OVER the crest rather than through a gated spillway** ← | ← |
| **So the weir must be designed to be OVERTOPPED regularly, as a normal condition** ← | ← |
| **Which makes it a very different structure from a dam, despite the superficial similarity** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE DEFINING DESIGN CONDITION AND IT REORDERS THE WHOLE ANALYSIS: for a dam, overtopping is a failure; for a weir, it is Tuesday.**

> **So the weir's design concerns are the ones that arise from flow over and past it: scour at its downstream toe, uplift and seepage beneath it, impact from boulders rolling over it, and abrasion of its crest.**

> **Stability against overturning with a full reservoir, which dominates dam design, barely arises — the water depth is small and the thrust is modest.**

> **And the energy dissipation and scour protection downstream, which is an appendage on a dam, is on a weir the largest part of the structure.**

**THE CLASSIC FAILURE MODES OF A DIVERSION WEIR, WHICH FOLLOW DIRECTLY:**

| Failure | Note |
|---|---|
| **SCOUR at the downstream toe, undermining the structure** ← | **The commonest failure by a wide margin** ← |
| **PIPING beneath the weir through the alluvial bed** ← | **Checked by Bligh's or Lane's creep theory, or by a flow net** ← |
| **OUTFLANKING — the river cutting a new channel around the end of the weir** ← | **Which leaves the weir standing in a dry bed** ← |
| **Abrasion and impact damage to the crest** ← | ← |
| **Uplift lifting the floor slabs of the apron** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST DEMORALISING FAILURE AND IT IS FULLY PREVENTABLE: the river simply goes round.**

> **A weir built across a river in an alluvial plain raises the water, and the raised water finds the lowest available path — which may be around the weir's flank rather than over its crest, particularly if there is an old channel or a low terrace there.**

> **Once flow begins around the end, it scours a channel, the channel deepens, and within a season the river has abandoned the weir.**

> **The prevention is adequate flank protection — substantial guide bunds and abutment walls tied well into high ground, extended far enough upstream and downstream, and founded below the deepest scour expected.**

> **The temptation is always to shorten them, because they cross dry land and appear to do nothing, and shortening them is the reason outflanking happens.**

> **THE SECOND ROW'S CREEP THEORIES DESERVE A WORD SINCE THEY ARE THE EXAMINABLE TOOL: Bligh's creep theory treats the seepage path along the base as a simple length and requires that length to exceed C·H, where H is the head difference and C is a coefficient depending on the soil.**

> **Lane's WEIGHTED creep theory refines it by counting VERTICAL path lengths at full value and horizontal ones at a third, recognising that vertical cutoffs are more effective per metre than horizontal aprons.**

> **That single correction is Lane's whole contribution and it is the practically important one, because it tells the designer to spend material on sheet piles and cutoffs rather than on lengthening the floor.**

> **Khosla's theory supersedes both with a proper potential-flow treatment, and it is what is actually used for design — but Lane's weighting captures the essential insight in a form that can be remembered and applied by eye.**
tags: toe scour is the commonest failure

examTip.trick: **No storage — it just raises the level to command the intake, and floods pass over the crest.**
examTip.trap: **For a dam overtopping is failure; for a weir it is normal** — so the design concerns are scour, uplift, abrasion and piping, not overturning.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lane counts vertical creep at full value and horizontal at a third** — spend on cutoffs, not on lengthening the floor. And never shorten the guide bunds.

questions.stem: An UNDERSLUICE (scouring sluice) provided in a diversion weir immediately adjacent to the intake serves to:
options: Provide an additional water supply during floods
Measure the discharge diverted into the intake
Raise the water level further during the dry season
Maintain a deep, SEDIMENT-FREE pocket in front of the intake by drawing the
questions.solution:
**To maintain a DEEP, SEDIMENT-FREE POCKET in front of the intake** by drawing the accumulated bed material through a low-level opening and returning it to the river.

**How the undersluice and the intake work together:**

| Element | Function |
|---|---|
| **The UNDERSLUICE is a gated opening with its sill LOWER than the weir crest** ← | **Typically at or near the original river bed level** ← |
| **It sits immediately beside the intake** ← | ← |
| **A DIVIDE WALL separates the undersluice pocket from the rest of the weir** ← | **So the scouring flow is concentrated in the pocket rather than spread across the weir** ← |
| **Opening the sluice draws a strong current along the bed past the intake** ← | ← |
| **Which carries the deposited sediment through and back to the river** ← | ← |
| **Leaving a deep, clean pocket from which the intake draws** ← | ← |

> **THE DIVIDE WALL IS THE ELEMENT THAT MAKES THE ARRANGEMENT WORK AND IT IS EASILY DISMISSED AS A DETAIL: without it, the scouring flow spreads across the whole weir width and its velocity falls below what is needed to move the bed material.**

> **With it, the same discharge is confined to a narrow pocket and the velocity there is high enough to scour.**

> **The principle is that scouring depends on VELOCITY, and velocity is discharge divided by area — so concentrating the flow into a small area is what creates the velocity, and the wall is what concentrates it.**

> **The wall must extend far enough upstream to guide the approach flow and far enough downstream to keep the two flows separate past the weir, and shortening it, as with the guide bunds, defeats it.**

**THE OPERATING RULE MATTERS AS MUCH AS THE STRUCTURE AND IT IS WORTH STATING:**

| Practice | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sluice FREQUENTLY and briefly rather than rarely and at length** ← | **Freshly deposited sediment moves easily; consolidated sediment does not** ← |
| **Sluice during the MONSOON, when water is abundant and sediment is arriving** ← | ← |
| **Sluice BEFORE the pocket fills to the intake sill, not after** ← | ← |
| **Keep a record of the sluicing and of the pocket's bed level** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE OPERATING PRINCIPLE THAT MATTERS MOST AND IT IS THE OPPOSITE OF WHAT NATURALLY HAPPENS: sediment that has lain and consolidated for months resists scouring; sediment deposited last week moves at once.**

> **So a short sluice every few days through the monsoon keeps the pocket clean with very little water.**

> **A long sluice once a season, after the pocket has filled and compacted, uses a great deal of water and may not clear it at all.**

> **The natural tendency is the second, because each individual sluicing costs water and generation and is easy to postpone — and the postponement is self-defeating, since the deferred operation is both less effective and more expensive than the timely one would have been.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON WHAT HAPPENS WHEN THE POCKET IS LOST, SINCE IT IS THE SITUATION MANY OLDER SCHEMES ARE IN: once the pocket has filled with consolidated material to the intake sill, the intake begins drawing bed load directly.**

> **That material goes to the gravel trap and the settling basin, overwhelming both, and from there some of it reaches the turbines.**

> **So the failure propagates through the whole sediment-handling chain, and the symptom appears at the runner while the cause is at the intake.**

> **An operator seeing accelerated runner wear should therefore look first at the intake pocket's bed level rather than at the settling basin, because the basin is more likely to be overwhelmed than defective — which is a diagnostic habit worth having, since the expensive component is rarely where the problem started.**
tags: sediment pocket in front of the intake

examTip.trick: **A low-sill gated opening beside the intake** that scours the pocket clean and returns the sediment to the river.
examTip.trap: **The DIVIDE WALL is what makes it work** — it confines the flow so the velocity is high enough to scour. Spread across the weir, the same discharge moves nothing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sluice often and briefly, never rarely and long** — fresh sediment moves, consolidated sediment does not. Deferring makes it both harder and dearer.

questions.stem: The TRASH RACK at the entrance to a power intake is inclined and provided with a raking mechanism principally because:
options: An inclined rack is stronger than a vertical one
Inclination increases the velocity through the rack
A blocked rack imposes a differential head across itself that can collapse it
The inclination prevents fish from approaching the intake
questions.solution:
**A blocked rack imposes a DIFFERENTIAL HEAD across itself that can collapse it, and the blockage also reduces the net head and hence the output** — so the rack must be cleanable while the plant runs.

**The two consequences of a blocked rack:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **STRUCTURAL: a differential head builds across the rack** ← | **A clean rack passes water with a head loss of a few centimetres; a blocked one can develop metres** ← |
| **A rack designed for 0.3 m differential and subjected to 3 m will BUCKLE** ← | ← |
| **And the collapsed rack, plus everything it was holding, enters the waterway** ← | **Which can destroy a turbine** ← |
| **HYDRAULIC: the head lost across the rack is head lost to the turbine** ← | ← |
| **A metre of blockage loss on a 50 m head is 2 per cent of the output, continuously** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS DESCRIBE A FAILURE THAT HAS DESTROYED TURBINES AND IT IS WORTH TAKING SERIOUSLY BECAUSE THE MECHANISM IS SO UNFORGIVING: the rack's load grows as it blocks, and its blockage grows because it is blocked.**

> **A partially blocked rack passes the same flow through a smaller area, so the velocity through the remaining gaps rises, so debris is pressed more firmly into them and more is drawn in.**

> **The differential head rises, which increases the force holding the debris there.**

> **So blockage is self-reinforcing once it begins, and a rack can go from clear to critical within hours during a flood carrying floating debris.**

> **This is why the raking mechanism must work while the plant runs, and why a rack that can only be cleaned by shutting down and dewatering is inadequate for any river carrying debris.**

**THE DESIGN PROVISIONS THAT FOLLOW:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **Design the rack structurally for a large differential — commonly 2 to 5 m, not the clean-rack loss** ← | **So that a blockage bends the plant's schedule rather than the rack** ← |
| **A DIFFERENTIAL HEAD ALARM across the rack** ← | **The direct measurement of blockage, and the trigger for raking** ← |
| **A mechanical RAKE, travelling or fixed, discharging to a debris chute** ← | ← |
| **INCLINE the rack, typically 60 to 80 degrees from horizontal** ← | **So the rake can travel up it and the debris lifts clear of the water** ← |
| **Approach velocity kept low — commonly below 1.0 m/s** ← | **High approach velocity presses debris on and makes raking harder** ← |
| **A log boom or floating debris barrier upstream** ← | **Intercepting the large floating material before it reaches the rack** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS A DESIGN CHOICE THAT PAYS FOR ITSELF REPEATEDLY AND IS OFTEN COMPROMISED TO SAVE STRUCTURE COST: a low approach velocity means a large rack area, which means a wide intake.**

> **That costs money at construction and it is the first thing trimmed when the budget tightens.**

> **A rack sized for 1.5 or 2 m/s works perfectly in clear water and becomes unrakeable in debris, because the flow holds the trash against the bars faster than the rake can lift it away.**

> **So the approach velocity criterion is not conservatism; it is what makes the raking mechanism able to do its job, and cutting it transfers a capital saving into a permanent operating problem.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE CHEAPEST PROVISION OF ALL AND IT IS FREQUENTLY OMITTED: a log boom — a floating chain of timbers or pontoons across the approach — stops trees, branches and the large floating debris that does the most damage.**

> **It is inexpensive, it needs no power, and it fails safely by being overtopped.**

> **The material it collects must be removed periodically, which requires access and a means of lifting, and providing those at the design stage is what makes the boom useful rather than an obstruction that itself becomes a problem.**

examTip.trick: **Blockage builds a differential head that can buckle the rack, and it steals head from the turbine** — so it must be rakeable while running.
examTip.trap: **Design the rack structurally for 2-5 m differential, not the clean-rack loss** — blockage is self-reinforcing and can go critical in hours.
examTip.mnemonic: **Keep approach velocity under about 1 m/s** — above that the flow holds trash on the bars faster than the rake can lift it. Trimming this buys a permanent problem.

questions.stem: A settling basin is to remove particles of settling velocity 0.02 m/s. The basin is 3.5 m deep and carries a mean through-velocity of 0.25 m/s. The minimum theoretical length required is:
questions.solution:
**43.8 m.**

**Using L = V D / w:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Substituting** | **L = 0.25 × 3.5 ÷ 0.02** ← |
| ** ** | **0.25 × 3.5 = 0.875** ← |
| ** ** | **0.875 ÷ 0.02 = 43.75 m** ← |
| **So** | **L ≈ 43.8 m** ← |

> **A CHECK BY THE TWO TIMES IS WORTH DOING BECAUSE IT CONFIRMS THE PHYSICS RATHER THAN THE ARITHMETIC: the particle takes 3.5 ÷ 0.02 = 175 seconds to fall to the floor.**

> **In 175 seconds the water travels 0.25 × 175 = 43.75 m.**

> **So the basin must be at least that long, and the two routes agree.**

> **Working it as two times rather than as a formula also makes the answer intuitive — nearly three minutes of settling, at a walking-pace-quarter flow, needs about forty metres — and an intuition of that kind is what makes an error visible.**

**THE WORD 'MINIMUM THEORETICAL' IS DOING REAL WORK IN THIS QUESTION AND THE PRACTICAL LENGTH IS GREATER:**

| Allowance | Typical factor |
|---|---|
| **TURBULENCE keeps particles in suspension and reduces the effective settling** ← | **A factor of 1.5 to 2.0 on the theoretical length is usual** ← |
| **Non-uniform velocity distribution across the section** ← | **Some water travels faster than the mean and carries its particles further** ← |
| **Inlet and outlet TRANSITIONS, which do not settle effectively** ← | **Added to the length, not counted within it** ← |
| **Accumulated deposit reducing the depth and raising the velocity** ← | **Unless the basin is flushed before that matters** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE LARGEST CORRECTION AND IT IS WHY REAL BASINS ARE NEARLY TWICE THE THEORETICAL LENGTH: the derivation assumes the water moves in smooth parallel layers and the particle falls steadily through them.**

> **Real flow is turbulent, and turbulent eddies carry particles back up as readily as down.**

> **Settling still occurs because there is a net downward drift, but it occurs more slowly than the quiescent settling velocity implies.**

> **Camp's and Dobbins' work provides the theoretical treatment, and for design purposes the practical answer is the empirical factor — so the 43.8 m theoretical basin becomes perhaps 70 to 90 m in construction, plus transitions.**

> **THE SECOND ROW POINTS TO THE DESIGN RESPONSE THAT ADDRESSES BOTH PROBLEMS AT ONCE: the velocity distribution should be made as UNIFORM as possible.**

> **A long gradual inlet transition, a distribution arrangement across the width, and a basin whose width does not change abruptly all serve this.**

> **A basin fed by an abrupt widening develops a jet down its centre and dead zones at its sides, so much of its plan area does no settling at all and the water that does pass through moves far faster than the nominal mean.**

> **That single defect can halve a basin's effectiveness, and it is entirely a matter of inlet geometry — which makes the inlet transition, rather than the basin's length, the most cost-effective place to spend attention on a settling basin design.**

examTip.trick: **0.25 × 3.5 ÷ 0.02 = 43.75 m.** Or as times: 175 s to fall, 43.75 m travelled in that time.
examTip.trap: **'Minimum theoretical' — a real basin is 1.5 to 2 times longer** for turbulence, plus the inlet and outlet transitions on top.
examTip.mnemonic: **A bad inlet transition halves the basin** — an abrupt widening makes a central jet and dead sides. Cheapest place to spend design attention.

questions.stem: A settling basin designed for CONTINUOUS (Dufour or Bieri type) flushing differs from an intermittently flushed basin in that it:
options: Removes a finer fraction of sediment than an intermittent basin can
Requires no flushing water at all
Withdraws a small continuous flow from hoppers along the basin floor
Operates only during the dry season
questions.solution:
**It withdraws a small CONTINUOUS flow from hoppers along the basin floor, carrying the settled sediment away without interrupting generation** — at the cost of that flow being permanently unavailable for power.

**The two flushing philosophies compared:**

| Aspect | INTERMITTENT flushing | CONTINUOUS flushing |
|---|---|---|
| **Operation** | **Isolate a bay, drain it, scour the deposit out, refill** ← | **A steady small withdrawal from floor hoppers, always running** ← |
| **Generation** | **Interrupted, unless the basin is duplicated** ← | **Uninterrupted** ← |
| **Water used** | **A large volume, briefly** ← | **A small percentage, continuously — typically 2 to 5 per cent of the flow** ← |
| **Structure** | **Simpler — bays, gates, a flushing channel** ← | **More complex — hoppers, a collector conduit, control** ← |
| **Reliability** | **High — few moving parts** ← | **Depends on the hoppers and conduit not blocking** ← |
| **Operator dependence** | **HIGH — someone must decide and act** ← | **Low — it runs by itself** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE CONTINUOUS SYSTEM'S STRONGEST ARGUMENT AND IT ADDRESSES THE FAILURE MODE IDENTIFIED THROUGHOUT THIS SUBCHAPTER: intermittent flushing depends on someone choosing to forgo generation, and that choice is deferred.**

> **A continuous system removes the decision entirely.**

> **The water is taken whether anyone attends to it or not, so the basin stays clean without anybody having to sacrifice anything on any particular day.**

> **That is a more robust design in an organisational sense, and organisational robustness is often what determines whether a sediment system actually works over decades — which makes this a case where the more complex structure may be the more reliable arrangement in practice, contrary to the usual presumption.**

**THE COST OF THE CONTINUOUS SYSTEM DESERVES TO BE STATED PLAINLY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Say 3 per cent of the design flow is withdrawn continuously** ← | ← |
| **That is 3 per cent of the energy, every hour of every year** ← | ← |
| **On a 20 MW plant at a 0.55 capacity factor, about 2.9 GWh a year** ← | **20 × 8.76 × 0.55 × 0.03** ← |
| **Which at any realistic tariff is a substantial annual sum** ← | ← |
| **Against which must be set the generation NOT lost to intermittent flushing** ← | ← |
| **And the runner wear NOT suffered because the basin actually stays clean** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST TWO ROWS ARE WHERE THE COMPARISON IS ACTUALLY DECIDED AND THEY ARE THE HARDEST TO QUANTIFY: the continuous system's 3 per cent is visible, certain and continuous, while the intermittent system's losses are intermittent, uncertain and easy to overlook.**

> **So the comparison is systematically biased against the continuous system by the visibility of its cost.**

> **An honest comparison must value the intermittent system's shutdowns at their realistic frequency, and must include the runner refurbishment cost that follows from a basin that is flushed less often than it should be.**

> **When that is done, continuous flushing frequently wins on a high-sediment river, and it loses on a clean one — which is the sensible answer, and it is not the answer that a comparison of the visible costs alone produces.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON WHAT NEITHER SYSTEM DOES: both remove the sand the basin was designed to catch, and neither removes the fine silt that passes.**

> **On a Himalayan river that silt contains a substantial quartz fraction, and quartz is harder than turbine steel.**

> **So the residual abrasion is accepted as a design consequence, and it is managed at the turbine rather than at the headworks — by hard coatings on the runner, by replaceable wearing parts, by designing for periodic refurbishment, and by accepting a runner life measured in years rather than decades.**

> **That acceptance should be explicit in the project's financial model, and a model that assumes a thirty-year runner on a Himalayan ROR scheme has omitted one of the larger operating costs the plant will actually face.**
tags: residual silt managed at the turbine

examTip.trick: **A steady small withdrawal from floor hoppers** — typically 2-5% of the flow, taken continuously, with no shutdown.
examTip.trap: **Its real advantage is removing the OPERATOR DECISION** — intermittent flushing requires someone to forgo generation, and that gets deferred.
examTip.mnemonic: **Its cost is visible and the alternative's is not** — so honest comparison must price the intermittent system's shutdowns and the extra runner wear.

questions.stem: In the layout of an ROR headworks, the FOREBAY at the downstream end of the headrace serves to:
options: Provide the final small reserve of water that absorbs the surge when the turbines change load
Act as the settling basin for fine sediment
Measure the discharge entering the penstock
Increase the head available to the turbines
questions.solution:
**To provide the final small reserve of water that absorbs the SURGE when the turbines change load, to keep the penstock intake submerged, and to act as the last point at which floating debris and excess water can be removed before the penstock.**

**The forebay's several functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **SURGE absorption on load change** ← | **When the turbines close, the headrace flow has nowhere to go until it slows — the forebay level rises to accommodate it** ← |
| **A reserve for load INCREASE** ← | **When the turbines open, the penstock draws more than the headrace is yet delivering, and the forebay makes up the difference** ← |
| **Maintaining SUBMERGENCE over the penstock intake** ← | **Preventing air-entraining vortices** ← |
| **A SPILLWAY to discharge excess water safely** ← | **Which is where the headrace flow goes when the plant shuts down** ← |
| **A final TRASH RACK before the penstock** ← | ← |
| **A GATE to close the penstock for maintenance** ← | ← |
| **Some final settling of any remaining coarse material** ← | **Incidental, not its purpose** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE FUNCTION WHOSE OMISSION CAUSES THE MOST DRAMATIC FAILURE AND IT IS WORTH THINKING THROUGH: when the plant trips, the turbines stop taking water within seconds.**

> **The headrace canal, however, is still delivering its full design flow, and a canal several kilometres long cannot be stopped quickly.**

> **That water arrives at the forebay with nowhere to go.**

> **Without an adequate forebay spillway it overtops the forebay walls or backs up and overtops the headrace canal along its length — and an overtopping canal on a hillside erodes its own embankment and can trigger a landslide.**

> **So the forebay spillway must be sized for the FULL design flow, not for some fraction, because a full and sudden rejection is a routine event that will occur many times a year.**

**THE SURGE FUNCTION DESERVES A NOTE ON WHERE IT APPLIES AND WHERE SOMETHING ELSE IS NEEDED:**

| Arrangement | Surge provision |
|---|---|
| **Open headrace CANAL ending in a forebay** ← | **The FOREBAY itself, with a free water surface open to atmosphere** ← |
| **Pressure TUNNEL leading to a penstock** ← | **A SURGE TANK, which serves the identical purpose for a closed conduit** ← |

> **THE TWO ARE THE SAME DEVICE IN DIFFERENT CLOTHING AND RECOGNISING THAT MAKES BOTH EASIER TO UNDERSTAND: each provides a free water surface close to the turbines, into which the conduit's momentum can discharge.**

> **A long conduit full of moving water has a great deal of momentum, and closing a valve at its end abruptly would generate a severe water hammer pressure.**

> **Providing a free surface near the valve gives that momentum somewhere to go — the water rises in the forebay or the surge tank instead of compressing against the closed valve.**

> **So both structures do the same job, and the choice between them is simply whether the conveyance is an open channel or a closed pressure conduit.**

> **THE THIRD ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE SETS THE FOREBAY'S MINIMUM DEPTH AND IT IS A SPECIFIC HYDRAULIC CRITERION RATHER THAN A JUDGEMENT: the submergence over the penstock intake must exceed the depth at which an air-entraining vortex forms.**

> **Several empirical criteria exist, relating the required submergence to the intake velocity and diameter — Gordon's formula being the commonly quoted one.**

> **Insufficient submergence draws air into the penstock, and air in a penstock causes pressure fluctuations, vibration, loss of efficiency and, in bad cases, damage when a pocket of air passes through the turbine.**

> **Since the criterion applies at the LOWEST forebay level, which occurs during the largest load increase at the lowest river flow, that is the combination the check must use — and checking it at normal level, which is the natural thing to do, passes a design that will draw air exactly when it is working hardest.**
tags: forebay spillway sized for full flow
forebay and surge tank are analogous

examTip.trick: **Surge absorption, submergence, spilling excess, final trash rack and gate** — the buffer between a slow canal and fast-acting turbines.
examTip.trap: **Size the forebay spillway for the FULL design flow** — on a trip the canal keeps delivering, and an overtopping hillside canal can trigger a landslide.
examTip.mnemonic: **Forebay is to a canal what a SURGE TANK is to a pressure tunnel** — a free surface near the turbines for the conduit's momentum to discharge into.

questions.stem: In choosing between an open HEADRACE CANAL and a pressure TUNNEL for the conveyance of an ROR scheme in mountainous terrain, the tunnel is often preferred despite its higher unit cost because it:
options: Takes a direct route through the ridges rather than contouring around every side valley
Requires no surge protection at its downstream end
Always has a lower head loss per kilometre than a canal
Can be constructed without any geological investigation
questions.solution:
**It takes a DIRECT route through the ridges rather than contouring around every side valley** — and it is immune to landslides, rockfall, erosion and the land acquisition that a hillside canal on unstable slopes entails.

**The comparison in mountainous terrain:**

| Aspect | OPEN CANAL | PRESSURE TUNNEL |
|---|---|---|
| **Route** | **Must CONTOUR — following every side valley in and out** ← | **DIRECT, straight through the ridges** ← |
| **Length for the same two endpoints** | **Often 2 to 3 times the tunnel's** ← | **The short route** ← |
| **Cost per metre** | **Low** ← | **High** ← |
| **Total cost** | **Can exceed the tunnel's, because of the length** ← | ← |
| **Vulnerability** | **Landslides, rockfall, erosion, washout at every stream crossing** ← | **Essentially none once lined** ← |
| **Land acquisition** | **A strip along the hillside, often through cultivated or settled land** ← | **Only at the portals** ← |
| **Maintenance** | **Continuous — clearing slips, repairing linings, desilting** ← | **Minimal** ← |
| **Construction risk** | **Low and predictable** ← | **HIGH — geology can differ from what was expected** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE DECISIVE ARITHMETIC AND IT IS FREQUENTLY MISJUDGED BY COMPARING UNIT RATES: a tunnel that costs four times as much per metre and is one third as long costs only a third more in total.**

> **And in deeply dissected Himalayan terrain the length ratio can be greater still, because a canal must enter and leave every tributary valley while a tunnel ignores them.**

> **So the comparison must always be made on the TOTAL cost of the whole conveyance, never on rates per metre, and the intuition that tunnels are expensive is derived from the rate and is often wrong about the total.**

> **THE FIFTH AND SEVENTH ROWS CARRY THE ARGUMENT FURTHER AND THEY ARE WHERE NEPAL'S EXPERIENCE HAS BEEN DECISIVE: a hillside canal in the Himalaya is exposed to the mountain for its whole life.**

> **Monsoon slips bury it, undercut it, and wash it away; each event costs generation as well as repair; and the repairs themselves are hard to reach and seasonally constrained.**

> **Several Nepali schemes have suffered repeated and expensive canal failures, and the industry has moved decisively toward tunnels for that reason rather than on first-cost grounds.**

> **So the availability and the maintenance cost, over decades, dominate a comparison that a construction-cost estimate alone would decide the other way.**

**THE COUNTERWEIGHT IS REAL AND DESERVES ITS OWN STATEMENT:**

| Risk | Note |
|---|---|
| **GEOLOGICAL uncertainty is the tunnel's great hazard** ← | **A fault zone, squeezing ground, high water inflow or a mixed face can stop progress for months** ← |
| **Himalayan geology is young, fractured and highly variable** ← | ← |
| **So tunnel cost and time overruns are common and can be severe** ← | ← |
| **And the risk is hard to transfer — contractors price it heavily or decline it** ← | ← |
| **The mitigation is INVESTIGATION: boreholes, geophysics, and probing ahead of the face** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE ONLY REAL ANSWER AND IT RETURNS TO THE POINT MADE ABOUT INVESTIGATION GENERALLY: the uncertainty cannot be eliminated and it can be greatly reduced, and the reduction is cheap relative to what it protects.**

> **Probing ahead of the tunnel face — drilling a long hole in advance of the excavation — converts a surprise into a forecast, and a forecast permits the ground treatment to be prepared before the face reaches the bad ground rather than after it has collapsed into it.**

> **That practice is standard in Himalayan tunnelling now and it was not always, and the schemes that learned it the hard way did so at considerable cost.**

> **It is worth noting the shape of the trade honestly: the canal has high, certain, recurring costs and low construction risk; the tunnel has low recurring costs and high construction risk — so the choice is partly about which kind of risk the project's financing can absorb, and a thinly capitalised developer may rationally prefer the canal even where the tunnel has the better expected outcome.**

examTip.trick: **A tunnel goes straight through the ridges; a canal contours round every side valley** — often two or three times the length.
examTip.trap: **Compare TOTAL cost, never cost per metre** — four times the rate over a third of the length is only a third more in total.
examTip.mnemonic: **Canal: certain recurring cost, low build risk. Tunnel: low recurring cost, high geological risk.** Which risk the financing can absorb may decide it.

questions.stem: A CROSS-DRAINAGE structure on a hillside headrace canal is required wherever the canal crosses a natural stream or gully. The arrangement most commonly adopted on a small Himalayan scheme is:
options: A siphon carrying the canal beneath the stream bed
A SUPER-PASSAGE carrying the stream over the canal, or a culvert carrying it under
Allowing the stream to discharge directly into the canal to augment its flow
Diverting the stream permanently into a new channel
questions.solution:
**A SUPER-PASSAGE carrying the stream OVER the canal, or a culvert carrying it under** — because the stream is a flashy, debris-laden torrent whose flow must be kept entirely separate from the canal water.

**Why the flows must be kept separate:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **The side stream is FLASHY — it can rise from nothing to a torrent in minutes** ← | ← |
| **It carries BOULDERS, gravel and debris** ← | ← |
| **Admitting it would overtop the canal within minutes of a cloudburst** ← | ← |
| **And would fill the canal, and then the settling basin, with the material it carries** ← | ← |
| **Undoing at a stroke everything the headworks did to exclude sediment** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE POINT MOST WORTH GRASPING AND IT IS WHY OPTION (c) IS SO WRONG DESPITE SOUNDING ECONOMICAL: a scheme goes to great expense at its headworks to exclude sediment, and a single unprotected stream crossing readmits it downstream of every one of those defences.**

> **The gravel trap and the settling basin are upstream; the stream enters below them; so its load goes straight to the penstock and the turbine.**

> **A scheme can therefore have an exemplary headworks and a badly abraded runner, and the cause is a culvert somebody omitted three kilometres along the canal.**

> **So every crossing, however small the gully looks in the dry season, must be a proper structure — and 'it only flows in the monsoon' is a description of exactly when the damage would occur, not a reason to omit the crossing.**

**THE FOUR CROSSING ARRANGEMENTS AND WHEN EACH APPLIES:**

| Structure | Arrangement | Used when |
|---|---|---|
| **AQUEDUCT** ← | **The CANAL is carried over the stream on a structure** ← | **The canal is higher than the stream bed** ← |
| **SUPER-PASSAGE** ← | **The STREAM is carried over the canal** ← | **The stream bed is higher than the canal** ← |
| **CULVERT (canal culvert)** ← | **The stream passes UNDER the canal in a pipe or box** ← | **The stream is small and the canal can be carried over it in fill** ← |
| **INVERTED SIPHON (canal siphon)** ← | **The CANAL drops under the stream bed in a pressure conduit and rises again** ← | **The canal is lower than the stream bed** ← |

> **THE MEMORY DEVICE IS TO ASK WHICH ONE GOES ON TOP AND WHETHER IT IS UNDER PRESSURE: an aqueduct and a super-passage are both open channels carried across, differing only in which flow is carried; a culvert and a siphon are both closed conduits, differing likewise.**

> **The word 'aqueduct' always means the CANAL is carried — the water being conducted is the canal's.**

> **The word 'super-passage' means something passes over the canal, and that something is the natural stream.**

> **And 'siphon' in this context means the canal dives under, running full and under pressure, which is why an inverted siphon must be watertight and must be designed for the internal pressure while an aqueduct need not.**

> **A DETAILING POINT WORTH CARRYING ON SMALL SCHEMES: a super-passage's chute must discharge clear of the canal's downstream embankment, and the discharge point must be protected.**

> **A stream dropped onto an unprotected hillside immediately below the canal will erode a gully there, and the gully will work back and undermine the canal from below.**

> **So the structure must carry the stream not merely across the canal but clear of everything the canal depends on, with an energy dissipator and a lined channel taking it down to the valley.**

> **That trailing element is frequently omitted as being outside the crossing proper, and its omission has undermined more hillside canals than the crossings themselves have failed.**
tags: cross drainage on a headrace canal

examTip.trick: **Keep the torrent and the canal water entirely separate** — super-passage over, or culvert under.
examTip.trap: **Admitting a side stream readmits sediment BELOW the gravel trap and settling basin** — an exemplary headworks and a ruined runner, caused by one missing culvert.
examTip.mnemonic: **Aqueduct carries the CANAL; super-passage carries the STREAM** — and a siphon is the canal diving under, so it alone is a pressure conduit.

questions.stem: A headrace canal is to carry 6 m³/s. It is a trapezoidal concrete-lined channel with a bed width of 2.5 m, side slopes of 1:1 and a depth of flow of 1.5 m. The mean velocity of flow is:
questions.solution:
**1.00 m/s.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Area of a trapezoid** | **A = (b + zy) y, with z = 1 for 1:1 side slopes** ← |
| ** ** | **A = (2.5 + 1 × 1.5) × 1.5** ← |
| ** ** | **A = 4.0 × 1.5 = 6.0 m²** ← |
| **Velocity** | **V = Q / A = 6 ÷ 6.0 = 1.00 m/s** ← |

> **THE AREA FORMULA IS THE ONLY THING THAT CAN GO WRONG HERE AND THE COMMONEST ERROR GIVES OPTION (a): using A = b·y + z·y², which is 2.5 × 1.5 + 1 × 2.25 = 6.0 — the same answer, correctly.**

> **The error that gives 3.75 m² and hence 1.6 m/s is using the bed width alone, A = b·y = 3.75, forgetting the triangular side portions entirely.**

> **So the check is to visualise the section: a rectangle 2.5 m wide plus two triangles each 1.5 m wide at the top and 1.5 m deep, contributing ½ × 1.5 × 1.5 × 2 = 2.25 m².**

> **Total 3.75 + 2.25 = 6.0 m², confirming the formula and the arithmetic together.**

**WHETHER 1.0 m/s IS AN APPROPRIATE DESIGN VELOCITY IS THE MORE INTERESTING QUESTION:**

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **MINIMUM velocity — to prevent sediment depositing in the canal** ← | **Usually 0.6 to 0.9 m/s for a canal carrying settled water** ← |
| **MAXIMUM velocity — to prevent erosion of the lining** ← | **Concrete lining tolerates 2 to 2.5 m/s; higher with good concrete** ← |
| **And the HEAD LOSS consideration** ← | **Higher velocity means more friction loss, and head is the product's value** ← |
| **So a power canal is designed toward the LOW end** ← | **1.0 to 1.5 m/s is typical** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS EXPLAIN A DIFFERENCE FROM IRRIGATION PRACTICE THAT IS WORTH NOTING: an irrigation canal is designed for a non-silting non-scouring velocity, and head loss is of secondary concern because the head is not being sold.**

> **A POWER canal's head loss is a direct and permanent loss of revenue, so it is designed slower and larger than an irrigation canal carrying the same discharge.**

> **The extra excavation and lining are paid for once and the head saved is earned every hour for fifty years.**

> **So the same hydraulic problem gives a different answer depending on what the head is worth, which is the same conclusion reached for the penstock diameter and is the general principle behind sizing any conveyance whose head has a price.**

**A NOTE ON THE FREEBOARD, WHICH THE QUESTION'S GEOMETRY OMITS AND A DESIGN MUST NOT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The canal must be built deeper than the flow depth** ← | ← |
| **Freeboard of 0.3 m for a small canal up to 0.75 m or more for a large one** ← | ← |
| **It accommodates wave action, surges on load rejection, and inflow from rain and minor slips** ← | ← |
| **On a hillside canal it is also the margin against a partial blockage** ← | ← |

> **The last row is the one that matters most on a Himalayan canal, and it argues for generosity: a slip that partly blocks the canal raises the water level upstream of it.**

> **With adequate freeboard the canal continues to flow past the obstruction, at reduced capacity, until someone clears it.**

> **With minimal freeboard it overtops immediately, and the overtopping water erodes the downhill embankment and takes the canal out entirely.**

> **So freeboard on a hillside canal converts a maintenance problem into a maintenance problem, rather than converting it into a reconstruction — and it is very cheap, being only a little extra height on a lining that is being built anyway.**

examTip.trap: **Forgetting the side triangles gives 3.75 m² and 1.6 m/s** — visualise the rectangle plus two triangles as a check.
examTip.mnemonic: **A POWER canal is designed slower than an irrigation canal** — its head loss is sold revenue, so the extra section pays for itself for fifty years.

questions.stem: The ANCHOR BLOCKS provided at bends and at intervals along an exposed surface penstock are required to:
options: Support the penstock's weight only, the sliding supports between them carrying nothing
Insulate the penstock from ground vibration
Resist the unbalanced forces at changes of direction
Allow the penstock to be dismantled in sections
questions.solution:
**To resist the UNBALANCED FORCES at changes of direction** — chiefly the resultant of the internal pressure acting on the bend, together with the component of the pipe's weight along the slope and the friction of thermal movement.

**The forces an anchor block must carry:**

| Force | Note |
|---|---|
| **The resultant of INTERNAL PRESSURE at a bend** ← | **Usually by far the largest — pressure times area, resolved through the bend angle** ← |
| **The momentum change of the flowing water at the bend** ← | **Small compared with the pressure term at hydropower velocities** ← |
| **The component of the PIPE AND WATER WEIGHT along the slope** ← | **Substantial on a steep penstock** ← |
| **FRICTION at the sliding supports as the pipe expands and contracts** ← | ← |
| **Forces from expansion joints** ← | ← |
| **Wind and seismic forces** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW DOMINATES AND ITS MAGNITUDE IS WORTH APPRECIATING BECAUSE IT IS LARGER THAN INTUITION SUGGESTS: a 1.5 m diameter penstock under 300 m of head has a pressure of about 2.94 MPa acting on an area of 1.77 m², which is 5,200 kN on each face of a bend.**

> **At a 90-degree bend the resultant of the two is 5,200 × √2 ≈ 7,350 kN — about 750 tonnes.**

> **An anchor block resisting that by its own weight alone would need to be enormous, so the blocks are keyed into rock or founded on piles wherever possible.**

> **And the same arithmetic explains why bends in a penstock are minimised in the first place: every bend is a large force that must be caught, and a straight penstock needs anchors only for the slope component.**

**THE DIVISION OF LABOUR BETWEEN ANCHORS AND SLIDING SUPPORTS IS THE POINT OF OPTION (a) AND IT DESERVES SETTING OUT:**

| Element | Carries |
|---|---|
| **ANCHOR BLOCKS** ← | **All LONGITUDINAL forces — the pipe is rigidly fixed to the block** ← |
| **SLIDING (saddle) SUPPORTS between them** ← | **Only the VERTICAL weight, while permitting free longitudinal movement** ← |
| **EXPANSION JOINTS, one between each pair of anchors** ← | **Allow the length between anchors to change with temperature without stressing the pipe** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ELEMENT THAT MAKES THE ARRANGEMENT WORK AND ITS OMISSION OR SEIZURE CAUSES REAL DAMAGE: a steel penstock 100 m long changes length by about 12 mm for every 10 °C of temperature change.**

> **An exposed penstock on a Himalayan hillside sees a daily range of 20 or 30 degrees and a seasonal range considerably more.**

> **Restrained completely, that thermal strain would generate stresses of the order of 24 MPa per 10 °C — enough to matter greatly when added to the pressure stresses.**

> **So an expansion joint between each pair of anchors lets the pipe breathe, and a seized expansion joint transfers those forces into the anchors and the pipe wall, which is why the joints' packing is a maintenance item rather than a fit-and-forget detail.**

> **A FINAL NOTE ON WHY PENSTOCKS ARE BURIED WHERE POSSIBLE, SINCE IT FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM ALL OF THIS: a buried penstock is held by the surrounding ground, which restrains it continuously rather than at points.**

> **Its temperature is nearly constant, so thermal movement almost disappears and expansion joints become unnecessary.**

> **It is protected from rockfall, landslide, vandalism and the sun, and it does not sever the hillside's access and grazing.**

> **Against that it cannot be inspected, and corrosion on its outside proceeds unseen — which is why a buried penstock needs a good external coating, cathodic protection where the ground is aggressive, and a means of monitoring, and why the choice between buried and exposed is a genuine one rather than a foregone conclusion.**

examTip.trick: **Unbalanced longitudinal forces — chiefly pressure × area resolved through the bend** — plus the slope weight component and support friction.
examTip.trap: **Sliding supports carry the WEIGHT only; anchors carry everything longitudinal.** One expansion joint between each pair of anchors lets the pipe breathe.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 1.5 m pipe under 300 m head pushes about 750 tonnes at a right-angle bend** — which is why bends are minimised and anchors are keyed into rock.

questions.stem: WATER HAMMER in a penstock is the pressure rise caused by a rapid change in flow velocity. Its severity is reduced principally by:
options: Increasing the penstock's wall thickness
Reducing the flow velocity in the penstock
Lengthening the closure time of the turbine's guide vanes or valve
Increasing the penstock's diameter alone
questions.solution:
**Lengthening the CLOSURE TIME of the turbine's guide vanes or valve, and by providing a SURGE TANK close to the powerhouse to shorten the length of conduit in which the pressure wave must travel.**

**The two governing relationships:**

| Case | Expression | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **SUDDEN closure (t < 2L/a)** | **Δh = a·ΔV / g — the JOUKOWSKY equation** ← | **The maximum possible rise; independent of closure time** ← |
| **GRADUAL closure (t > 2L/a)** | **Δh ≈ 2LV / (g·t) — the Michaud/Allievi form** ← | **Inversely proportional to closure time** ← |

> **THE CRITICAL TIME 2L/a IS THE DIVIDING LINE AND IT IS THE KEY IDEA: it is the time for the pressure wave to travel to the reservoir and back.**

> **If the valve shuts before the reflected wave returns, the valve never 'knows' the reservoir is there and the full Joukowsky pressure develops.**

> **If closure takes longer, the returning negative wave arrives while the valve is still closing and progressively relieves the pressure.**

> **So the whole art of water hammer control is to make the closure slower than the round-trip wave travel time, by a comfortable margin — and the wave speed a in a steel penstock is around 1,000 to 1,200 m/s, so a 600 m penstock has a critical time of about 1.1 seconds and a closure of 5 or 6 seconds is comfortably gradual.**

**THE SURGE TANK'S ROLE IS TO SHORTEN L AND THAT IS ITS WHOLE PURPOSE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A surge tank provides a FREE WATER SURFACE partway along the conduit** ← | ← |
| **The pressure wave reflects at that free surface, exactly as at a reservoir** ← | ← |
| **So the effective L becomes the distance from the TURBINE to the SURGE TANK** ← | **Not to the reservoir** ← |
| **On a scheme with a 4 km tunnel and a 500 m penstock, that reduces L eightfold** ← | ← |
| **And the water hammer pressure falls correspondingly** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW SHOWS WHY THE SURGE TANK IS PLACED AS CLOSE TO THE POWERHOUSE AS THE TOPOGRAPHY ALLOWS, and it is a straightforward consequence of the formula.**

> **The tank must also be tall enough that the surge does not overflow it and that its downsurge does not draw air into the conduit, and it must be at a point where the ground is high enough to contain the upsurge — which in practice means it goes at the top of the penstock, where the pressure tunnel ends and the steep descent begins.**

> **That location is usually a topographic feature rather than a free choice, and the tunnel's alignment is often set partly by where a surge tank can be accommodated.**

> **THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE NOT WRONG SO MUCH AS ADDRESSING THE WRONG THING, AND THE DISTINCTION IS WORTH DRAWING: a thicker wall does not reduce the pressure, it merely withstands it.**

> **A larger diameter reduces the velocity V, which does reduce Δh — so option (d) helps a little, by the route option (b) names.**

> **But the velocity is set by the economic diameter calculation and cannot be reduced much without cost, and it appears linearly while closure time also appears linearly and can be changed by a factor of ten at almost no cost.**

> **So the effective measures are the ones that act on the TIME and the LENGTH, which is why they are the answer — and the closure time is limited in turn by the governor's need to control overspeed, which brings in the flywheel effect and sets up the classic conflict between pressure rise and speed rise that turbine governing must resolve.**
tags: pressure rise versus speed rise conflict

examTip.trick: **Slow the closure and shorten the conduit** — Δh = aΔV/g if closure beats 2L/a, and about 2LV/gt if it does not.
examTip.trap: **2L/a is the wave's round trip to the reservoir** — close faster than that and the valve never learns the reservoir exists, giving full Joukowsky pressure.
examTip.mnemonic: **A surge tank reflects the wave, so L is measured to the TANK, not the reservoir** — hence it sits as close to the powerhouse as the topography allows.

questions.stem: The economic diameter of a penstock is the diameter at which:
options: The velocity in the penstock equals 4 m/s
The head loss equals 5 per cent of the gross head
The wall thickness is minimised
The sum of the annual cost of the pipe and the annual value of the energy lost to friction is a minimum
questions.solution:
**The sum of the ANNUAL COST OF THE PIPE and the ANNUAL VALUE OF THE ENERGY LOST to friction is a MINIMUM** — a larger pipe costing more and losing less, a smaller one the reverse.

**The structure of the optimisation:**

| Component | Behaviour with diameter D |
|---|---|
| **Annual capital charge on the pipe** | **INCREASES with D — roughly with D to the power 1.5 for a pipe of constant pressure rating** ← |
| **Annual value of energy lost to friction** | **DECREASES steeply with D — head loss varies as 1/D⁵ for a given discharge** ← |
| **Their SUM** | **Falls, reaches a minimum, then rises** ← |
| **The minimum is the economic diameter** | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW'S 1/D⁵ IS THE RELATIONSHIP THAT MAKES THE OPTIMISATION SHARP AND IT IS WORTH SEEING WHERE IT COMES FROM: by Darcy-Weisbach, h = f L V² / (2gD).**

> **For a fixed discharge Q, V = Q/A ∝ 1/D², so V² ∝ 1/D⁴.**

> **Substituting: h ∝ (1/D⁴)/D = 1/D⁵.**

> **So increasing the diameter by 15 per cent halves the head loss, which is why enlarging a penstock is such an effective way of recovering head and why the optimum is reached quite quickly as D grows.**

**WHAT MOVES THE OPTIMUM, WHICH IS THE PRACTICALLY USEFUL PART:**

| Factor | Effect on the economic diameter |
|---|---|
| **A HIGHER energy tariff** ← | **LARGER pipe — the head saved is worth more** ← |
| **A higher steel price** ← | **SMALLER pipe** ← |
| **A higher discount rate** ← | **SMALLER pipe — future energy is worth less today than present steel costs** ← |
| **A higher plant capacity factor** ← | **LARGER pipe — the loss is incurred for more hours a year** ← |
| **A LONGER penstock** ← | **LARGER pipe — the loss is proportional to length while the cost per metre is not affected** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED AND IT HAS A CLEAR CONSEQUENCE: a peaking plant running 1,500 hours a year loses far less energy to friction than a base-load plant running 6,000 hours, even at the same rated flow.**

> **So the peaking plant's economic diameter is smaller, and applying a base-load plant's sizing rule to it over-invests in pipe.**

> **This is another instance of the general point that a hydraulic component's correct size depends on how the plant will be OPERATED, not only on its rated conditions.**

> **And it is a reason to settle the operating regime before sizing the waterway, rather than treating the regime as something decided later by the system operator.**

> **SEVERAL EMPIRICAL FORMULAE EXIST FOR A FIRST ESTIMATE AND THEY ARE WORTH HAVING, WITH THE PROPER CAVEAT: expressions such as D = 0.72 Q^0.5 for low head, or Fahlbusch's and Sarkaria's formulae relating D to P and H, give a starting diameter within perhaps 10 per cent.**

> **They embed particular assumptions about energy prices, steel prices and discount rates prevailing where and when they were derived.**

> **So they are legitimate for a first pass and should never be the final answer, because the underlying economics have moved since and differ between countries.**

> **The proper procedure is to cost three or four candidate diameters explicitly, compute the annual energy loss for each from the actual flow duration curve and tariff, and plot the total — which takes an afternoon and gives an answer that can be defended, unlike a formula whose provenance nobody in the room can state.**
tags: tariff and discount rate move the optimum
empirical formulae as a first pass

examTip.trick: **Minimise annual pipe cost plus annual value of friction losses** — bigger pipe costs more and loses less.
examTip.trap: **Head loss goes as 1/D⁵** — so 15% more diameter halves the loss. From h ∝ V²/D with V ∝ 1/D².
examTip.mnemonic: **A peaking plant needs a SMALLER pipe than a base-load one** — fewer hours of loss. Size the waterway after deciding the operating regime, not before.

questions.stem: A penstock of 1.2 m internal diameter is to withstand a maximum internal pressure of 3.0 MPa including water hammer allowance. Taking the permissible hoop stress in the steel as 120 MPa and ignoring corrosion allowance and joint efficiency, the required wall thickness is:
options: 7.5 mm
15 mm
30 mm
3.8 mm
questions.solution:
**15 mm.**

**Using the thin-cylinder hoop stress formula:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Hoop stress** | **σ = p D / (2 t)** ← |
| **Rearranged for thickness** | **t = p D / (2 σ)** ← |
| **Substituting** | **t = 3.0 × 1200 ÷ (2 × 120)** ← |
| ** ** | **3.0 × 1200 = 3600** ← |
| ** ** | **2 × 120 = 240** ← |
| ** ** | **t = 3600 ÷ 240 = 15 mm** ← |

> **KEEPING THE UNITS CONSISTENT IS THE WHOLE TRICK HERE AND IT IS WORTH SPELLING OUT: with p in MPa (which is N/mm²), D in mm and σ in MPa, the thickness comes out in millimetres directly.**

> **Mixing metres and megapascals is where errors arise, and converting the diameter to millimetres at the start avoids it entirely.**

> **The factor of 2 in the denominator is the hoop-stress 2 and not the longitudinal-stress 4 — hoop stress is pD/2t and longitudinal stress is pD/4t, the hoop being twice the longitudinal.**

> **Using the longitudinal formula by mistake gives 7.5 mm, which is option (a), and a pipe of that thickness would burst along a longitudinal seam — which is precisely the failure the hoop stress governs and the reason it is the one designed for.**

**WHY A REAL PENSTOCK WOULD BE THICKER THAN 15 mm, WHICH THE QUESTION'S EXCLUSIONS FLAG:**

| Addition | Note |
|---|---|
| **CORROSION allowance** ← | **Typically 1 to 2 mm, on the internal surface** ← |
| **JOINT EFFICIENCY** ← | **A welded seam may be credited at 0.85 to 1.0 depending on the inspection regime; the thickness is divided by it** ← |
| **A MINIMUM thickness for handling, transport and rolling** ← | **Often quoted as t ≥ (D + 500)/400 in mm, giving 4.25 mm here — not governing** ← |
| **BUCKLING resistance against external pressure or vacuum** ← | **Can govern for a large-diameter, low-head pipe, and for buried pipes** ← |
| **Stiffening at bends and supports** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE CONSIDERATION MOST LIKELY TO CATCH SOMEONE OUT BECAUSE IT INVERTS THE USUAL REASONING: a penstock can fail by COLLAPSING INWARD as well as by bursting outward.**

> **If the pipe is drained faster than air can enter, or if a valve closes downstream while the pipe continues to drain, an internal vacuum develops and the external atmospheric pressure crushes it.**

> **A thin large-diameter pipe has very little resistance to that, and pipes have been destroyed this way — flattened along their length by nothing more than being emptied carelessly.**

> **The provisions are an AIR VALVE at the upstream end of the penstock, sized to admit air as fast as the pipe can drain, and stiffening rings on large-diameter pipe.**

> **The air valve is the cheaper and more important of the two, and a penstock without one is at risk during every drain-down for maintenance — a low-probability, high-consequence event caused by an omitted fitting costing a tiny fraction of the pipe.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON WHY THICKNESS VARIES DOWN A PENSTOCK: the internal pressure increases with depth below the hydraulic grade line, so the thickness required increases steadily toward the powerhouse.**

> **A penstock is therefore built in several thickness classes, thinnest at the top and thickest at the bottom, changing at convenient intervals.**

> **Using a uniform thickness throughout would waste a great deal of steel, since the upper reaches need a fraction of what the lower ones do — and on a high-head penstock the bottom plate may be three or four times the thickness of the top.**

examTip.trick: **t = pD/2σ = 3.0 × 1200 / 240 = 15 mm.** Convert D to mm and MPa reads as N/mm², so t comes out in mm.
examTip.trap: **Hoop is pD/2t, longitudinal is pD/4t** — using the 4 gives 7.5 mm, and a pipe that thin bursts along its longitudinal seam.
examTip.mnemonic: **A penstock can also COLLAPSE inward** — drain it faster than air enters and atmospheric pressure flattens it. The air valve is the cheap, essential fitting.

questions.stem: A SURGE TANK on a hydropower waterway performs two distinct functions. These are:
options: To reflect the water hammer pressure wave, shortening the effective conduit length
To measure the flow and to provide access to the tunnel
To remove air from the tunnel and to filter the water
To raise the head on the turbines and to store water overnight
questions.solution:
**To reflect the WATER HAMMER pressure wave, shortening the effective conduit length; and to provide a water RESERVE and a free surface that allow the tunnel's flow to accelerate or decelerate gradually as the turbine load changes.**

**The two functions are distinct and both matter:**

| Function | Timescale | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **WATER HAMMER reflection** ← | **Seconds — the elastic pressure wave** ← | **Limits the pressure rise in the penstock, as shown earlier** ← |
| **MASS OSCILLATION damping** ← | **Minutes — the slow surging of the whole water mass between tank and reservoir** ← | **Lets the tunnel flow change gradually and lets the governor work** ← |

> **THE SECOND FUNCTION IS THE ONE MORE OFTEN MISSED AND IT IS WORTH SEEING SEPARATELY FROM THE FIRST: a long pressure tunnel is full of water with enormous inertia.**

> **When the turbines demand more flow, that whole mass must accelerate, and it cannot do so quickly.**

> **Without a surge tank the turbine would simply be starved until the tunnel caught up, which could take minutes — during which the plant could not respond to a load increase at all.**

> **The surge tank supplies the difference in the meantime, emptying while the tunnel accelerates and refilling once it has.**

> **So the surge tank is what makes a long-tunnel plant able to follow load at all, and a plant without one would be limited to slow, gradual load changes regardless of its governor.**

**THE MASS OSCILLATION ITSELF IS A SLOW PENDULUM AND ITS BEHAVIOUR SETS THE TANK'S SIZE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **After a load change, the level in the tank oscillates up and down about the new steady level** ← | ← |
| **The period is typically one to several MINUTES** ← | **Far slower than water hammer** ← |
| **The oscillation is damped by friction in the tunnel** ← | ← |
| **The tank must be tall enough to contain the maximum UPSURGE without overflowing** ← | **After a full load rejection** ← |
| **And deep enough that the maximum DOWNSURGE does not draw air into the tunnel** ← | **After a full load acceptance** ← |
| **THOMA's criterion gives the minimum cross-sectional area for the oscillation to be STABLE** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW POINTS TO A GENUINE INSTABILITY THAT IS NOT INTUITIVE AND IS WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: a surge tank that is too SMALL in area can produce oscillations that GROW rather than decay.**

> **The mechanism involves the governor: as the tank level falls, the head falls, so the governor opens the gates further to maintain power, which draws more water, which lowers the level further.**
