> **That is positive feedback, and below Thoma's critical area it overcomes the frictional damping and the oscillation diverges.**

> **So there is a MINIMUM tank area for stability, and it is a stability criterion rather than a capacity one — a tank can be tall enough to contain the surge and still be too narrow to be stable, which is a distinction the two requirements make easy to confuse.**

> **Designers commonly provide 1.5 to 1.8 times the Thoma area as a margin, because the criterion is derived under idealised assumptions about the governor's behaviour.**

**THE TANK TYPES FOLLOW FROM THESE REQUIREMENTS AND EACH ADDRESSES A PARTICULAR DIFFICULTY:**

| Type | Feature |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE surge tank** ← | **A plain vertical shaft open at the top — the baseline** ← |
| **RESTRICTED ORIFICE tank** ← | **A throttle at the tank's base, which damps the oscillation faster but transmits some pressure rise to the tunnel** ← |
| **DIFFERENTIAL (Johnson) tank** ← | **An inner riser and an outer tank — the riser responds fast for water hammer, the outer chamber gives volume for mass oscillation** ← |
| **EXPANSION CHAMBER tank** ← | **Widened upper and lower chambers, so the extremes of surge need little height** ← |

> **The third row is an elegant resolution of the conflict between the two functions: water hammer needs a fast-responding free surface right at the conduit, and mass oscillation needs a large volume.**

> **A single simple shaft must be large to serve the second and would be sluggish for the first.**

> **The differential tank separates them — a narrow riser that responds immediately, surrounded by a wide chamber that provides the volume more slowly.**

> **The fourth row addresses the topographic problem instead, and it is what is used where the ground is not high enough for a tall simple shaft: widening the tank at the surge extremes means less height is needed for the same volume, at the cost of a more complicated excavation.**

examTip.trick: **Two timescales: reflect the pressure wave (seconds) and absorb the mass oscillation (minutes)** — the second is what lets a long-tunnel plant follow load.
examTip.trap: **Thoma's criterion is a STABILITY minimum, not a capacity one** — too narrow a tank makes the governor drive a growing oscillation. Provide 1.5-1.8 times it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Differential tank = fast riser plus slow chamber** — separating the two functions that a single simple shaft must compromise between.

questions.stem: A hydropower tunnel is described as being under a 'pressure' rather than 'free-flow' regime when:
options: Its velocity exceeds 3 m/s
It is lined with concrete rather than shotcrete
It flows full, with the water under pressure greater than atmospheric
It is excavated by a tunnel boring machine
questions.solution:
**It flows FULL, with the water under pressure greater than atmospheric** — so the hydraulic grade line lies above the tunnel crown and the tunnel's slope need not match the hydraulic gradient.

**The two regimes compared:**

| Aspect | FREE-FLOW (open channel) tunnel | PRESSURE tunnel |
|---|---|---|
| **Flow condition** | **Partly full, free water surface, atmospheric pressure** ← | **Full, under pressure** ← |
| **Slope** | **Must follow the hydraulic gradient — a fixed, gentle grade** ← | **Free — it can rise and fall to suit the geology** ← |
| **Alignment freedom** | **Constrained by the need to maintain grade** ← | **Much greater — it can avoid bad ground** ← |
| **Lining** | **Needs lining on the invert and sides for hydraulics; crown may be unlined** ← | **Must resist INTERNAL pressure as well as ground load** ← |
| **Size for a given flow** | **Larger, since only part of the section carries water** ← | **Smaller — the whole section is used** ← |
| **Surge protection** | **A forebay** ← | **A surge tank** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS ARE THE PRESSURE TUNNEL'S PRACTICAL ADVANTAGE AND THEY MATTER GREATLY IN DIFFICULT GEOLOGY: a free-flow tunnel must hold a constant gentle grade, so it goes where the grade takes it.**

> **A pressure tunnel can dip beneath a bad zone or rise over one, because the water is pushed through by pressure rather than drawn along by gravity.**

> **In Himalayan geology, where a fault zone or a weak band may be discovered during driving, that freedom is worth a great deal — the tunnel can be realigned around the problem.**

> **A free-flow tunnel in the same situation must either go through the bad ground or abandon its grade, and neither is attractive.**

**THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRESSURE TUNNEL'S CENTRAL DESIGN PROBLEM AND IT DESERVES SETTING OUT PROPERLY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Internal water pressure pushes OUTWARD on the lining and the rock** ← | ← |
| **The rock can take that, provided it is confined by sufficient overburden** ← | ← |
| **The classic requirement is that the vertical rock cover exceeds the internal pressure head** ← | **With a factor, and measured to the ground surface** ← |
| **Expressed as the NORWEGIAN (or Bergh-Christensen) criterion for the side cover on a valley slope** ← | **Which is the governing case where a tunnel runs along a hillside** ← |
| **If the cover is insufficient, the water HYDRAULICALLY FRACTURES the rock and escapes** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW DESCRIBES A FAILURE THAT HAS OCCURRED ON REAL SCHEMES AND IT CAN BE SPECTACULAR: pressurised water finds its way out through the rock mass, and it can emerge on the hillside as a spring, or wash out a slope, or simply be lost.**

> **The condition arises where a pressure tunnel approaches a valley side and the horizontal cover becomes small even though the vertical cover looks adequate.**

> **So the criterion must be applied to the SHORTEST distance to the ground surface, measured perpendicular to the slope, not to the vertical depth — and a tunnel following a hillside can satisfy the vertical check everywhere and fail the true one.**

> **Where the cover is genuinely insufficient, the answer is a STEEL LINER embedded in concrete, which contains the pressure itself rather than relying on the rock — which is why the last stretch of a pressure tunnel before the penstock is commonly steel-lined.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON THE UNLINED PRESSURE TUNNEL, WHICH IS A NORWEGIAN SPECIALITY AND A GENUINE OPTION: where the rock is sound, tight and has ample cover, a pressure tunnel can be left entirely UNLINED.**

> **The rock takes the pressure and the leakage is acceptable, and the saving is very large — lining is a substantial fraction of a tunnel's cost.**

> **The price is a higher friction factor, so the tunnel must be bored somewhat larger, and the trade is usually favourable.**

> **It requires rock of a quality that Himalayan geology often does not offer, which is why the practice is common in Scandinavia and rare in Nepal — a reminder that a technique's suitability is a property of the site's geology rather than of the technique itself.**

examTip.trick: **Flows full under pressure, so the tunnel's slope is free** — it can rise and fall to dodge bad ground.
examTip.trap: **Rock cover must be checked PERPENDICULAR to the hillside, not vertically** — a tunnel along a valley side can pass the vertical check and still hydro-fracture.
examTip.mnemonic: **Steel-line where the cover runs out** — which is why the last reach before the penstock is normally steel-lined.

questions.stem: In the NEW AUSTRIAN TUNNELLING METHOD (NATM), the principle is to:
options: Mobilise the rock mass itself as the main load-carrying element
Excavate the full face and immediately install a rigid, heavy concrete lining that carries the whole ground load
Avoid all support and rely on the rock standing unaided
Freeze the ground before excavation in every case
questions.solution:
**To mobilise the ROCK MASS ITSELF as the main load-carrying element** — installing a flexible initial support of shotcrete and rock bolts that allows controlled deformation, monitoring that deformation, and adjusting the support to what the ground actually requires.

**The principles that define the method:**

| Principle | Note |
|---|---|
| **The rock around the opening is the primary structure, not the lining** ← | **The lining helps the rock support itself** ← |
| **Support must be FLEXIBLE enough to allow some deformation** ← | **Deformation lets the ground arch and shed load onto itself** ← |
| **But not so much that the rock loosens and loses strength** ← | **There is an optimum — too stiff is as bad as too soft** ← |
| **Support is installed EARLY, close to the face** ← | **To prevent loosening before it begins** ← |
| **Deformation is MEASURED continuously** ← | **Convergence measurement is central to the method, not an optional extra** ← |
| **And the support is ADJUSTED according to what the measurements show** ← | ← |
| **A closed RING is formed, with an invert where necessary** ← | **An unclosed ring is not a structure** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE IDEA THAT MAKES NATM COUNTER-INTUITIVE AND IT IS WORTH DWELLING ON: a very stiff lining attracts a very large load.**

> **If the tunnel is prevented from converging at all, the ground's full in-situ stress must be carried by the lining.**

> **If a small, controlled convergence is permitted, the rock around the opening redistributes its stress into an arch and carries most of the load itself, and the lining need only carry the remainder.**

> **So allowing some movement REDUCES the support required, which is the opposite of the structural engineer's usual instinct that stiffer is safer.**

> **The qualification in the same row is essential though — beyond a certain deformation the rock mass loosens, the joints open, the blocks lose interlock and the strength falls away, so the support must intervene before that point.**

> **The ground reaction curve, plotted against the support characteristic curve, is the formal expression of this and it shows the optimum as the intersection of the two.**

**THE MONITORING REQUIREMENT IS NOT NEGOTIABLE AND IT IS WHERE THE METHOD IS MOST OFTEN MISAPPLIED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The method DEPENDS on measuring convergence and adjusting support accordingly** ← | ← |
| **Applying shotcrete and bolts without measuring is not NATM** ← | **It is merely shotcrete and bolts** ← |
| **Measurements must be taken frequently and close behind the face** ← | ← |
| **And there must be an engineer empowered to CHANGE the support on the basis of them** ← | ← |
| **Which requires a contract that permits the support class to vary and pays for it** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE COMMERCIAL CONDITION THAT MAKES THE METHOD POSSIBLE AND ITS ABSENCE IS WHY NATM SOMETIMES FAILS ON PROJECTS THAT CLAIM TO USE IT: the method requires the support to vary with the ground, so the contract must price support by class and measure it as executed.**

> **A lump-sum contract for a fixed support specification gives the contractor every incentive to install the minimum specified regardless of what the rock is doing, and no mechanism to install more when it is needed.**

> **So the observational method requires an observational contract, and combining NATM's engineering with a fixed-price contract's commercial logic produces the worst of both.**

> **This is worth stating because it is a general truth about observational design methods — they are as much a contractual arrangement as a technical one, and the technical method cannot function inside the wrong commercial structure.**

> **A NOTE ON TERMINOLOGY, SINCE IT CAUSES CONFUSION: NATM is often used loosely to mean 'sprayed concrete lining' or 'drill and blast with shotcrete support'.**

> **Those are the method's usual tools and they are not the method.**

> **The method is the philosophy — rock as the structure, controlled deformation, measurement, and adjustment — and it can in principle be pursued with other tools.**

> **The distinction matters when assessing whether a project is genuinely applying it, because the tools are visible on site and the philosophy is visible only in the monitoring records and the decisions taken from them.**
tags: rock as the load carrying element
observational method needs an observational contract

examTip.trick: **The rock is the structure; the support helps it support itself** — flexible shotcrete and bolts, measured convergence, adjusted support.
examTip.trap: **Allowing controlled deformation REDUCES the load** — a rigid lining attracts the full in-situ stress. Stiffer is not safer here.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shotcrete and bolts without monitoring is not NATM** — and the method needs a contract that lets the support class vary and pays for it.

questions.stem: The ROCK MASS RATING (RMR) and the Q-SYSTEM are used in tunnel design to:
options: Determine the tunnel's hydraulic roughness
Calculate the tunnel's cost per metre
Estimate the rock's chemical composition
Classify the rock mass from a set of measured parameters
questions.solution:
**To CLASSIFY the rock mass from a set of measured parameters, and from that classification estimate the STAND-UP TIME and recommend a support pattern** — converting qualitative geological description into a quantitative design basis.

**The two systems and what they count:**

| System | Parameters |
|---|---|
| **RMR (Bieniawski)** ← | **Six: intact rock strength, RQD, joint spacing, joint condition, groundwater, and a correction for joint orientation. Rated 0 to 100** ← |
| **Q-SYSTEM (Barton)** ← | **Q = (RQD/Jn) × (Jr/Ja) × (Jw/SRF), six parameters in three ratios** ← |

> **THE Q-SYSTEM'S THREE RATIOS EACH HAVE A PHYSICAL MEANING AND KNOWING THEM MAKES THE FORMULA MEMORABLE RATHER THAN ARBITRARY: RQD/Jn represents the BLOCK SIZE — how much intact rock there is, divided by the number of joint sets breaking it up.**

> **Jr/Ja represents the SHEAR STRENGTH between blocks — joint roughness over joint alteration, so a rough clean joint scores well and a smooth clay-filled one badly.**

> **Jw/SRF represents the ACTIVE STRESS — water pressure reduction against the stress reduction factor for squeezing, swelling or faulted ground.**

> **So Q is block size times inter-block friction times a stress condition, which is a reasonable summary of what determines whether a tunnel stands up, and the formula becomes a statement rather than a string of symbols.**

**WHAT THE CLASSIFICATIONS ARE USED FOR:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Estimating STAND-UP TIME for a given unsupported span** ← | **Bieniawski's chart — how long the excavation will hold before support is needed** ← |
| **Recommending a SUPPORT PATTERN** ← | **Bolt length and spacing, shotcrete thickness, whether steel ribs are needed** ← |
| **Estimating rock mass DEFORMATION MODULUS** ← | **Through empirical correlations** ← |
| **Comparing ground conditions between locations and projects** ← | **A common language** ← |
| **CONTRACTUALLY, to define the support class payable for a given reach** ← | **Which is how the observational contract described earlier is made to work** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE SYSTEMS' MOST PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT USE AND IT IS SELDOM MENTIONED IN TEXTBOOKS: the rock classification provides the objective trigger for a change in support and therefore for a change in payment.**

> **Without it, 'the ground got worse' is an assertion that the contractor makes and the engineer disputes.**

> **With it, the face is mapped, the Q value or RMR is computed from countable parameters, and the support class follows from a schedule agreed before the work began.**

> **So the classification turns a matter of judgement into a matter of measurement, which is what allows the support to vary honestly with the ground — and that is a contractual achievement at least as valuable as the engineering one.**

**AND THE SYSTEMS' LIMITATIONS DESERVE STATING, SINCE THEY ARE OFTEN APPLIED BEYOND THEM:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **They are EMPIRICAL, derived from case histories** ← | **Mostly from particular geological settings** ← |
| **They handle JOINTED rock well and squeezing or swelling ground poorly** ← | **The SRF term is a crude handle on a complex behaviour** ← |
| **They say nothing about a single adverse feature** ← | **A classification can be good and one badly oriented wedge can still drop out** ← |
| **And they are no substitute for understanding the geology** ← | ← |

> **The third row is the most important caution and it applies to every classification system: an average is not a guarantee.**

> **A reach of tunnel may rate as good rock throughout and contain one intersection of three joint sets forming a wedge that is kinematically free to fall.**

> **The classification does not see it, because it counts joint sets and spacings rather than analysing the geometry.**

> **So the classification sets the general support pattern and a separate KINEMATIC analysis of the wedges formed by the mapped joint sets must be done alongside it — which is why the tunnel face is mapped geologically and not merely scored.**
tags: Q as block size times friction times stress

examTip.trick: **Score the rock mass, get stand-up time and a support pattern** — RMR out of 100, or Q from three ratios.
examTip.trap: **Q = block size (RQD/Jn) × inter-block friction (Jr/Ja) × active stress (Jw/SRF)** — three physical ideas, not six arbitrary symbols.
examTip.mnemonic: **A good average hides a bad wedge** — classification sets the general pattern; kinematic wedge analysis of the mapped joints must run alongside it.

questions.stem: The head loss due to friction in a hydropower tunnel or penstock is most commonly computed using the Darcy-Weisbach equation h = f L V² / (2gD). For a given discharge, doubling the diameter reduces the friction head loss by a factor of:
questions.solution:
**32.**

**The reasoning:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **h = f L V² / (2gD)** | ← |
| **For fixed Q, V = Q/A = 4Q/(πD²), so V ∝ 1/D²** | ← |
| **Therefore V² ∝ 1/D⁴** | ← |
| **And h ∝ (1/D⁴)/D = 1/D⁵** | ← |
| **Doubling D** | **h falls by 2⁵ = 32** ← |

> **THE FIFTH POWER IS THE RESULT WORTH COMMITTING TO MEMORY AND IT EXPLAINS A GREAT DEAL ABOUT CONVEYANCE DESIGN: head loss is extraordinarily sensitive to diameter.**

> **A 10 per cent increase in diameter reduces the loss by about 38 per cent, since 1.1⁵ = 1.61.**

> **A 20 per cent increase reduces it by nearly 60 per cent.**

> **So when a scheme is found to be losing more head than expected, enlarging the conduit is disproportionately effective — and conversely, a conduit built slightly undersized loses disproportionately more than the shortfall in diameter would suggest.**

**THE DISTRACTORS EACH CORRESPOND TO A PARTIAL ANALYSIS AND NAMING THEM IS INSTRUCTIVE:**

| Answer | The analysis that produces it |
|---|---|
| **2** | **Treating h ∝ 1/D and forgetting that V changes with D at all** ← |
| **4** | **Taking V² ∝ 1/D² — squaring only one power of D** ← |
| **8** | **Getting to 1/D³ — a common half-way error** ← |
| **32** | **The complete analysis, 1/D⁵** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE ERROR AND IT IS ONE OF FORGETTING WHAT IS HELD CONSTANT: h = fLV²/2gD does contain 1/D explicitly, and if V were held constant the answer would indeed be 2.**

> **But the question fixes the DISCHARGE, not the velocity, and fixing Q makes V depend on D.**

> **So the explicit D in the formula is only one of three, the other two arriving through V.**

> **Being clear about which quantity is held constant is the whole of this problem, and it is worth a deliberate moment on any question of the form 'if X doubles, what happens to Y' — the answer always depends on what is held fixed, and the question usually says so in a single word.**

**A NOTE ON WHICH FRICTION FORMULA TO USE, SINCE BOTH APPEAR IN PRACTICE:**

| Formula | Note |
|---|---|
| **DARCY-WEISBACH with f from the Colebrook-White equation or the Moody chart** ← | **Dimensionally rational, valid over all regimes, and the correct choice** ← |
| **MANNING with n** ← | **Empirical, strictly for fully rough turbulent open-channel flow, but widely used for tunnels** ← |
| **HAZEN-WILLIAMS with C** ← | **Empirical, calibrated for water in pipes at ordinary temperatures — common in water supply** ← |

> **The first row is the correct general tool and the other two persist because they are convenient and because a great deal of practical experience is encoded in their coefficients.**

> **For a hydropower tunnel, Manning's n is very commonly used — around 0.012 for a smooth concrete lining, 0.033 or more for an unlined blasted rock tunnel — and the corresponding Darcy f can be derived from it.**

> **The wide range between lined and unlined values is exactly the trade noted earlier for unlined pressure tunnels: the unlined tunnel is cheaper and rougher, so it must be bored larger to pass the same flow at the same loss.**

> **Quantifying that trade needs the roughness values, and getting them wrong by using a lined tunnel's n for an unlined one understates the required diameter substantially — a mistake whose consequence is a permanent head loss that cannot be corrected without re-excavating the tunnel.**

examTip.trick: **h ∝ 1/D⁵ at fixed Q, so doubling D divides the loss by 32.**
examTip.trap: **The formula's explicit 1/D is only one of three powers** — the other two arrive through V ∝ 1/D². Note what is held constant: Q, not V.
examTip.mnemonic: **Manning n ≈ 0.012 lined, 0.033+ unlined blasted rock** — which is why an unlined tunnel must be bored larger for the same loss.

questions.stem: In a long pressure tunnel, an ADIT is provided principally to:
options: Provide additional storage volume for surge
Allow air to escape from the tunnel crown during filling
Give access to an intermediate point of the tunnel
Reduce the tunnel's friction losses
questions.solution:
**To give ACCESS to an intermediate point of the tunnel** — creating additional working faces so the tunnel can be driven from several points at once, and providing ventilation, spoil removal and later maintenance access.

**Why adits matter so much to a tunnel's programme:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A tunnel driven from its two portals has TWO working faces** ← | ← |
| **Each adit meeting the tunnel adds TWO more** ← | **One in each direction** ← |
| **So one adit doubles the number of faces and roughly halves the driving time** ← | ← |
| **Which on a critical-path tunnel translates directly into a shorter project** ← | ← |
| **And into a large IDC saving, by the mechanism described earlier** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE THE ECONOMIC ARGUMENT AND IT IS USUALLY DECISIVE: a tunnel is very often the critical path of a hydropower project, and its duration is set by its length divided by the advance rate per face.**

> **An adit costs a few hundred metres of excavation and saves perhaps a year on a long tunnel.**

> **Against a year's interest during construction on a project costing billions, the adit is almost free.**

> **So the question is rarely whether an adit is worth providing but how many and where — and the answer is generally as many as the topography permits access to at reasonable cost.**

**THE OTHER FUNCTIONS ARE REAL AND SOME ARE PERMANENT:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Additional working faces** ← | **The main construction reason** ← |
| **VENTILATION** ← | **A long single-ended drive becomes very difficult to ventilate** ← |
| **SPOIL removal over a shorter haul** ← | ← |
| **Material and equipment delivery** ← | ← |
| **DRAINAGE of construction water** ← | **Where the adit is lower than the drive** ← |
| **Permanent MAINTENANCE access after commissioning** ← | **The adit is plugged with a bulkhead and a door, or a gate** ← |
| **Emergency escape during construction** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS OFTEN THE BINDING CONSTRAINT ON A LONG DRIVE AND IT IS EASY TO UNDERESTIMATE: ventilating a single-ended tunnel means pushing air down a duct for the tunnel's whole length and letting it return along the bore.**

> **Beyond a couple of kilometres that becomes expensive in power and marginal in effectiveness, particularly with diesel plant at the face.**

> **An adit converts the arrangement into a through-ventilation circuit, which is far more effective and much cheaper to run.**

> **So on a long tunnel the adit may be required for ventilation alone, before the programme argument is even considered.**

> **THE SIXTH ROW DESERVES DESIGN ATTENTION AT THE OUTSET AND IS FREQUENTLY AN AFTERTHOUGHT: a pressure tunnel must be sealed at the adit junction, and that bulkhead must resist the full internal pressure.**

> **It also needs a door or gate through which the tunnel can be entered when it is dewatered for inspection.**

> **Designing that from the start — with the bulkhead's location, the door's size, and the dewatering and refilling arrangements settled — produces a tunnel that can be inspected.**

> **Plugging an adit with mass concrete because nobody thought about maintenance produces a tunnel that can be entered only through its ends, which on a long tunnel may mean it is never inspected at all — and an uninspected pressure tunnel is a substantial asset whose condition is simply unknown.**

examTip.trick: **Intermediate access giving two more working faces** — plus ventilation, spoil haul and later maintenance entry.
examTip.trap: **One adit roughly halves the driving time of a critical-path tunnel** — against a year's IDC on a billion-rupee project, the adit is almost free.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design the adit bulkhead with a DOOR** — plug it with mass concrete and the pressure tunnel can never be inspected again.

questions.stem: CONSOLIDATION GROUTING and CONTACT GROUTING around a concrete-lined pressure tunnel are carried out respectively to:
options: Seal the tunnel against water entry and to colour the lining for inspection
Strengthen and tighten the surrounding rock mass by filling its fissures
Both do the same thing under different names
Reduce the tunnel's roughness and to provide reinforcement
questions.solution:
**To strengthen and tighten the surrounding ROCK MASS by filling its fissures; and to fill the VOID between the lining's extrados and the rock, particularly at the crown where the concrete shrinks away.**

**The two operations distinguished:**

| Operation | Target | Pressure | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| **CONTACT grouting** ← | **The gap between the lining and the rock** ← | **LOW — just enough to fill the void** ← | **Restore continuity so the lining bears on the rock** ← |
| **CONSOLIDATION grouting** ← | **The fissured rock mass itself, through holes drilled into it** ← | **HIGHER — to penetrate the rock's joints** ← | **Stiffen and tighten the rock so it shares the load and leaks less** ← |

> **THE CONTACT GROUTING NEED ARISES FROM A SIMPLE PHYSICAL FACT THAT IS EASY TO OVERLOOK: concrete SHRINKS as it cures, and it settles under gravity while plastic.**

> **So the lining pulls away from the rock at the crown, leaving a gap of a few millimetres to a few centimetres over the top of the tunnel.**

> **A lining not in contact with the rock cannot transfer load to it, so the lining alone must carry whatever comes — which it was never designed to do.**

> **Contact grouting through holes drilled up into that gap fills it and restores the load path, and it is a modest operation whose omission undermines the whole design assumption that lining and rock act together.**

**WHY CONSOLIDATION GROUTING MATTERS PARTICULARLY FOR A PRESSURE TUNNEL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A pressure tunnel's lining is thin and cannot carry the internal pressure alone** ← | ← |
| **It relies on transferring that pressure OUTWARD into the rock** ← | ← |
| **A fissured rock mass is compressible, so it deflects and the lining cracks** ← | ← |
| **Grouting the fissures stiffens the rock, reducing the deflection** ← | ← |
| **And it reduces the leakage of pressurised water out into the rock** ← | ← |
| **So it serves both structurally and hydraulically** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS DESCRIBE THE CENTRAL DESIGN RELATIONSHIP FOR A LINED PRESSURE TUNNEL AND IT IS A STIFFNESS PROBLEM RATHER THAN A STRENGTH ONE: how the internal pressure is shared between lining and rock depends on their relative stiffnesses.**

> **A stiff rock takes most of it and the lining is lightly stressed; a soft rock takes little and the lining must take the rest.**

> **So the rock's deformation modulus is the governing parameter, and consolidation grouting is a way of increasing it.**

> **This is why the grouting is not a finishing operation but a structural one, and why grout takes and pressures are recorded and interpreted rather than merely executed — the records tell the designer whether the rock is behaving as the design assumed.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON GROUTING PRACTICE THAT IS WORTH CARRYING: grouting is done in a SEQUENCE of split spacing — primary holes at a wide spacing, then secondary holes between them, then tertiaries if the takes justify it.**

> **Each series' grout take is recorded, and the takes should DIMINISH as the spacing closes.**

> **Diminishing takes mean the rock is being progressively filled and the treatment is working.**

> **Takes that do not diminish mean the grout is going somewhere else — into a large open feature, or out to the surface, or along a fault — and the treatment is not achieving what it appears to be.**

> **So the pattern of takes across the series is the quality check on the whole operation, and grouting that is executed without that analysis has consumed the materials without demonstrating any result.**
tags: load sharing between lining and rock
diminishing takes as the quality check

examTip.trick: **Consolidation tightens the ROCK; contact fills the GAP between lining and rock at the crown.**
examTip.trap: **Concrete shrinks away from the crown, so the lining is not in contact** — and a lining not touching the rock must carry alone what it was never designed for.
examTip.mnemonic: **Grout in split spacing and watch the takes DIMINISH** — takes that do not fall mean the grout is escaping somewhere, not filling the rock.

questions.stem: A circular tunnel 3.2 km long carries 16 m³/s at a mean velocity of 2.0 m/s. Taking the Darcy friction factor as f = 0.020, the friction head loss is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 4.1 m.**

**First the diameter, which the question supplies indirectly through Q and V:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Area** | **A = Q/V = 16 ÷ 2.0 = 8.0 m²** ← |
| **Diameter** | **A = πD²/4, so D = √(4A/π) = √(32 ÷ 3.1416)** ← |
| ** ** | **= √10.186 = 3.19 m** ← |

**Then the Darcy-Weisbach loss:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **h = f L V² / (2 g D)** | ← |
| **Numerator** | **0.020 × 3200 × 2.0² = 0.020 × 3200 × 4 = 256** ← |
| **Denominator** | **2 × 9.81 × 3.19 = 62.6** ← |
| **So** | **h = 256 ÷ 62.6 = 4.09 m ≈ 4.1 m** ← |

> **THE FIRST TABLE IS THE STEP THE QUESTION IS REALLY TESTING AND IT IS EASY TO MISS: the diameter is not given, and it must be recovered from the discharge and the velocity before Darcy-Weisbach can be applied at all.**

> **A = Q/V is the continuity equation, and it is available whenever any two of the three are known.**

> **So a question that gives Q and V has given the area, and a question that gives Q and D has given the velocity — recognising which two are supplied is the first move on any conveyance problem.**

> **The arithmetic of √(4A/π) is worth doing carefully; a quick check is that a 3.19 m tunnel has an area of about 8 m², which matches.**

**THE DISTRACTORS EACH CORRESPOND TO A SPECIFIC ERROR AND THEY ARE WORTH IDENTIFYING:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **8.2 m** | **Using the RADIUS (1.60 m) in place of the diameter — which doubles the loss exactly** ← |
| **16.4 m** | **Both the radius error and the omission of the 2 in 2gD** ← |
| **2.0 m** | **Using 2D instead of D, or halving somewhere in the chain** ← |
| **4.1 m** | **Correct** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE COMMONEST SUBSTANTIVE ERROR IN DARCY-WEISBACH WORK AND IT IS WORTH GUARDING AGAINST DELIBERATELY: the D in the formula is the DIAMETER, and for a non-circular section it is the EQUIVALENT diameter 4R, where R is the hydraulic radius A/P.**

> **Substituting the hydraulic radius directly, instead of four times it, gives a loss four times too large.**

> **So for a horseshoe or D-shaped tunnel — which most hydropower tunnels are — the sequence is: compute the area and the wetted perimeter, form R = A/P, then use D = 4R in Darcy-Weisbach.**

> **That step is where non-circular tunnel calculations most often go wrong, and it is worth writing out on its own line rather than folding it into the substitution.**

> **A useful confirmation is that for a CIRCLE, R = (πD²/4) ÷ (πD) = D/4, so 4R returns D exactly — which shows the equivalent-diameter rule is consistent with the circular case rather than a separate convention.**

**A CLOSING CHECK ON WHETHER THE ANSWER IS REASONABLE, WHICH IS ALWAYS WORTH THE FEW SECONDS:**

| Check | Working |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic gradient** | **4.09 m over 3200 m = 1 in 782** ← |
| **Typical power tunnel gradient** | **Between about 1 in 500 and 1 in 1500** ← |
| **So the answer sits comfortably in the normal range** ← | ← |
| **Whereas 16.4 m would be 1 in 195** ← | **Far too steep — an uneconomically small tunnel** ← |

> **THE GRADIENT CHECK IS MORE USEFUL THAN CHECKING THE HEAD LOSS ITSELF BECAUSE IT CAN BE COMPARED AGAINST A REMEMBERED NORM, and the norm is easy to carry: roughly a metre of loss per kilometre, give or take a factor of two.**

> **A tunnel losing 5 m per kilometre is either very small for its flow or very rough, and either way something should be questioned.**

> **One losing 0.2 m per kilometre is unusually generous, which is not wrong but invites the question of whether the extra excavation was justified by the head it saves.**

> **So the gradient is the figure to form a judgement on, and the absolute head loss is what that judgement is then converted into for the energy calculation.**

examTip.trap: **The D in Darcy-Weisbach is the DIAMETER, or 4R for a non-circular tunnel** — putting the hydraulic radius in directly makes the loss four times too big.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the hydraulic gradient: about 1 m per km** — a power tunnel runs roughly 1 in 500 to 1 in 1500. That norm catches a wrong answer instantly.

questions.stem: The DRAFT TUBE fitted below a reaction turbine serves to:
options: Provide a support for the turbine's weight
Recover the kinetic energy remaining in the water leaving the runner, by expanding it gradually
Prevent air from entering the turbine casing
Increase the velocity of the water leaving the runner
questions.solution:
**To RECOVER the kinetic energy remaining in the water leaving the runner, by expanding it gradually; and to allow the turbine to be set ABOVE the tailwater level while still using the head down to that level.**

**The two functions, both of which are substantial:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **KINETIC ENERGY recovery** ← | **Water leaves the runner with significant velocity; a gradually expanding tube converts that velocity head into pressure** ← |
| **Effectively creating a partial VACUUM below the runner** ← | **Which is why the draft tube is said to 'suck'** ← |
| **HEAD recovery** ← | **The head between the runner and the tailwater is made available to the turbine, though the runner sits above the tailwater** ← |
| **Permitting the runner to be set at a convenient, accessible level** ← | **Rather than drowned below tailwater** ← |

> **THE SECOND FUNCTION IS WHAT MAKES A REACTION TURBINE PRACTICAL AND IT DESERVES A CLEAR STATEMENT: without a draft tube, a turbine discharging freely to atmosphere loses all the head below its runner.**

> **A runner set 5 m above the tailwater would waste 5 m of head, which on a 40 m scheme is an eighth of the output.**

> **The draft tube, running full and sealed to the tailwater, transmits the tailwater's suction up to the runner exit — so the effective head becomes the full distance from headwater to tailwater, regardless of where the runner sits.**

> **This is why an impulse turbine like a Pelton, which discharges freely to atmosphere and has no draft tube, must be set just above the maximum tailwater level and does lose the head below it — a real loss that is negligible at 400 m head and would be intolerable at 40 m, which is part of why Pelton wheels are high-head machines.**

**THE KINETIC RECOVERY FUNCTION IS WHERE THE DESIGN CARE GOES:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The tube must expand GRADUALLY** ← | **A sudden expansion dissipates the energy instead of recovering it** ← |
| **Typical total included angle of 8 to 12 degrees** ← | **Beyond that the flow separates from the walls** ← |
| **Separation destroys the recovery and causes vibration** ← | ← |
| **The ELBOW type is used where excavation depth must be limited** ← | **Turning the flow horizontal in a shaped bend** ← |
| **Its efficiency is lower than a straight conical tube's** ← | **But it needs far less excavation** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW'S ANGLE LIMIT IS THE CRITICAL DETAIL AND IT IS THE SAME CONSTRAINT THAT GOVERNS EVERY DIFFUSER, from a wind tunnel to a carburettor: expand too fast and the boundary layer separates.**

> **Once it separates, the flow no longer fills the widening section, the pressure recovery stops, and the energy that should have been recovered is lost in turbulence instead.**

> **So the recovery depends on keeping the expansion gentle enough for the flow to follow, which sets the tube's length — and a short, steeply expanding draft tube recovers less than a long gentle one, which is the trade against excavation cost.**

**AND THE VACUUM THE DRAFT TUBE CREATES BRINGS ITS OWN HAZARD, WHICH IS THE CLOSING POINT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The pressure at the runner exit is BELOW atmospheric** ← | ← |
| **If it falls to the water's VAPOUR PRESSURE, cavitation occurs** ← | ← |
| **So the runner's height above tailwater is LIMITED** ← | **Set by the cavitation criterion, not by convenience** ← |
| **The governing parameter is THOMA's cavitation coefficient σ** ← | **σ = (Ha − Hv − Hs) / H, which must exceed a critical value for the machine** ← |
| **And Ha is lower at ALTITUDE, which matters greatly in Nepal** ← | ← |

> **The last row is a consideration that is easy to omit and that bites hard in a mountainous country: atmospheric pressure at 2,000 m is about 8 m of water rather than 10.3 m at sea level.**

> **So the permissible suction head is reduced by more than two metres, and a turbine setting that is perfectly safe at sea level will cavitate at altitude.**

> **The consequence is that high-altitude powerhouses must set their runners LOWER relative to tailwater — sometimes below it — which means deeper excavation and a more expensive powerhouse.**

> **A manufacturer's standard setting quoted without reference to altitude is therefore not applicable in the Himalaya, and confirming that the σ calculation used the site's actual atmospheric pressure is a check worth making explicitly on any imported turbine specification.**
tags: recovers the head below the runner

examTip.trick: **Recovers exit kinetic energy by gradual expansion, and recovers the head between runner and tailwater.**
examTip.trap: **Expansion angle 8-12° total** — steeper and the flow separates, so the recovery stops and the energy is lost to turbulence instead.
examTip.mnemonic: **Atmospheric pressure is ~8 m of water at 2,000 m, not 10.3** — so Himalayan powerhouses must set runners lower or they cavitate.

questions.stem: A BIFURCATION or MANIFOLD in a penstock, where the single pipe divides to feed two or more turbines, requires special structural attention because:
options: The opening in the main pipe's wall interrupts the hoop stress path
The velocity increases sharply at the junction
The water temperature rises at the junction
Bifurcations are always made of cast iron
questions.solution:
**The opening in the main pipe's wall interrupts the HOOP STRESS path, so the load must be carried around the opening by reinforcement** — a sickle plate, crescent rib or external girder — and the junction is a region of complex three-dimensional stress.

**Why an opening in a pressure shell is structurally awkward:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A cylindrical shell carries internal pressure by continuous HOOP tension** ← | ← |
| **Cutting a hole interrupts that tension path** ← | ← |
| **The load that the removed material was carrying must divert around the opening** ← | ← |
| **Producing stress CONCENTRATIONS at the edges** ← | ← |
| **So material must be added to carry the diverted load** ← | **At least equal to the area removed, and placed close to the opening** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE COMPENSATION PRINCIPLE AND IT APPLIES TO EVERY PENETRATION OF EVERY PRESSURE VESSEL, so it is worth carrying beyond penstocks: replace the metal you removed, and put it near the hole.**

> **Placing it near the hole matters because reinforcement far from the opening does not participate — the stress diverts only a limited distance, so material outside that zone is dead weight.**

> **Pressure vessel codes define an effective reinforcement zone for precisely this reason, and material outside it does not count toward the compensation.**

> **The same rule governs manholes in penstocks, branch connections for valves, and instrument tappings — any hole in a pressure shell — which makes it one of the more generally useful principles in this subchapter.**

**THE STANDARD BIFURCATION ARRANGEMENTS:**

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| **SICKLE (crescent) PLATE bifurcation** ← | **An internal curved plate along the line of intersection of the two branches, carrying the unbalanced load in tension** ← |
| **External GIRDER or ring reinforcement** ← | **Rings around the junction, carrying the load externally** ← |
| **SPHERICAL manifold** ← | **A sphere from which the branches spring — structurally efficient but a large hydraulic loss** ← |
| **Simple wye with thickened plate** ← | **For small pipes and low heads only** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE ARRANGEMENT USED FOR MOST LARGE HIGH-HEAD BIFURCATIONS AND ITS ACTION IS WORTH PICTURING: the sickle plate sits in the plane of the two branch axes, along the curve where the two cylinders intersect.**

> **The internal pressure tries to push the two branches apart, and the sickle plate ties them together, carrying that force in direct tension.**

> **It is shaped like a crescent because the unbalanced force varies around the intersection, being greatest at the crotch and least at the flanks.**

> **So the plate is deepest at the crotch and tapers to nothing, which is why it is called a sickle — the shape follows the force distribution, which is the mark of an efficient structural element.**

> **THE HYDRAULIC SIDE DESERVES A NOTE TOO, SINCE THE STRUCTURAL AND HYDRAULIC REQUIREMENTS PULL AGAINST EACH OTHER: a small branch angle is hydraulically good and structurally awkward, because the intersection curve is long and the crotch is sharp.**

> **A large branch angle — approaching 90 degrees — is structurally simpler and hydraulically poor, because the flow must turn abruptly.**

> **Branch angles of 45 to 60 degrees are the usual compromise for a symmetrical wye.**

> **And the bifurcation's head loss, though small in absolute terms, is incurred continuously for the plant's life, so the hydraulic side of the compromise is worth more than its apparent magnitude suggests — which is the same argument made for the penstock diameter and it applies to every fitting in the waterway.**
tags: reinforcement must be near the opening

examTip.trick: **The hole interrupts the hoop tension path** — so the diverted load needs reinforcement, and the junction is a 3D stress problem.
examTip.trap: **Replace the metal removed and put it NEAR the hole** — reinforcement outside the effective zone does not participate. True of every pressure-shell penetration.
examTip.mnemonic: **The sickle is deepest at the crotch because the unbalanced force is** — the shape follows the force distribution.

questions.stem: The MAIN INLET VALVE (MIV) installed immediately upstream of each turbine is provided principally to:
options: Regulate the flow to the turbine in normal operation
Measure the flow entering the turbine
Isolate that unit for maintenance without dewatering the whole penstock
Reduce the pressure entering the turbine casing
questions.solution:
**To isolate that unit for maintenance without dewatering the whole penstock, and to close as a SAFETY device if the turbine's own guide vanes fail to shut on a runaway.**

**Its functions, and what it is NOT for:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **ISOLATION for maintenance of one unit** ← | **Essential in a multi-unit station sharing a penstock** ← |
| **EMERGENCY closure if the guide vanes or the nozzle fail to close** ← | **The last line of defence against a runaway** ← |
| **Closure on a serious fault — bearing failure, loss of cooling, fire** ← | ← |
| **NOT flow regulation** ← | **That is the guide vanes' or the nozzle's job** ← |
| **NOT normal starting and stopping under load** ← | **Though it is opened and closed as part of the sequence** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE POINT THE QUESTION TURNS ON AND THE DISTINCTION IS A REAL OPERATIONAL ONE: a main inlet valve is designed to be either fully open or fully closed.**

> **Operating it partly open subjects the disc or the gate to severe vibration and cavitation, and it wears the seals rapidly.**

> **Flow control is done by the turbine's own guide vanes, which are designed for continuous modulation and are shaped to do it efficiently.**

> **So the MIV is a stop valve rather than a control valve, and treating it as the latter damages it — a distinction worth carrying to valves generally, since gate and butterfly valves throughout an installation are frequently misused for throttling duties they were not designed for.**

**THE VALVE TYPES AND WHERE EACH SUITS:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **BUTTERFLY valve** ← | **A disc rotating on a shaft across the pipe — compact, cheap, but the disc obstructs the flow permanently** ← |
| **SPHERICAL (rotary) valve** ← | **A rotating sphere with a full-bore passage — ZERO obstruction when open, and much better sealing at high head** ← |
| **GATE (sluice) valve** ← | **A sliding gate — used at lower heads and smaller sizes** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHAT IS USED AT HIGH HEAD AND THE REASON IS BOTH HYDRAULIC AND SEALING: a butterfly valve's disc remains in the flow when the valve is open, causing a permanent head loss and, at high velocity, cavitation and vibration.**

> **A spherical valve's passage is clear, matching the pipe bore exactly, so its loss when open is negligible.**

> **Its seals can also be pressed home hydraulically, giving a tight shut-off against very high pressure that a butterfly valve cannot match.**

> **So butterfly valves serve up to moderate heads and spherical valves take over above roughly 200 m — the crossover being economic rather than sharp, since the spherical valve costs considerably more.**

> **THE SECOND FUNCTION IN THE FIRST TABLE DESERVES ELABORATION BECAUSE IT IS THE SAFETY CASE: if a turbine loses its load and its guide vanes fail to close, the runner accelerates to RUNAWAY speed — perhaps 1.8 times normal for a Francis machine and over 2 times for some others.**

> **The generator is designed to survive runaway, but the situation must be ended.**

> **The MIV closing under its own stored energy — a weight, an accumulator or a spring, never mains power — stops the water and the machine.**

> **The requirement that the closing energy be STORED rather than supplied is the essential part: the emergency that requires the valve to close may be the same event that removed the station's power supply, so a valve needing power to close is a valve that will not close when it matters most.**

examTip.trick: **Isolation for maintenance, and emergency closure if the guide vanes fail** — a stop valve, not a control valve.
examTip.trap: **Never throttle with an MIV** — fully open or fully closed. Partial opening brings vibration, cavitation and rapid seal wear.
examTip.mnemonic: **Closing energy must be STORED — weight, accumulator or spring** — because the emergency may be the very event that cut the power.

questions.stem: In an underground waterway, a SURGE SHAFT is sometimes replaced by an AIR CUSHION SURGE CHAMBER, which works by:
options: Venting the tunnel to atmosphere through a vertical borehole
Confining a volume of compressed air in a sealed rock cavern connected to the tunnel
Injecting air continuously into the flowing water
Using a rubber bladder inside the penstock
questions.solution:
**By confining a volume of COMPRESSED AIR in a sealed rock cavern connected to the tunnel** — the air acting as the compressible element that a free water surface would otherwise provide, so no shaft to the surface is needed.

**Why the arrangement is attractive:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **No SHAFT to the surface is required** ← | **Which on a deep tunnel under a high mountain may be hundreds of metres** ← |
| **The chamber can be placed where the GEOLOGY is good, not where the topography allows** ← | ← |
| **It can be located close to the powerhouse** ← | **Which is hydraulically ideal, as the surge tank discussion showed** ← |
| **No surface structure, so no visual impact and no access road to a mountain top** ← | ← |
| **And it is excavated from the tunnel itself, using the same plant** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER ARE THE DECISIVE ADVANTAGE AND THEY SOLVE A GENUINE TOPOGRAPHIC PROBLEM: a conventional surge shaft must rise to above the maximum upsurge level and must reach the ground surface.**

> **Where the tunnel runs deep beneath a mountain, that shaft may be 300 or 400 m deep, expensive to sink, and it may emerge somewhere inaccessible.**

> **Worse, the topography may simply not allow the shaft to be where hydraulics wants it — near the powerhouse — so the designer must compromise the surge tank's position against where a shaft can be built.**

> **The air cushion chamber removes that constraint entirely, placing the compressible volume exactly where it is wanted, and it is one of the more elegant solutions in underground hydropower engineering.**

**THE REQUIREMENTS AND RISKS ARE SIGNIFICANT AND THEY EXPLAIN WHY THE TYPE IS NOT UNIVERSAL:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **The rock must be TIGHT — air leaks far more readily than water** ← | **The governing difficulty** ← |
| **Sufficient rock cover to contain the pressure, as for any pressure tunnel** ← | ← |
| **A COMPRESSOR plant to make up the inevitable air losses** ← | **A permanent operating requirement** ← |
| **Water curtains are sometimes used above the chamber** ← | **Boreholes kept full of water, raising the pore pressure so air cannot escape upward** ← |
| **And instrumentation to monitor the air volume and pressure** ← | **Since a loss of air is a loss of surge protection** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN INGENIOUS DEVICE WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: the WATER CURTAIN.**

> **Air escapes from the chamber by pushing water out of the rock's joints and migrating upward through them.**

> **Keeping a set of boreholes above the chamber filled with water at a pressure exceeding the chamber's air pressure means the joints there are held full of water at higher pressure, and air cannot displace it.**

> **So a curtain of pressurised water forms a barrier to air migration, and it is maintained by a small continuous supply rather than by any physical seal.**

> **The same technique is used for unlined pressurised gas and oil storage caverns, and it is a good example of using a fluid pressure gradient to do the work of an impermeable membrane.**

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE OPERATIONAL CONCERN AND IT DEFINES THE FAILURE MODE: if the air volume falls without anyone noticing, the chamber's compressibility falls with it, and the surge protection degrades silently.**

> **The plant continues to run normally and appears fine, until a load rejection produces a larger surge than the system was designed for.**

> **So continuous monitoring of the air pressure and level, with an alarm, is not optional.**

> **This is the fourth instance in this chapter of a protective provision that fails invisibly — blocked drains, de-tensioned anchors, seized expansion joints, and now a leaking air cushion — and the common lesson is that any safety provision whose degradation is not directly observable needs instrumentation deliberately added to make it observable.**
tags: compressed air as the compressible element

examTip.trick: **A sealed cavern of compressed air replaces the free water surface** — so no shaft to the surface is needed.
examTip.trap: **Air leaks where water would not** — hence water curtains: boreholes held at higher pressure above the chamber, blocking upward air migration.
examTip.mnemonic: **Its failure is silent** — lose air and the surge protection degrades while the plant runs normally. Monitor the pressure, as with drains and anchors.

questions.stem: A surge tank of 8 m diameter experiences an upsurge of 12 m above its steady level following a full load rejection. The volume of water that has entered the tank during the upsurge is approximately:
options: 603 m³
301 m³
96 m³
questions.solution:
**About 603 m³.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Cross-sectional area of the tank** | **A = πD²/4 = π × 8² ÷ 4** ← |
| ** ** | **= 3.1416 × 64 ÷ 4 = 50.27 m²** ← |
| **Volume of the upsurge** | **V = A × rise = 50.27 × 12** ← |
| ** ** | **= 603.2 m³** ← |

> **THE DISTRACTORS ARE THE STANDARD CIRCULAR-AREA ERRORS AND THEY ARE WORTH NAMING BECAUSE THEY RECUR CONSTANTLY: 301 m³ is half the answer, from using πD²/8 or from halving somewhere.**

> **2413 m³ is four times the answer, from using πD² without the /4 — that is, treating the diameter as the radius.**

> **96 m³ is D × rise, from treating the tank as though its area were its diameter — a dimensional slip.**

> **The guard is to compute the area first as a separate step and sanity-check it: an 8 m circle has an area of about 50 m², which is roughly 80 per cent of the 64 m² square that contains it, and the ratio π/4 = 0.785 is worth carrying for exactly this check.**

**WHAT THE FIGURE MEANS FOR THE TANK'S DESIGN:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **603 m³ arrived in perhaps 60 to 90 seconds** ← | **The quarter-period of the mass oscillation** ← |
| **That is an average inflow of roughly 7 to 10 m³/s** ← | ← |
| **Which is the tunnel's flow decelerating from its full value to zero** ← | ← |
| **So the volume is roughly half the tunnel's design flow times the quarter-period** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A USEFUL APPROXIMATE RELATIONSHIP FOR CHECKING A SURGE COMPUTATION AND IT FOLLOWS FROM THE OSCILLATION'S SHAPE: during the upsurge the tunnel flow falls from Q to zero, so its average over that period is about Q/2.**

> **Multiplying by the time to reach maximum surge gives the volume, and that volume divided by the tank's area gives the surge height.**

> **It is only approximate, since the deceleration is not linear and friction damps the motion, but it lands within perhaps 20 per cent and it catches gross errors in a full surge analysis.**

> **Having such a check available matters because surge calculations are usually done by numerical integration or by software, and a result from software with no independent check is a result nobody has verified.**

**AND THE DESIGN CONSEQUENCE OF THE UPSURGE HEIGHT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The tank must extend above the maximum upsurge, with freeboard** ← | ← |
| **A 12 m upsurge on top of the static level sets the tank's top** ← | ← |
| **Which must be below the ground surface at that location, or the tank must be a surface structure** ← | ← |
| **And the DOWNSURGE sets the tank's bottom, which must stay above the tunnel crown** ← | **Or air enters the tunnel, which is a serious matter** ← |

> **The last row is the constraint that most often governs the tank's overall height, and it is worth noting that the two extremes are produced by OPPOSITE events: maximum upsurge follows full load REJECTION, and maximum downsurge follows full load ACCEPTANCE.**

> **So the tank must be designed for both, and the worst case for each is a different operating incident.**

> **A further subtlety is that the worst case of all is often a SEQUENCE — a rejection followed by an acceptance timed to coincide with the oscillation, which reinforces it.**

> **Analysing single events therefore understates the extremes, and a proper surge study examines credible sequences of load changes rather than isolated ones, which is where the numerical analysis earns its keep.**
tags: circular area pi D squared over 4
upsurge and downsurge from opposite events

examTip.trick: **A = πD²/4 = 50.27 m², times 12 m = 603 m³.**
examTip.trap: **2413 is πD² without the /4** — treating the diameter as the radius. Carry π/4 = 0.785: a circle is 79% of its bounding square.
examTip.mnemonic: **Upsurge follows REJECTION, downsurge follows ACCEPTANCE** — opposite events set the tank's top and bottom, and a timed sequence beats either alone.

questions.stem: The TAILRACE of a hydropower plant should be designed so that:
options: Its water level is as high as possible to provide submergence
Its water level is kept as low as practicable, since every metre of tailwater level is a metre of head lost
Its velocity is as high as possible to carry sediment away
It discharges into a different river from the one the intake draws on
questions.solution:
**Its water level is kept as LOW as practicable, since every metre of tailwater level is a metre of head lost** — while still maintaining the submergence the draft tube requires.

**The tension the design must resolve:**

| Pushing the level DOWN | Pushing the level UP |
|---|---|
| **Every metre gained is a metre of head, earned for the plant's whole life** ← | **The draft tube must remain submerged, or it loses its function and cavitates** ← |
| **Directly increases the output at all flows** ← | **The tailrace channel must have enough depth to carry the flow** ← |
| ← | **The river's own level varies and rises in flood** ← |

> **THE SECOND COLUMN'S THIRD ROW IS THE CONSTRAINT THAT USUALLY DECIDES THE MATTER AND IT IS OFTEN UNDERESTIMATED: the tailrace discharges into the river, so its level is governed by the river's level, which the designer does not control.**

> **In flood the river rises, the tailwater rises with it, and the plant's head falls.**

> **On a low-head plant this can be severe enough to force a shutdown — the head falls below the turbine's operating minimum while the river is in full flood.**

> **So the tailrace design must be based on the river's RATING CURVE across the full range of flows, and the plant's energy calculation must use the tailwater level appropriate to each flow rather than a single figure.**

**THE DESIGN PROVISIONS THAT FOLLOW:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **A tailrace channel of generous section, so its own friction loss is small** ← | **Loss in the tailrace is head lost exactly as loss in the headrace is** ← |
| **A low, wide channel rather than a narrow deep one** ← | **Lower velocity, lower loss** ← |
| **Protection against the river's SCOUR at the outfall** ← | ← |
| **Protection against the river DEPOSITING material in the tailrace** ← | **Which raises the level and is harder to fix than scour** ← |
| **And a location where the river's level is as LOW as possible** ← | **Which may mean carrying the tailrace some distance downstream** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A REAL AND PERSISTENT PROBLEM ON HIMALAYAN RIVERS AND IT IS WORTH ANTICIPATING: a tailrace discharging into a river that is aggrading will be progressively buried.**

> **The river's bed rises, the tailwater level rises with it, and the plant loses head permanently and gradually.**

> **Nothing in the plant deteriorates; the river simply comes up around it.**

> **The defences are to discharge into a reach that is scouring rather than depositing, to keep the tailrace velocity high enough to resist deposition from the river's backwater, and to provide for periodic dredging — and the first of these is a siting decision that must be made before construction, because it cannot be revisited.**

> **THE LAST ROW POINTS TO A GENUINE DESIGN OPTION THAT IS SOMETIMES OVERLOOKED: the tailrace need not discharge at the powerhouse.**

> **Extending it as a tunnel or channel downstream to a point where the river is lower gains head, and on a steep river that can be several metres for a modest length.**

> **The gain is permanent and it applies to every cubic metre the plant ever passes, so it is weighed against the tailrace's construction cost by exactly the economic calculation used for the penstock diameter.**

> **On some schemes the tailrace tunnel is longer than the headrace for this reason, and an underground powerhouse sited well downstream of the dam, discharging through a long tailrace tunnel, is a standard high-head layout in which this consideration is a major part of the logic.**
tags: extending the tailrace to gain head

examTip.trick: **As low as practicable — every metre of tailwater is a metre of head** — subject to keeping the draft tube submerged.
examTip.trap: **The river's flood level sets the tailwater, and the designer does not control it** — use the rating curve across all flows, not one figure.
examTip.mnemonic: **An aggrading river buries a tailrace** — the plant does not deteriorate, the river comes up around it. Choose a scouring reach at the siting stage.

questions.stem: During the FIRST FILLING of a long pressure tunnel, the rate of filling must be strictly controlled principally because:
options: The water must be chemically treated before it enters
Rapid filling would erode the concrete lining
Trapped air must be able to escape ahead of the rising water
The turbines must be run in slowly at the same time
questions.solution:
**Trapped AIR must be able to escape ahead of the rising water — a pocket of compressed air suddenly released can blow out a lining or a bulkhead — and the lining and rock need time to take up the pressure gradually so that any distress is detected before full pressure is reached.**

**The hazards of a rapid first filling:**

| Hazard | Note |
|---|---|
| **Trapped AIR at high points, compressed as the water rises** ← | **It can reach great pressure and release violently** ← |
| **Air pockets driven along the tunnel, arriving at the turbine or a valve** ← | ← |
| **The lining loaded to full pressure before anyone can observe its response** ← | ← |
| **Rapid pressurisation of the surrounding rock, with no time for pore pressures to equalise** ← | ← |
| **And, on the eventual EMPTYING, the reverse problem of external pressure collapsing the lining** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST IMMEDIATELY DANGEROUS AND ITS MECHANISM IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: a tunnel is not perfectly uniform in gradient, and air collects at every local high point.**

> **As the water rises, that air is compressed rather than expelled, and a pocket compressed to a high pressure holds a great deal of stored energy.**

> **When it finally finds a path — past a bulkhead, through a vent, or by displacing water — it releases that energy suddenly, and compressed air expands far faster and more violently than water.**

> **Serious accidents have occurred this way, and the provision against it is AIR VENTS at every high point, opened before filling begins and closed only when water flows from them.**

**THE FILLING PROCEDURE ITSELF IS A DEFINED OPERATION AND ITS ELEMENTS ARE STANDARD:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Fill at a controlled, SLOW rate — often specified as a maximum rise in metres per hour** ← | ← |
| **Through a small BYPASS around the main gate, not by opening the gate** ← | **A small opening gives a controllable rate** ← |
| **Air vents open at all high points** ← | ← |
| **HOLD at intermediate levels while instruments are read** ← | ← |
| **Inspect the adits, the portals and the hillside for leakage at each hold** ← | ← |
| **And only proceed when the readings at each stage are satisfactory** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND SIXTH ROWS ARE THE SAME STAGED PHILOSOPHY APPLIED TO A DAM'S FIRST FILLING AND THE REASONING IS IDENTICAL: the structure is being loaded for the first time and there is no way to know how it will respond except by loading it and watching.**

> **Doing that in increments, with holds, means that if something is wrong it is discovered at partial load, when the consequence is small and the tunnel can be drained easily.**

> **Filling straight to full pressure means that if something is wrong it is discovered at full load, and the tunnel is then full and pressurised and the problem is much harder to address.**

> **So the staged filling converts an unknown into a sequence of small tests, and the few days it costs are the cheapest risk reduction available at that point in the project.**

> **THE LAST ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE DESERVES ITS OWN MENTION BECAUSE IT CATCHES PEOPLE OUT LATER: the DEWATERING of a pressure tunnel is as hazardous as its filling and for the mirror-image reason.**

> **Emptying it faster than air can enter creates a partial vacuum, and the external groundwater pressure — which may be substantial — then acts inward on a lining designed for internal pressure.**

> **Concrete linings have been collapsed inward this way, and so have steel liners.**

> **So the dewatering rate is specified as strictly as the filling rate, with adequate air admission, and the drainage provisions behind the lining that relieve external groundwater pressure must be working — which is another reason those drains are inspected and their functioning recorded rather than being forgotten once the tunnel is commissioned.**

examTip.trick: **Let the air out ahead of the water, and load the lining in stages so distress shows before full pressure.**
examTip.trap: **Compressed air stores energy and releases violently** — vents at every high point, open before filling and closed only when water flows.
examTip.mnemonic: **Dewatering is as dangerous as filling** — empty it faster than air enters and external groundwater pressure collapses the lining inward.

questions.stem: An UNDERGROUND POWERHOUSE is chosen in preference to a surface powerhouse principally where:
options: The rock is weak and easily excavated
Construction cost alone is to be minimised
There is no suitable rock at the site
The valley is steep and narrow with no safe surface site clear of rockfall
questions.solution:
**The valley is steep and narrow with NO SAFE SURFACE SITE clear of rockfall, landslide and flood** — and where placing the machine hall in sound rock also shortens the waterway, protects against seismic and security threats, and avoids surface land acquisition.

**The reasons for going underground:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **NO SAFE SURFACE SITE in a steep narrow valley** ← | **Often the decisive reason in the Himalaya** ← |
| **Protection from ROCKFALL, LANDSLIDE, avalanche and flood** ← | ← |
| **A SHORTER waterway is sometimes possible** ← | **Since the cavern can sit where the tunnel naturally arrives** ← |
| **Better SEISMIC performance** ← | **Underground structures shake with the rock rather than being shaken by it** ← |
| **No surface land acquisition or visual impact** ← | ← |
| **Security, which historically mattered a great deal** ← | ← |
| **And the excavated rock can serve as construction aggregate** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A GENUINE AND SOMETIMES SURPRISING ADVANTAGE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING WHY: a surface structure responds to ground motion by vibrating, and its response can amplify the input several times.**

> **An underground cavern is confined by rock on all sides and moves essentially with it, so the relative motion — which is what damages a structure — is much smaller.**

> **Recorded underground damage in major earthquakes has been consistently less than surface damage at the same location, provided the cavern is in competent rock and away from an active fault.**

> **So in a highly seismic country, going underground buys seismic performance as well as protection from the slopes above, and the two reasons reinforce each other.**

**THE COSTS AND DIFFICULTIES ARE REAL AND OPTION (b) IS THERE TO BE REJECTED:**

| Difficulty | Note |
|---|---|
| **Excavation of a large cavern is EXPENSIVE and slow** ← | **A machine hall may be 20 m wide, 40 m high and 100 m long** ← |
| **It demands GOOD ROCK — a large cavern in poor rock is very costly to support** ← | ← |
| **Access tunnels, cable tunnels, ventilation shafts and a transformer cavern are all additional** ← | ← |
| **Ventilation, lighting, drainage and fire safety are all harder underground** ← | ← |
| **And a FIRE underground is a far more serious event than a fire on the surface** ← | **Escape is limited and smoke has nowhere to go** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS OPTION (a) AND THE CONTRADICTION IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT ABOUT: weak, easily excavated rock is a reason NOT to build a cavern, not a reason to build one.**

> **A large span in weak rock requires heavy support — long tensioned anchors, thick shotcrete, steel arches — and the support cost rises far faster than the excavation cost falls.**

> **The governing dimension is the cavern's SPAN, and the stand-up time for a 20 m span in poor rock may be measured in hours.**

> **So an underground powerhouse requires competent rock as a precondition, and where the rock is poor the surface option becomes relatively more attractive even in a difficult valley.**

> **THE LAST ROW DESERVES SERIOUS WEIGHT AND IT SHAPES A GREAT DEAL OF THE DETAILED DESIGN: an underground powerhouse contains transformers, oil-filled equipment, cables and generators, all of which can burn.**

> **The standard responses are to place the TRANSFORMERS in a separate cavern, to use oil-free or low-flammability transformers and cables where possible, to provide a dedicated smoke extraction system, to compartment the cavern with fire doors, and to provide at least two independent escape routes.**

> **The separate transformer cavern is the single most valuable of these, because transformer oil is the largest fire load in the station and separating it protects the machine hall from the worst credible fire.**

> **And two independent escape routes is an absolute requirement rather than a preference — a single access tunnel that is also the only escape route is not acceptable, however inconvenient the second one is to construct.**
tags: fire safety and separate transformer cavern

examTip.trick: **No safe surface site in a steep valley** — plus protection from rockfall and flood, seismic benefit, and no land acquisition.
examTip.trap: **Weak rock argues AGAINST a cavern, not for it** — support cost rises faster than excavation cost falls, and SPAN is the governing dimension.
examTip.mnemonic: **Separate transformer cavern and two escape routes** — transformer oil is the biggest fire load, and underground a fire has nowhere to vent.

questions.stem: A penstock is to be replaced on an operating scheme. The head loss through the existing pipe is 9 m out of a gross head of 180 m. Replacing it with a pipe of 20 per cent greater diameter would reduce the loss to approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 3.6 m.**

**Using h ∝ 1/D⁵ at constant discharge:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Ratio of diameters** | **D₂/D₁ = 1.20** ← |
| **Ratio of losses** | **h₂/h₁ = (D₁/D₂)⁵ = (1/1.20)⁵** ← |
| ** ** | **1.20⁵ = 1.2 × 1.2 × 1.2 × 1.2 × 1.2** ← |
| ** ** | **1.44, 1.728, 2.0736, 2.4883** ← |
| **So** | **h₂ = 9 ÷ 2.4883 = 3.62 m** ← |

> **THE ARITHMETIC OF 1.2⁵ IS WORTH DOING STEP BY STEP RATHER THAN GUESSING, and the intermediate values are useful to recognise: 1.2² = 1.44, 1.2³ = 1.728, 1.2⁴ ≈ 2.07, 1.2⁵ ≈ 2.49.**

> **So a 20 per cent diameter increase cuts the loss to about 40 per cent of its previous value — it reduces it by 60 per cent.**

> **That is a large return for a modest enlargement and it is the practical import of the fifth-power relationship.**

> **The distractor at 7.2 m corresponds to assuming h ∝ 1/D, which gives 9/1.2 = 7.5 — close to 7.2 and representing the error of ignoring the velocity's dependence on diameter.**

**WHETHER THE REPLACEMENT IS WORTH MAKING IS THE REAL QUESTION AND IT CAN BE ANSWERED FROM THESE FIGURES:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Head recovered** | **9 − 3.62 = 5.38 m** ← |
| **As a fraction of the gross head** | **5.38 ÷ 180 = 3.0 per cent** ← |
| **So the plant's output rises by about 3 per cent** ← | **Net head rising from 171 m to 176.4 m** ← |
| **On a 50 MW plant at a 0.55 capacity factor** | **50 × 8.76 × 0.55 = 241 GWh a year, so 3 per cent is about 7.2 GWh** ← |
| **Which is the annual benefit against which the pipe's cost is weighed** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS A POINT WORTH BEING CAREFUL ABOUT: the output rises in proportion to the NET head, not the gross.**

> **The net head goes from 180 − 9 = 171 m to 180 − 3.62 = 176.4 m, an increase of 5.38 m on 171, which is 3.15 per cent.**

> **Expressing the gain as a fraction of the gross head gives 2.99 per cent, which is close but not identical, and on a scheme with larger losses the two would differ noticeably.**

> **So the correct denominator is the net head the plant currently achieves, since that is what the output is currently proportional to.**

> **A CLOSING OBSERVATION ON THE ECONOMICS OF SUCH A RETROFIT, WHICH DIFFERS FROM A NEW-BUILD DECISION: the original penstock's cost is SUNK and must not enter the comparison.**

> **The question is only whether the new pipe's cost is repaid by the additional energy, and the old pipe's residual value — as scrap, or by sale — counts as a credit.**

> **That is a different and usually harder test than the original sizing decision faced, because the original decision compared the incremental cost of a larger pipe against the energy gained, and the retrofit must justify an ENTIRE pipe against only the incremental energy.**

> **So a penstock that was undersized at construction frequently cannot be economically replaced afterwards, even though it was clearly the wrong size — which is a strong argument for getting the diameter right the first time, and a good illustration of why decisions that are cheap to make correctly and expensive to correct deserve disproportionate attention at the design stage.**
tags: gain as a fraction of net head

examTip.trick: **h₂ = h₁/(1.2)⁵ = 9/2.49 = 3.6 m** — a 20% larger pipe loses 60% less.
examTip.trap: **7.2 m comes from assuming h ∝ 1/D** — forgetting that velocity also falls with diameter. Keep 1.2⁵ ≈ 2.49 handy.
examTip.mnemonic: **The old pipe's cost is SUNK** — a retrofit must justify a whole pipe against only the incremental energy, which is why undersized penstocks stay undersized.

questions.stem: The fundamental distinction between an IMPULSE turbine and a REACTION turbine is that in an impulse turbine:
options: The entire available head is converted to kinetic energy in the nozzle before the water strikes the runner
The runner is always mounted on a horizontal shaft
The water flows radially rather than axially
The efficiency is always higher than a reaction turbine's
questions.solution:
**The entire available head is converted to KINETIC ENERGY in the nozzle before the water strikes the runner**, so the runner operates at ATMOSPHERIC pressure and is not enclosed in pressurised water.

**The distinction and everything that follows from it:**

| Aspect | IMPULSE (Pelton, Turgo, crossflow) | REACTION (Francis, Kaplan, propeller) |
|---|---|---|
| **Where the head is converted** | **Entirely in the NOZZLE, before the runner** ← | **PARTLY in the guide vanes and partly across the runner itself** ← |
| **Pressure at the runner** | **ATMOSPHERIC throughout** ← | **Drops across the runner — the runner is pressurised** ← |
| **Runner filled with water?** | **NO — only the buckets being struck** ← | **YES — completely full** ← |
| **Draft tube** | **None — discharges freely to air** ← | **Essential** ← |
| **Head below the runner** | **LOST** ← | **Recovered by the draft tube** ← |
| **Flow control** | **By moving a SPEAR in the nozzle** ← | **By rotating the GUIDE VANES (wicket gates)** ← |
| **Suits** | **HIGH head, low flow** ← | **Low to medium head, higher flow** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST VIVID WAY TO HOLD THE DISTINCTION AND IT IS WORTH PICTURING: a Pelton runner spins in AIR, and a jet strikes its buckets one after another.**

> **A Francis runner is completely submerged and the water passes continuously through every passage at once.**

> **So an impulse runner is a wheel being hit, and a reaction runner is a passage being flowed through.**

> **From that single image the rest of the table can be reconstructed — a wheel in air needs no draft tube and loses the head below it; a submerged runner must be sealed, pressurised, and connected to the tailwater by a draft tube.**

**THE NAME 'REACTION' DESERVES EXPLAINING SINCE IT IS OFTEN TAKEN ON TRUST:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water ACCELERATES as it passes through a reaction runner's passages** ← | **The passages narrow** ← |
| **That acceleration requires a force on the water** ← | ← |
| **By Newton's third law, the water exerts an equal and opposite REACTION on the runner** ← | ← |
| **That reaction is part of the torque driving the machine** ← | ← |
| **So the runner is driven by both the impulse of the changing momentum AND the reaction of the accelerating flow** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE HONEST STATEMENT AND IT SHOWS WHY THE NAMES ARE SLIGHTLY MISLEADING: a reaction turbine works by impulse AND reaction, while an impulse turbine works by impulse alone.**

> **The degree of reaction — the fraction of the head converted within the runner rather than before it — is the formal measure, and it is zero for a Pelton wheel by definition.**

> **A Francis turbine has a degree of reaction of roughly 0.5, and a Kaplan rather more.**

> **So the two families are the endpoints and the middle of a continuum rather than two wholly different principles, which is worth knowing because it explains why specific speed varies smoothly across them rather than jumping.**

> **AND OPTION (d) MUST BE REJECTED EXPLICITLY BECAUSE IT INVERTS THE FACTS: peak efficiencies are comparable, with Francis turbines reaching 94 or 95 per cent and Pelton wheels around 90 to 92.**

> **What genuinely differs is the shape of the efficiency curve at PART LOAD: a Pelton wheel holds its efficiency remarkably flat from about 20 per cent of full flow upward, because reducing the jet changes its velocity very little.**

> **A Francis turbine's efficiency falls away sharply below about 40 or 50 per cent of design flow, because the flow no longer matches the fixed runner blade angles.**

> **That part-load characteristic, not the peak figure, is what matters on a variable Himalayan river — and it is a second reason, alongside head, why Pelton wheels suit Nepali schemes so well.**

examTip.trick: **All the head becomes velocity in the nozzle, so the runner spins in AIR at atmospheric pressure** — no draft tube, and the head below it is lost.
examTip.trap: **A reaction turbine works by impulse AND reaction** — 'degree of reaction' is zero for Pelton, about 0.5 for Francis. A continuum, not two principles.
