examTip.mnemonic: **Pelton holds efficiency flat down to 20% flow; Francis falls away below 40-50%** — which matters more than peak efficiency on a variable river.

questions.stem: The SPECIFIC SPEED of a turbine, Ns = N√P / H^1.25, is used in turbine selection because it:
options: Is a single number combining speed, power and head that characterises the shape of the runner
Determines the turbine's efficiency directly
Gives the actual rotational speed the turbine will run at
Measures the turbine's resistance to cavitation
questions.solution:
**It is a single number combining SPEED, POWER and HEAD that characterises the SHAPE of the runner** — so each turbine family occupies a characteristic range of specific speed, and computing it for a site points directly to the family required.

**The characteristic ranges (with Ns in metric units, N in rpm, P in kW, H in m):**

| Turbine | Specific speed range |
|---|---|
| **PELTON, single jet** ← | **About 8 to 30** ← |
| **PELTON, multi-jet** ← | **Up to about 70, rising with the number of jets** ← |
| **FRANCIS, slow runner** ← | **About 60 to 150** ← |
| **FRANCIS, fast runner** ← | **About 150 to 400** ← |
| **KAPLAN / propeller** ← | **About 300 to 1000** ← |

> **THE PROGRESSION FROM TOP TO BOTTOM IS A PROGRESSION IN RUNNER SHAPE AND SEEING IT THAT WAY MAKES THE TABLE MEMORABLE: low specific speed means a NARROW runner handling little water at great head, and high specific speed means a WIDE, OPEN runner handling a great deal of water at small head.**

> **A Pelton wheel is a rim of buckets — almost no through-passage at all, which is the extreme of narrowness.**

> **A Francis runner opens progressively as specific speed rises, its passages becoming wider and its flow turning from radial toward axial.**

> **A Kaplan is a propeller in a tube — fully axial and completely open.**

> **So the specific speed is literally a shape parameter, and the sequence Pelton → Francis → Kaplan is a continuous opening-out of the runner rather than three unrelated designs.**

**WHY THE PARAMETER IS SO USEFUL IN DESIGN:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Selecting the turbine FAMILY for a given site** ← | **Compute Ns for the required P, H and a candidate N** ← |
| **Choosing the ROTATIONAL SPEED** ← | **N must suit the generator's pole number and the grid frequency** ← |
| **Scaling MODEL test results to the prototype** ← | **Machines of equal Ns are geometrically similar and share performance characteristics** ← |
| **Estimating cavitation limits** ← | **Thoma's σ correlates with Ns** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CONSTRAINT THAT MAKES THE SELECTION AN ITERATION RATHER THAN A CALCULATION AND IT IS OFTEN OVERLOOKED: the rotational speed is not free.**

> **A synchronous generator's speed is N = 120f/p, with f the frequency and p the number of poles, and p must be an even integer.**

> **At 50 Hz this gives the permissible speeds 3000, 1500, 1000, 750, 600, 500, 428.6, 375, 333.3 rpm and so on.**

> **So the designer computes Ns for each permissible speed, sees which turbine family each implies, and chooses — and the choice trades a higher speed, which gives a smaller and cheaper machine, against the turbine type that speed forces and the cavitation risk that comes with it.**

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PARAMETER'S ORIGINAL PURPOSE AND IT IS WORTH APPRECIATING: specific speed exists so that a model tested in a laboratory can predict a prototype's behaviour.**

> **Two machines with the same specific speed are hydraulically similar, so the model's efficiency, its cavitation behaviour and its characteristic curves transfer to the full-size machine with known scaling corrections.**

> **Every large turbine is model-tested before manufacture for exactly this reason, and the model test is a contractual acceptance milestone on major contracts.**

> **So specific speed is not merely a selection chart's axis; it is the similarity parameter that makes turbine development possible at laboratory scale, which is why it is defined as it is rather than in some more intuitive form.**

examTip.trick: **Ns characterises runner SHAPE** — low Ns is a narrow high-head runner, high Ns a wide open low-head one. Pelton 8-70, Francis 60-400, Kaplan 300-1000.
examTip.trap: **N is not free — N = 120f/p with p even** — so at 50 Hz only 3000, 1500, 1000, 750, 600, 500, 375... are available. Selection is an iteration.
examTip.mnemonic: **Equal Ns means hydraulically similar** — which is why a laboratory model predicts the prototype, and why every large turbine is model-tested.

questions.stem: A generator is to run at 600 rpm on a 50 Hz system. The number of poles required is:
questions.solution:
**10 poles.**

**Using the synchronous speed relation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **N = 120 f / p** | **N in rpm, f in Hz, p the number of POLES** ← |
| **Rearranged** | **p = 120 f / N** ← |
| **Substituting** | **p = 120 × 50 ÷ 600** ← |
| ** ** | **= 6000 ÷ 600 = 10 poles** ← |

> **THE COMMONEST ERROR IS CONFUSING POLES WITH POLE PAIRS AND IT GIVES OPTION (a): the relation in terms of pole PAIRS is N = 60f/(pole pairs), which gives 5 pole pairs — that is, 10 poles.**

> **So 5 pole pairs and 10 poles are the same machine described two ways, and 6 is simply wrong by either route.**

> **The safest habit is to use N = 120f/p with p meaning poles, and to remember that the number of poles is always EVEN because poles occur in north-south pairs.**

> **That evenness is itself a useful check — any calculation yielding an odd number of poles has gone wrong somewhere.**

**THE PERMISSIBLE SPEEDS AT 50 Hz ARE WORTH TABULATING SINCE THEY RECUR CONSTANTLY:**

| Poles | Speed (rpm) |
|---|---|
| **2** | **3000** ← |
| **4** | **1500** ← |
| **6** | **1000** ← |
| **8** | **750** ← |
| **10** | **600** ← |
| **12** | **500** ← |
| **16** | **375** ← |
| **20** | **300** ← |
| **24** | **250** ← |

> **THE PATTERN IS THAT 3000 IS DIVIDED BY THE NUMBER OF POLE PAIRS, and holding the first few in memory — 3000, 1500, 1000, 750, 600, 500 — covers most hydropower applications.**

> **Large low-head machines run slowly and therefore have many poles: a big Kaplan at 100 rpm needs 60 poles, which is why such generators are physically enormous in diameter.**

> **High-head Pelton machines run fast and need few, which is why they are comparatively compact.**

> **So the generator's physical size is driven by the turbine's speed, and a slow turbine implies a large expensive generator — which is a cost that must be included when comparing a low-head and a high-head scheme, and which reinforces the point that low-head plants cost more per kilowatt.**

**A NOTE ON WHY SYNCHRONOUS OPERATION MATTERS AT ALL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A synchronous generator's rotor turns in exact step with the grid's frequency** ← | ← |
| **So its speed is FIXED by the grid once synchronised** ← | ← |
| **The governor therefore controls POWER, not speed, when the machine is on the grid** ← | ← |
| **It controls SPEED only when the machine is isolated or being synchronised** ← | ← |

> **The third and fourth rows describe a distinction that confuses many people and it is worth stating clearly: a governor's function changes depending on whether the machine is connected.**

> **On an isolated system, opening the gates makes the machine speed up, so the governor regulates gate opening to hold the frequency.**

> **On a large grid, the machine cannot speed up — the grid holds it — so opening the gates simply makes it generate more power.**

> **Hence the same governor acts as a speed controller in one situation and a load controller in the other, and understanding which regime applies is essential to interpreting a plant's behaviour during a disturbance.**
tags: governor role changes on and off grid

examTip.trap: **Poles, not pole pairs** — 10 poles is 5 pole pairs. And the pole count is always EVEN, which is a free check on the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **3000, 1500, 1000, 750, 600, 500** — the 50 Hz ladder. Slow machines need many poles and are therefore physically huge.

questions.stem: The GOVERNOR of a hydro turbine must reconcile two conflicting requirements when the load is suddenly rejected. These are:
options: Closing slowly to limit the water hammer pressure rise in the penstock
Maintaining voltage and maintaining frequency
Cooling the bearings and lubricating the seals
Opening the guide vanes and closing the main inlet valve
questions.solution:
**Closing SLOWLY to limit the water hammer pressure rise in the penstock, and closing QUICKLY to limit the runaway speed rise of the unit** — the two pulling in opposite directions.

**The conflict set out:**

| Requirement | Wants the closure | Because |
|---|---|---|
| **Limit PRESSURE rise** ← | **SLOW** ← | **Δh ≈ 2LV/gt — the longer the closure, the smaller the rise** ← |
| **Limit SPEED rise** ← | **FAST** ← | **While water still drives the runner with no load on it, the unit accelerates** ← |

> **THE TWO ARE IRRECONCILABLE BY TIMING ALONE AND THAT IS THE WHOLE PROBLEM: any closure time chosen is a compromise between a pressure the penstock must withstand and a speed the generator must survive.**

> **Typical design limits are a pressure rise of 25 to 50 per cent above static and a speed rise of 30 to 60 per cent above rated.**

> **The closure time that satisfies both may not exist for a long penstock and a low-inertia machine, in which case something else must be provided.**

> **That is where the additional devices come in, and each of them relaxes one side of the conflict so that a workable closure time exists.**

**THE DEVICES THAT BREAK THE DEADLOCK:**

| Device | How it helps |
|---|---|
| **Increased FLYWHEEL EFFECT (GD² or WR²) of the rotating mass** ← | **A heavier rotor accelerates more slowly, so a slower closure is tolerable** ← |
| **A SURGE TANK** ← | **Shortens the effective L, so the pressure rise for a given closure time falls** ← |
| **A PRESSURE RELIEF VALVE, opening as the guide vanes close** ← | **Keeps the total flow steady while the flow to the runner stops — no water hammer at all** ← |
| **A DEFLECTOR on a Pelton wheel** ← | **Swings between the jet and the runner instantly, cutting the torque while the spear closes slowly** ← |
| **A bypass or synchronous bypass valve** ← | **Same principle as the relief valve** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST ELEGANT SOLUTION OF THE SET AND IT IS SPECIFIC TO IMPULSE MACHINES: a Pelton wheel's jet can be DEFLECTED away from the buckets without changing the flow at all.**

> **So the torque is removed in a fraction of a second, ending the overspeed risk immediately, while the spear valve takes as many seconds as it likes to close and the penstock sees no rapid deceleration.**

> **The conflict is not compromised but dissolved — the two requirements are separated onto two different devices, each of which can then be optimised alone.**

> **This is a recurring pattern in engineering worth recognising: when two requirements conflict because one mechanism must serve both, the best solution is often to provide two mechanisms rather than to find the optimal compromise.**

> **THE FIRST ROW DESERVES A NOTE BECAUSE IT IS A DESIGN VARIABLE THAT IS PURCHASED RATHER THAN CALCULATED: the generator's rotor can be made deliberately heavier than electrically necessary, to add inertia.**

> **That costs money and it buys a slower permissible closure and hence a lower pressure rise.**

> **So the penstock's wall thickness and the generator's rotor mass are economically linked — spending on one saves on the other — and the optimum is found by considering them together.**

> **A specification that fixes the flywheel effect before the penstock is designed, or vice versa, forgoes that optimisation, which is a good reason for the hydraulic and electromechanical designs to proceed in dialogue rather than in sequence.**

examTip.trick: **Slow closure limits pressure; fast closure limits overspeed** — and no single closure time serves both well.
examTip.trap: **A Pelton DEFLECTOR dissolves the conflict** — it cuts the torque instantly while the spear closes slowly. Two mechanisms beat one compromise.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rotor inertia and penstock thickness are economically linked** — spend on one and save on the other. Design them together, not in sequence.

questions.stem: CAVITATION in a reaction turbine is best described as:
options: Erosion caused by sand particles in the water striking the runner
Corrosion of the runner due to dissolved oxygen
Air leaking into the turbine casing through the shaft seal
The formation of vapour bubbles where the local pressure falls to the water's vapour pressure
questions.solution:
**The formation of VAPOUR BUBBLES where the local pressure falls to the water's vapour pressure, and their violent COLLAPSE as they are carried into a higher-pressure region** — the collapse pitting and eroding the metal surface.

**The mechanism, step by step:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water accelerating over a curved blade experiences a local pressure DROP** ← | **By Bernoulli — higher velocity, lower pressure** ← |
| **If that pressure reaches the VAPOUR pressure, the water boils locally** ← | **At ambient temperature — it is boiling by pressure reduction, not by heating** ← |
| **Vapour bubbles form and are carried downstream by the flow** ← | ← |
| **Reaching a region of higher pressure, they COLLAPSE — implode — almost instantaneously** ← | ← |
| **The collapse near a surface produces a microjet and a shock wave of enormous local intensity** ← | **Pressures of the order of gigapascals, momentarily** ← |
| **Repeated millions of times, this fatigues and removes metal, leaving a spongy pitted surface** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS WHY CAVITATION DAMAGES EVEN VERY HARD MATERIALS AND IT SURPRISES PEOPLE: the damage is not caused by the water's velocity but by the implosion.**

> **A collapsing bubble adjacent to a surface collapses asymmetrically, forming a microjet that strikes the metal at enormous speed and very small area.**

> **The local stress exceeds the yield strength of any engineering metal, so each collapse removes or work-hardens a minute amount, and the accumulation is a fatigue process.**

> **Hardness alone therefore does not confer immunity — resistance depends on toughness and work-hardening capacity as well, which is why austenitic stainless steels resist cavitation better than harder but more brittle materials.**

**DISTINGUISHING CAVITATION FROM SAND ABRASION IS PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT AND OPTION (a) IS THERE FOR THAT REASON:**

| Feature | CAVITATION | SAND ABRASION |
|---|---|---|
| **Appearance** | **Spongy, pitted, honeycombed — material removed from within** ← | **Smooth, polished, wave-patterned grooves following the flow** ← |
| **Location** | **Where pressure is LOWEST — blade suction side outlet, draft tube cone, runner band** ← | **Where velocity and particle concentration are highest — leading edges, labyrinth seals, nozzle tips** ← |
| **Cause** | **Setting too high, running off design point, low tailwater** ← | **Sediment in the water** ← |
| **Remedy** | **Lower the setting, restrict the operating range, aerate, use resistant steel** ← | **Better settling, hard coatings, replaceable parts** ← |

> **THE APPEARANCE ROW IS HOW THE TWO ARE TOLD APART ON A DISMANTLED RUNNER AND THE DIAGNOSIS MATTERS BECAUSE THE REMEDIES ARE DIFFERENT: treating cavitation damage by improving the settling basin achieves nothing, and lowering the turbine setting does nothing for sand abrasion.**

> **In Nepal the two very often occur TOGETHER and they reinforce each other — abrasion roughens the blade surface, the roughness triggers local flow separation, separation lowers the local pressure, and cavitation begins where it otherwise would not.**

> **So a runner suffering sand abrasion becomes progressively more prone to cavitation, and the combined damage rate exceeds the sum of the two acting alone.**

> **That interaction is why Himalayan runners deteriorate faster than either mechanism alone would predict, and it is an argument for repairing abrasion damage promptly rather than letting it accumulate to a convenient overhaul date.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON THE OPERATING RANGE, WHICH IS THE CHEAPEST CONTROL AVAILABLE: cavitation is worst at part load and at overload, and least near the design point.**

> **So restricting the machine's permitted operating range — refusing to run it below, say, 50 per cent of rated output — avoids much of the damage at the cost of some operational flexibility.**

> **Turbine manufacturers supply a permitted operating range on the hill chart for exactly this purpose, and operating outside it to meet a system need is a decision that trades runner life for immediate energy.**

> **Making that trade knowingly is legitimate; making it because nobody consulted the hill chart is how runners are destroyed in a fraction of their intended life.**

examTip.trick: **Bubbles form at vapour pressure and IMPLODE in higher pressure** — the microjet and shock wave pit the metal. Damage is from collapse, not velocity.
examTip.trap: **Cavitation is spongy and pitted; abrasion is smooth and grooved** — different causes, different remedies. Improving settling does nothing for cavitation.
examTip.mnemonic: **In the Himalaya they compound** — abrasion roughens the blade, roughness triggers separation, separation triggers cavitation. Repair abrasion promptly.

questions.stem: The SPIRAL (scroll) CASING of a Francis turbine is shaped with a progressively DECREASING cross-sectional area around the runner in order to:
options: Reduce the casing's weight and cost
Increase the water's pressure as it approaches the runner
Deliver the water to the guide vanes uniformly around the whole circumference at constant velocity
Allow the casing to be cast in a single piece
questions.solution:
**To deliver the water to the guide vanes UNIFORMLY around the whole circumference at constant velocity** — since the flow remaining in the casing diminishes as water is progressively drawn off into the runner.

**The reasoning, which is pure continuity:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Water enters the casing at one point and travels around the runner** ← | ← |
| **At every angular position, some of it turns inward through the guide vanes** ← | ← |
| **So the flow REMAINING in the casing decreases steadily around the circumference** ← | ← |
| **To keep the velocity constant, the area must decrease in the same proportion** ← | **A = Q/V, with V fixed and Q falling** ← |
| **Which gives the characteristic spiral, tapering to nothing at the far side** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DESIGN RULE AND IT PRODUCES THE SHAPE DIRECTLY: if a quarter of the flow has been drawn off by the time the water has travelled a quarter of the way round, the casing's area at that point should be three-quarters of its inlet area.**

> **Applying that at every angle traces out the spiral.**

> **The purpose of holding the velocity constant is to give every guide vane the same approach conditions, so that the runner is loaded uniformly all the way round.**

> **Non-uniform approach would load the runner unevenly, producing a rotating force on the shaft, vibration and bearing wear — so the casing's shape is what allows the machine to run smoothly, and it is a hydraulic requirement rather than a structural or manufacturing one.**

**THE COMPLETE WATER PATH THROUGH A FRANCIS TURBINE IS WORTH HAVING IN ORDER:**

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **1. SPIRAL CASING** ← | **Distributes the flow uniformly around the circumference** ← |
| **2. STAY VANES (speed ring)** ← | **Structural — they carry the casing's pressure load; shaped to disturb the flow as little as possible** ← |
| **3. GUIDE VANES (wicket gates)** ← | **Adjustable — they set the flow rate and impart the correct swirl to the water** ← |
| **4. RUNNER** ← | **Extracts the energy, turning the flow from radial to axial** ← |
| **5. DRAFT TUBE** ← | **Recovers the exit kinetic energy and the head to tailwater** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN ROWS 2 AND 3 IS FREQUENTLY BLURRED AND IT IS WORTH KEEPING SHARP: stay vanes are FIXED and structural, guide vanes are MOVABLE and hydraulic.**

> **The stay ring holds the spiral casing together against the internal pressure trying to burst it, and its vanes are aerofoil-shaped purely so that this structural necessity costs as little head as possible.**

> **The guide vanes do the hydraulic work — rotating together on a regulating ring to vary the flow and to set the angle at which water meets the runner blades.**

> **Only the guide vanes move, and they are what the governor actuates.**

> **THE THIRD ROW'S SECOND FUNCTION IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN FORGOTTEN AND IT IS THE MORE IMPORTANT OF THE TWO: guide vanes do not merely throttle, they set the SWIRL.**

> **A Francis runner extracts energy by changing the water's angular momentum, so the water must arrive with the right tangential velocity component for the blade angle it meets.**

> **At the design flow the guide vane angle produces exactly that, and the water enters the runner smoothly with no shock.**

> **At part flow the vanes close, the approach angle changes, and the water no longer meets the fixed blade angle correctly — so it enters with shock loss, and that is precisely why a Francis turbine's efficiency falls away at part load while a Kaplan's, whose blades also turn to match, does not.**

examTip.trick: **Flow is drawn off all the way round, so the area must shrink to hold the velocity constant** — pure continuity, A = Q/V.
examTip.trap: **Stay vanes are FIXED and structural; guide vanes MOVE and are hydraulic** — only the guide vanes are actuated by the governor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Guide vanes set the SWIRL, not just the flow** — which is why a fixed-blade Francis loses efficiency at part load and an adjustable-blade Kaplan does not.

questions.stem: A KAPLAN turbine is described as 'double regulated' because:
options: It has two runners on the same shaft
Both the guide vanes and the runner blades are adjustable
It can operate in both directions of rotation
It is regulated by both a governor and a manual control
questions.solution:
**Both the GUIDE VANES and the RUNNER BLADES are adjustable, and they are moved in a coordinated relationship** — which keeps the flow entering the blades at the correct angle over a wide range of load and gives the machine a very flat efficiency curve.

**Why the second adjustment matters so much:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A fixed-blade propeller turbine has one flow at which the blade angle is correct** ← | ← |
| **Away from it, water strikes the blades at the wrong angle and shock loss occurs** ← | ← |
| **So a propeller turbine's efficiency curve is PEAKED — excellent at one point, poor away from it** ← | ← |
| **A Kaplan turns the blades to match the flow** ← | ← |
| **So the correct entry angle is maintained at every load** ← | ← |
| **Giving a broad, FLAT efficiency curve over perhaps 30 to 100 per cent of load** ← | ← |

> **THE CONTRAST BETWEEN THE THIRD AND SIXTH ROWS IS THE WHOLE VALUE OF THE KAPLAN AND IT IS WORTH QUANTIFYING: a fixed propeller at half load may be at 70 per cent efficiency, and a Kaplan at the same load at 90.**

> **On a plant whose flow varies through the year, that difference dominates the annual energy.**

> **So the Kaplan's additional mechanical complexity — a hub containing the blade-operating mechanism, oil passages down the shaft, and a servomotor — is repaid in energy on any site with variable flow.**

> **And where the flow is steady, as below a regulating reservoir, the fixed propeller's simplicity and lower cost may win — which is why both machines remain in use rather than the Kaplan having simply superseded the propeller.**

**THE COORDINATION BETWEEN THE TWO ADJUSTMENTS IS THE MACHINE'S DEFINING FEATURE AND IT DESERVES DETAIL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **For each guide vane opening there is one blade angle giving peak efficiency** ← | ← |
| **That relationship is established by MODEL TESTING and is called the CAM or the combinator curve** ← | ← |
| **The governor holds the two in that relationship automatically** ← | **Originally by a mechanical cam, now in software** ← |
| **The relationship also depends on the HEAD** ← | **So the combinator is a three-dimensional relationship: gate, blade and head** ← |
| **A mis-set combinator loses efficiency invisibly** ← | **The machine runs and generates, just less than it should** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS AN OPERATIONAL POINT WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE THE LOSS IS EASY TO OVERLOOK: a Kaplan whose combinator relationship has drifted, or which is running on a curve set for a different head, loses a few per cent of its output continuously.**

> **Nothing alarms, nothing trips, and the machine appears perfectly healthy.**

> **The loss shows only in the energy figures, and only if somebody compares the actual output against what the head and flow should be producing.**

> **So periodic verification of the combinator — an index test comparing output against flow at various gate openings — is a worthwhile maintenance activity, and it is one of the few that pays for itself directly in recovered energy.**

**THE RELATED MACHINE TYPES ARE WORTH PLACING ALONGSIDE IT:**

| Machine | Regulation |
|---|---|
| **PROPELLER (fixed blade)** ← | **Single regulated — guide vanes only** ← |
| **KAPLAN** ← | **Double regulated — guide vanes and blades** ← |
| **BULB turbine** ← | **A Kaplan with the generator in a bulb in the waterway — for very low heads** ← |
| **Semi-Kaplan** ← | **Adjustable blades, FIXED guide vanes — a low-cost compromise for small schemes** ← |

> **The last row is a useful option that is often overlooked on small low-head schemes: if only one adjustment can be afforded, adjusting the BLADES and fixing the guide vanes preserves most of the flat efficiency curve.**

> **The blade angle is the more influential of the two for part-load performance, so fixing the cheaper-to-fix element retains most of the benefit.**

> **That kind of partial adoption — taking the more valuable half of a two-part improvement — is worth looking for generally, and it is how a technology developed for large plant is often made affordable at small scale.**

examTip.trick: **Guide vanes AND runner blades both adjust, in a coordinated relationship** — keeping the entry angle right at every load.
examTip.trap: **The combinator depends on HEAD as well as gate opening** — a curve set for the wrong head loses a few per cent silently, with nothing alarming.
examTip.mnemonic: **Semi-Kaplan: adjust the BLADES, fix the guide vanes** — the blade angle matters more at part load, so half the mechanism keeps most of the benefit.

questions.stem: A Pelton turbine operates under a net head of 320 m. The theoretical velocity of the jet issuing from the nozzle, taking the nozzle velocity coefficient as 0.98, is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 77.7 m/s.**

**Using the jet velocity relation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Ideal velocity from Torricelli** | **V = √(2gH) = √(2 × 9.81 × 320)** ← |
| ** ** | **2 × 9.81 = 19.62; 19.62 × 320 = 6278.4** ← |
| ** ** | **√6278.4 = 79.24 m/s** ← |
| **With the velocity coefficient** | **V = Cv √(2gH) = 0.98 × 79.24** ← |
| ** ** | **= 77.66 m/s ≈ 77.7 m/s** ← |

> **THE DISTRACTOR AT 79.2 m/s IS THE IDEAL VELOCITY WITH THE COEFFICIENT NOT APPLIED, and it is the same class of trap as the earlier question where the efficiencies were supplied and ignored.**

> **The question gave Cv, so Cv must appear in the answer.**

> **The other two distractors come from √(gH) = 56.0 — omitting the factor of 2 — and from a mis-rooted value.**

> **So the guard is the same as before: check that every quantity the question supplied has been used, and check the structure of the formula rather than only its arithmetic.**

**THE JET VELOCITY LEADS DIRECTLY TO THE RUNNER SPEED AND THAT IS THE NEXT STEP IN ANY PELTON DESIGN:**

| Relationship | Note |
|---|---|
| **Optimum bucket speed u = φ × V, with φ ≈ 0.46 to 0.48** ← | **Theoretically 0.5; slightly less in practice because of friction and the need to clear the bucket** ← |
| **Here u ≈ 0.46 × 77.7 ≈ 35.7 m/s** ← | ← |
| **And u = πDN/60 gives the relationship between wheel diameter and speed** ← | ← |
| **So a fixed synchronous speed determines the wheel diameter, or vice versa** ← | ← |

> **THE THEORETICAL 0.5 IN THE FIRST ROW IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING RATHER THAN MEMORISING BECAUSE THE DERIVATION IS SHORT AND SATISFYING: the power delivered is the force on the bucket times the bucket's speed.**

> **The force depends on the RELATIVE velocity (V − u), so it falls as u rises; the power is that force times u, so it rises with u.**

> **The product u(V − u) is maximised when u = V/2, which is the classic result.**

> **At u = 0 the bucket is stationary and delivers no power despite the maximum force; at u = V the bucket runs away with the jet and feels no force at all; and halfway between is the optimum — which is a satisfying piece of mechanics and it generalises to any impulse device.**

**AND THE JET VELOCITY'S OTHER IMPLICATION IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST IN NEPAL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **77.7 m/s is about 280 km/h** ← | ← |
| **Any sand carried in that jet strikes the bucket at that speed** ← | ← |
| **Abrasive wear rises very steeply with velocity — roughly with its cube** ← | ← |
| **So the same sediment concentration does vastly more damage at 320 m head than at 80 m** ← | **Twice the velocity, roughly eight times the wear** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW'S CUBIC RELATIONSHIP IS THE REASON HIGH-HEAD HIMALAYAN SCHEMES SUFFER SO BADLY AND IT IS WORTH CARRYING AS A NUMBER: doubling the head raises the jet velocity by √2, and raising velocity by √2 raises wear by about 2.8 times.**

> **So a 400 m scheme wears roughly three times as fast as a 200 m scheme in the same river, all else being equal.**

> **That is why the settling basin's design particle size must be chosen with reference to the HEAD, and why a basin specification transferred from a medium-head scheme to a high-head one on the same river is inadequate.**

> **It also explains why Pelton buckets on Nepali schemes are commonly hard-coated with tungsten carbide and are treated as replaceable wearing parts, budgeted for renewal rather than expected to last the plant's life.**
tags: optimum bucket speed half the jet
abrasive wear rises with velocity cubed

examTip.trap: **79.2 is the ideal velocity with Cv ignored** — the question supplied it, so it must appear in the answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **Optimum bucket speed is half the jet** — maximise u(V − u). And wear goes roughly as velocity cubed, which is why high head punishes sediment so hard.

questions.stem: The EXCITATION system of a hydro generator is provided to:
options: Start the turbine rotating from rest
Supply the direct current to the rotor's field winding that produces the magnetic field
Cool the stator windings
Synchronise the generator's frequency with the grid
questions.solution:
**To supply the DIRECT CURRENT to the rotor's field winding that produces the magnetic field** — and by varying that current, to control the generator's TERMINAL VOLTAGE and its reactive power output.

**What excitation does and how it divides from governing:**

| Control | Acts on | Governs |
|---|---|---|
| **The GOVERNOR, through the guide vanes** ← | **The mechanical power input** ← | **FREQUENCY when isolated, ACTIVE POWER (MW) when on the grid** ← |
| **The EXCITER, through the field current** ← | **The magnetic field strength** ← | **VOLTAGE when isolated, REACTIVE POWER (MVAr) when on the grid** ← |

> **THE SYMMETRY BETWEEN THE TWO ROWS IS THE CLEANEST WAY TO HOLD THE WHOLE SUBJECT AND IT IS WORTH MEMORISING IN THIS FORM: the governor handles the real power and the frequency; the exciter handles the reactive power and the voltage.**

> **And in each case, which of the pair is controlled depends on whether the machine is connected to a large grid.**

> **Isolated, the machine sets its own frequency and voltage, so the two controls regulate those directly.**

> **Connected, the grid imposes both, so the same two controls instead determine how much active and reactive power the machine contributes — a single change of circumstance that reverses what each control appears to do.**

**THE REACTIVE POWER FUNCTION DESERVES EXPLANATION SINCE IT IS LESS FAMILIAR THAN THE REAL POWER ONE:**

| Condition | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| **OVER-excited (field current high)** ← | **The machine EXPORTS reactive power — it acts like a capacitor, supporting the system voltage** ← |
| **Normally excited** ← | **Unity power factor, no reactive exchange** ← |
| **UNDER-excited (field current low)** ← | **The machine ABSORBS reactive power — acting like an inductor, reducing the system voltage** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS A GENUINELY VALUABLE SERVICE THAT HYDRO PLANT PROVIDES AND IT IS OFTEN UNCOMPENSATED: a grid needs reactive power to support its voltage, particularly when heavily loaded, and generators are the most controllable source of it.**

> **A hydro generator can supply or absorb reactive power rapidly and continuously, adjusting as the system requires.**

> **It can even do so while generating no real power at all — running as a SYNCHRONOUS CONDENSER, with the runner dewatered by compressed air so that it spins in air with minimal drag, drawing a little power from the grid and supplying a great deal of reactive support.**

> **That capability is valuable in a weak grid and it costs almost nothing to provide on a machine that already exists, which makes it one of the better-value services an existing hydro station can offer.**

**AND THE EXCITER'S OWN ARRANGEMENT HAS CHANGED IN A WAY WORTH KNOWING:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Rotating DC exciter on the main shaft** ← | **The traditional arrangement — a DC generator feeding the field through slip rings** ← |
| **STATIC excitation** ← | **Power taken from the generator's own terminals, rectified, and fed to the field through slip rings** ← |
| **BRUSHLESS excitation** ← | **An AC exciter with rotating rectifiers on the shaft — no slip rings or brushes at all** ← |

> **The second row is the common modern arrangement for large machines and its advantage is response SPEED: a static exciter using thyristors can change the field current within a cycle or two, which a rotating exciter's own inductance prevents.**

> **Fast excitation response improves the machine's transient stability — its ability to stay in step with the grid after a fault — because the field can be boosted, or 'forced', immediately to hold the machine synchronised.**

> **Its one weakness follows from where it takes its supply: a static exciter fed from the generator's own terminals loses its supply when a nearby fault collapses the terminal voltage, which is precisely when the forcing is needed.**

> **The remedy is a compound arrangement drawing partly from the line CURRENT, which is high during a fault, so the exciter is supplied exactly when the voltage source fails — an elegant piece of design in which the fault itself powers the response to it.**
tags: field current controls voltage and MVAr

examTip.trick: **DC to the rotor field — controlling voltage when isolated, reactive power when on the grid.**
examTip.trap: **Governor = MW and frequency; exciter = MVAr and voltage** — and which of each pair applies depends on whether the machine is grid-connected.
examTip.mnemonic: **Over-excited exports MVAr like a capacitor** — and a dewatered machine spinning in air is a synchronous condenser, valuable in a weak grid for almost nothing.

questions.stem: The POWERHOUSE CRANE is one of the first items that must be settled in a powerhouse layout because:
options: It is the most expensive single item in the station
It must be installed before the walls are built
Its required capacity and hook height are set by the heaviest single piece to be lifted
Cranes have very long delivery periods
questions.solution:
**Its required CAPACITY and HOOK HEIGHT are set by the heaviest single piece to be lifted — usually the generator rotor** — and those in turn fix the height of the machine hall, the strength of the crane beams and the size of the erection bay.

**How the crane propagates through the whole building:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The HEAVIEST LIFT sets the crane's capacity** ← | **Normally the generator rotor, which on a large machine is hundreds of tonnes** ← |
| **The crane's capacity sets the size and strength of the CRANE BEAMS and their columns** ← | ← |
| **The HOOK HEIGHT needed to lift the rotor clear of the stator sets the crane rail level** ← | ← |
| **Which sets the HEIGHT of the machine hall** ← | ← |
| **And the height of an underground cavern is very expensive, so this matters greatly there** ← | ← |
| **The ERECTION BAY must be large enough to lay out the largest components** ← | ← |
| **And the ACCESS route must admit the heaviest piece from the road** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN WHY THIS IS A FIRST-ORDER LAYOUT DECISION RATHER THAN AN EQUIPMENT DETAIL: cavern height is one of the most expensive dimensions in an underground powerhouse, because excavation volume and support requirements both grow with it.**

> **The height is determined by stacking the draft tube, the turbine, the generator, the crane clearance and the crane itself, and the crane's contribution is substantial.**

> **So a decision to use two smaller cranes lifting in tandem instead of one large one, or to split the rotor for transport and assemble it in situ, can reduce the cavern's height by several metres and save a great deal of excavation.**

> **Those decisions must be taken early, because they cannot be revisited once the cavern's profile is fixed.**

**THE LAST ROW IS FREQUENTLY THE BINDING CONSTRAINT IN NEPAL AND IT DESERVES ITS OWN TREATMENT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The heaviest indivisible component must travel from the port to the site by ROAD** ← | ← |
| **Every bridge, culvert, bend and tunnel on that route sets a limit** ← | ← |
| **In Nepal that means from Kolkata or Haldia through India and up a hill road** ← | ← |
| **Hill road bends limit the LENGTH as much as bridges limit the weight** ← | ← |
| **So the transport study must be done before the machine is specified, not after** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL RULE AND ITS VIOLATION HAS DELAYED REAL PROJECTS: a transformer or a rotor that cannot reach the site is not a procurement problem to be solved later, it is a specification error.**

> **The remedies — splitting the component, strengthening bridges, building a bypass, or in extreme cases airlifting — are all expensive and slow.**

> **So the route survey is done early, the governing weight and dimension are established, and the equipment is specified within them.**

> **Where the site's constraint is severe, that may mean choosing more, smaller units rather than fewer large ones — which raises the cost per kilowatt and is nonetheless the right answer when the alternative is a machine that cannot be delivered.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON THE NUMBER OF UNITS, SINCE THE TRANSPORT QUESTION FEEDS INTO IT: the choice between two large units and three or four smaller ones involves several considerations at once.**

> **More units give better part-load efficiency on a variable river, more redundancy when one is under maintenance, smaller and more transportable components, and a lower minimum operating flow.**

> **Fewer units give lower cost per kilowatt, a smaller powerhouse, and less equipment to maintain.**

> **Two or three units is the usual resolution for a Nepali ROR scheme, with the variable flow argument generally outweighing the cost per kilowatt — and it is worth noting that this is the same conclusion reached earlier from the turbine's minimum operating flow, arrived at now from an entirely different direction.**

Usually the generator rotor — and those in turn fix the height of the machine hall, the strength of the crane beams and the size of the erection bay.

examTip.trick: **The heaviest lift — usually the rotor — sets capacity and hook height, and those set the hall's height and the crane beams.**
examTip.trap: **Do the TRANSPORT route survey before specifying the machine** — a rotor that cannot pass a hill bend is a specification error, not a procurement problem.
examTip.mnemonic: **More smaller units: better part-load, more redundancy, transportable parts. Fewer large: cheaper per kW.** Two or three usually wins on a variable river.

questions.stem: A THRUST BEARING in a vertical-shaft hydro generating unit carries:
options: Only the radial forces from the shaft's rotation
The combined weight of the entire rotating assembly
The torque generated by the turbine
The electromagnetic forces in the generator air gap
questions.solution:
**The combined WEIGHT of the entire rotating assembly — rotor, shaft and runner — plus the downward HYDRAULIC THRUST on the runner**, transferring that load to the powerhouse structure.

**The bearing arrangement of a vertical unit:**

| Bearing | Carries |
|---|---|
| **THRUST bearing** ← | **The whole AXIAL load: rotating weight plus hydraulic thrust — often several hundred to a few thousand tonnes** ← |
| **UPPER GUIDE bearing** ← | **Radial load above the rotor — keeps the shaft centred** ← |
| **LOWER GUIDE bearing** ← | **Radial load below the rotor** ← |
| **TURBINE GUIDE bearing** ← | **Radial load close to the runner, resisting the hydraulic side forces** ← |

> **THE MAGNITUDE IN THE FIRST ROW IS WHAT MAKES THE THRUST BEARING THE MOST CRITICAL MECHANICAL COMPONENT IN THE STATION: on a large unit it carries a load comparable to a small building, on an oil film a fraction of a millimetre thick, while rotating continuously.**

> **It works on the hydrodynamic principle — tilting pads that form a converging wedge of oil as the runner plate slides over them, and the pressure generated in that wedge supports the load.**

> **The film is created by the ROTATION itself, so it exists only while the machine is turning.**

> **Which leads directly to the arrangement's critical vulnerability, and to the provision that answers it.**

**THE STARTING AND STOPPING PROBLEM AND ITS SOLUTION:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **At rest and at very low speed, no hydrodynamic film forms** ← | ← |
| **So the pads and the runner plate are in metal-to-metal contact under the full load** ← | ← |
| **Starting under those conditions scores the bearing surfaces** ← | ← |
| **The provision is HIGH-PRESSURE OIL INJECTION (jacking oil) beneath the pads before starting** ← | ← |
| **Which lifts the assembly hydrostatically until rotation establishes the hydrodynamic film** ← | ← |
| **And is applied again during shutdown, until the machine stops** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN ESSENTIAL AUXILIARY ON ANY LARGE UNIT AND ITS FAILURE IS SERIOUS: starting a large machine without jacking oil can damage the thrust bearing on a single start.**

> **So the starting sequence interlocks on the jacking oil pressure, and the machine will not start without it.**

> **This is a good instance of a protective interlock that must NOT be defeatable, because the temptation to bypass it during commissioning or a fault investigation is real and the consequence of doing so is immediate and expensive.**

> **The same logic applies to the cooling water flow interlock and the bearing temperature trips — protections whose bypass produces no immediate symptom and a large eventual cost.**

**AND THE HYDRAULIC THRUST COMPONENT DESERVES A NOTE SINCE IT IS NOT CONSTANT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The downward thrust on a reaction runner varies with the load and the head** ← | ← |
| **It can be large — comparable to the rotating weight on some machines** ← | ← |
| **On a Kaplan it also varies with the blade angle** ← | ← |
| **And during transients it can momentarily reverse, trying to LIFT the rotating assembly** ← | ← |

> **The last row is the condition that requires some units to have an arrangement resisting UPWARD movement as well, and it is easily overlooked because the steady-state load is so overwhelmingly downward.**

> **A load rejection on some machine types produces a transient upthrust, and a rotating assembly that lifts even slightly and drops back damages the bearing and the seals.**

> **So the thrust bearing or a separate arrangement must hold the assembly down as well as up, and the transient analysis that establishes whether this is needed is part of the machine's design rather than the civil engineer's — but its consequence, a hold-down provision anchored into the structure, appears in the civil drawings and must not be value-engineered out by someone who sees only the steady-state load.**

examTip.trick: **Rotating weight plus hydraulic thrust — the whole axial load** — on an oil film a fraction of a millimetre thick.
examTip.trap: **The hydrodynamic film only exists while rotating** — hence high-pressure JACKING OIL before starting and during shutdown, interlocked so it cannot be skipped.
examTip.mnemonic: **Transients can momentarily UPTHRUST** — so a hold-down provision may be needed, and it must not be value-engineered away.

questions.stem: The step-up TRANSFORMER at a hydropower station raises the generator's output voltage — typically 6.6 to 13.8 kV — to transmission voltage because:
options: Transmission line losses are proportional to the square of the current
High voltage is safer for personnel to work with
Generators cannot be built to produce high voltage under any circumstances
The grid frequency changes with voltage
questions.solution:
**Transmission line LOSSES are proportional to the square of the CURRENT, so raising the voltage for the same power reduces the current proportionately and the losses as its square** — making long-distance transmission economic.

**The arithmetic that justifies the whole transmission system:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Power transmitted P = √3 × V × I × cos φ for three phase** ← | ← |
| **So for a given P, the current I is inversely proportional to V** ← | ← |
| **Line loss = 3 I² R** ← | ← |
| **Therefore loss ∝ 1/V²** ← | ← |
| **Raising the voltage from 11 kV to 132 kV — a factor of 12 — cuts the loss by a factor of 144** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS WHY TRANSMISSION AT HIGH VOLTAGE IS NOT MERELY PREFERABLE BUT NECESSARY: transmitting 50 MW at 11 kV over 50 km would lose most of it as heat, and would require conductors of absurd size.**

> **At 132 kV the same power travels the same distance with a few per cent loss and a conductor of ordinary dimensions.**

> **So the transformer is what makes it possible to generate power where the water is and consume it where the people are, and those two places in Nepal are typically far apart.**

> **The cost of the transformers at each end is repaid many times over by the conductor saved and the energy not lost — and the higher the voltage, the further the economic transmission distance, which is why the choice of transmission voltage follows from the line's length and the power carried.**

**WHY GENERATORS ARE NOT SIMPLY BUILT AT TRANSMISSION VOLTAGE, WHICH OPTION (c) OVERSTATES:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Generator voltage is limited by the INSULATION that can be fitted in the stator slots** ← | ← |
| **Higher voltage needs thicker insulation, which displaces copper** ← | ← |
| **So a high-voltage generator would be larger, more expensive and less efficient** ← | ← |
| **The economic optimum for the machine itself lies in the 6.6 to 25 kV range** ← | ← |
| **So it is an economic limit rather than an absolute one** ← | **High-voltage generators have been built experimentally and are not economic** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHY OPTION (c) IS WRONG AS STATED RATHER THAN MERELY IMPRECISE: it is not that generators cannot be built at high voltage, but that it is uneconomic to do so.**

> **The Powerformer concept demonstrated generation directly at transmission voltage using cable-wound stators, eliminating the step-up transformer altogether.**

> **It worked, and it did not displace the conventional arrangement, because the machine's extra cost exceeded the transformer's.**

> **So the standard arrangement persists because the optimum is where it is, and knowing that the alternative exists and was rejected on cost is more useful than believing it impossible.**

**THE TRANSFORMER'S OTHER FUNCTIONS AND ITS PRACTICAL CONCERNS DESERVE A CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **It provides galvanic ISOLATION between the generator and the grid** ← | ← |
| **Its winding connection — usually delta on the generator side, star with earthed neutral on the HV side — sets the EARTHING arrangement** ← | **And blocks zero-sequence currents and triplen harmonics** ← |
| **TAP CHANGERS allow the ratio to be adjusted as system conditions vary** ← | ← |
| **It is the largest FIRE risk in the station, being full of oil** ← | **Hence separate transformer caverns or bays, oil containment bunds and deluge systems** ← |
| **And it is often the heaviest single item to transport** ← | ← |

> **The fourth row connects back to the underground powerhouse discussion and it is worth restating because it drives real layout decisions: the transformer's oil is the station's principal fire load.**

> **Separating it — in its own cavern underground, or in an outdoor bay with blast walls at a surface station — limits the worst credible fire to equipment that can be replaced without destroying the machine hall.**

> **The oil containment bund beneath it serves the same purpose for a leak, keeping oil out of the drainage and the river.**

> **Both provisions are cheap relative to what they protect, and both are occasionally omitted at small stations where the same reasoning applies at a smaller scale.**
tags: loss varies as 1 over V squared
generator voltage is an economic limit

examTip.trick: **Loss = 3I²R and I ∝ 1/V, so loss ∝ 1/V²** — 11 kV to 132 kV cuts losses by 144 times.
examTip.trap: **Generators COULD be built at high voltage — it is uneconomic, not impossible** — insulation displaces copper, so the optimum sits at 6.6-25 kV.
examTip.mnemonic: **The transformer is the station's biggest fire load** — separate cavern or bay, oil bund, deluge. Cheap relative to the machine hall it protects.

questions.stem: A hydro plant of 24 MW installed capacity generates 105 GWh in a year. Its capacity factor is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 0.50.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Energy at 100 per cent capacity factor** | **24 MW × 8.76 GWh per MW-year = 210.24 GWh** ← |
| **Capacity factor** | **105 ÷ 210.24 = 0.4994** ← |
| **So** | **CF ≈ 0.50** ← |

> **THE 8.76 GWh PER MW-YEAR SHORTCUT MAKES THIS A SINGLE DIVISION, and it is the third time in this bank that the figure has done the work — which is reason enough to have it committed.**

> **The longer route is identical: 24,000 kW × 8760 h = 210,240,000 kWh = 210.24 GWh, and 105 ÷ 210.24 = 0.4994.**

> **A rougher mental check is that half of 210 is 105 exactly, so the answer is precisely a half — which is the kind of round result worth noticing because it confirms the arithmetic instantly.**

> **When a calculation lands on a suspiciously clean number, that is usually because the question was constructed to do so, and it is a signal that the method was right rather than a coincidence to be distrusted.**

**WHAT A 0.50 CAPACITY FACTOR SAYS ABOUT THIS PLANT:**

| Interpretation | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is a typical figure for a well-sized ROR plant in Nepal** ← | **The range being roughly 0.45 to 0.60** ← |
| **Equivalent to 4,380 full-load hours a year** ← | **0.5 × 8760** ← |
| **Consistent with a design flow around Q40 to Q50 on a monsoon river** ← | ← |
| **A much lower figure would suggest an oversized plant or a curtailment problem** ← | ← |
| **A much higher one would suggest storage, a very steady river, or an undersized plant** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS ARE THE DIAGNOSTIC USE OF THE FIGURE AND IT IS THE REASON TO COMPUTE IT AT ALL: the capacity factor is a summary statistic that invites a question rather than answering one.**

> **A plant reporting 0.30 on a river that should support 0.50 is losing energy somewhere — to curtailment, to outages, to a silted intake, to a worn runner, or to a design flow chosen too ambitiously.**

> **Each of those has a different remedy, and the capacity factor does not distinguish between them; it merely says that something is worth investigating.**

> **So the figure's value is as a screening indicator, tracked year on year, where a DECLINE is more informative than any absolute level — a plant whose capacity factor falls from 0.52 to 0.44 over five years has a developing problem, and identifying it early is far cheaper than discovering it at an overhaul.**

> **A CLOSING NOTE ON THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN CAPACITY FACTOR AND AVAILABILITY, SINCE TRACKING BOTH IS WHAT MAKES THE DIAGNOSIS POSSIBLE: availability is the fraction of time the plant was ABLE to run, and capacity factor is the fraction of possible energy it actually produced.**

> **A plant with 98 per cent availability and a 0.44 capacity factor is being limited by WATER or by the market, not by its own condition.**

> **One with 85 per cent availability and the same capacity factor is being limited by breakdowns.**

> **The two figures together separate the hydrological and commercial causes from the mechanical ones, which neither figure achieves alone — and reporting both is therefore a great deal more useful than reporting either, a point that applies to performance indicators generally.**
tags: capacity factor as a screening indicator

examTip.trap: **A clean answer usually means the method was right** — half of 210 is 105 exactly, which confirms the arithmetic at a glance.
examTip.mnemonic: **Track capacity factor AND availability** — high availability with a low CF means water or market; low availability means breakdowns. Neither figure separates them alone.

questions.stem: The SWITCHYARD of a hydropower station contains circuit breakers, isolators, instrument transformers, surge arresters and busbars. The essential distinction between a CIRCUIT BREAKER and an ISOLATOR is that:
options: An isolator operates faster than a circuit breaker
A circuit breaker is used only at low voltage
A circuit breaker can interrupt current
They are two names for the same device
questions.solution:
**A circuit breaker can INTERRUPT current — including fault current — under load, whereas an isolator has no arc-quenching capability and may only be operated OFF-LOAD**, to provide a visible break for safety.

**The two devices compared:**

| Aspect | CIRCUIT BREAKER | ISOLATOR (disconnector) |
|---|---|---|
| **Can break load current?** | **YES** ← | **NO** ← |
| **Can break FAULT current?** | **YES — that is its purpose** ← | **NO** ← |
| **Arc quenching** | **SF6, vacuum, oil or air blast** ← | **NONE** ← |
| **Operated** | **Under load, automatically by protection** ← | **OFF-LOAD only, after the breaker has opened** ← |
| **Purpose** | **Protection — clearing faults and switching** ← | **ISOLATION — a visible, verifiable air gap for safe working** ← |
| **Speed** | **A few cycles** ← | **Slow — seconds** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW OF PURPOSE IS THE CRUCIAL SAFETY DISTINCTION AND IT IS WHY BOTH DEVICES EXIST RATHER THAN JUST THE CAPABLE ONE: a circuit breaker interrupts current but does not provide a guaranteed, VISIBLE break.**

> **Its contacts are inside a sealed chamber and nobody can see whether they have actually opened.**

> **A person about to work on the equipment needs certainty, and certainty means an air gap that can be SEEN, or a position that is positively verified.**

> **So the isolator's job is not to break current at all — it is to prove, visibly, that the circuit is open, and that is why the sequence for taking equipment out of service is always: open the BREAKER first, then the ISOLATOR, then earth.**

**THE OPERATING SEQUENCE AND ITS INTERLOCKING:**

| To de-energise | To re-energise |
|---|---|
| **1. Open the circuit BREAKER** ← | **1. Remove the EARTH** ← |
| **2. Open the ISOLATOR** ← | **2. Close the ISOLATOR** ← |
| **3. Apply the EARTHING switch** ← | **3. Close the BREAKER** ← |
| **4. Prove dead, then work** ← | ← |

> **THE ORDER IS REVERSED BETWEEN THE COLUMNS AND IT IS ENFORCED BY MECHANICAL AND ELECTRICAL INTERLOCKS FOR THE BEST OF REASONS: opening an isolator under load draws an arc that the device cannot extinguish.**

> **That arc can persist, escalate into a phase-to-phase fault, and destroy the switchyard and anyone standing near it.**

> **Isolator-under-load incidents are among the most severe accidents in substation work, and they happen when the interlocking is defeated or absent.**

> **So the interlock preventing isolator operation while the breaker is closed is a life-safety device, in the same category as the jacking-oil interlock noted earlier, and it is likewise one that must never be bypassed for convenience.**

> **THE EARTHING STEP DESERVES ITS OWN EMPHASIS BECAUSE IT IS THE ONE THAT ACTUALLY PROTECTS THE WORKER: an isolated circuit can still become live — through induction from adjacent circuits, through a switching error elsewhere, or through backfeed from a low-voltage source.**

> **The earthing switch connects the isolated conductor solidly to earth, so that any such energisation causes an immediate fault and trips the source rather than electrocuting the person working.**

> **So isolation proves the circuit is dead now, and earthing ensures it stays dead.**

> **The two are complementary and neither substitutes for the other — which is why the permit-to-work procedure requires both, along with proving dead at the point of work with an instrument that is itself proved before and after use.**

examTip.trick: **A breaker interrupts current; an isolator only provides a visible off-load break** — no arc quenching at all.
examTip.trap: **Breaker first, then isolator, then earth — reversed to restore** — opening an isolator on load draws an arc it cannot extinguish. Never bypass the interlock.
examTip.mnemonic: **Isolation proves it is dead now; EARTHING keeps it dead** — against induction, switching errors and backfeed. Both are required, neither substitutes.

questions.stem: A hydro plant delivers 18 MW at a net head of 95 m with an overall efficiency of 0.86. The discharge through the turbines is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About 22.5 m³/s.**

**Rearranging the power equation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **P = 9.81 η Q H, with P in kW** | ← |
| **So Q = P ÷ (9.81 η H)** | ← |
| **Substituting** | **Q = 18,000 ÷ (9.81 × 0.86 × 95)** ← |
| ** ** | **9.81 × 0.86 = 8.437** ← |
| ** ** | **8.437 × 95 = 801.5** ← |
| ** ** | **Q = 18,000 ÷ 801.5 = 22.46 m³/s** ← |

> **THE REARRANGEMENT IS THE ONLY DIFFICULTY AND THE CHECK IS TO SUBSTITUTE BACK: 9.81 × 0.86 × 22.46 × 95 = 18,003 kW, which recovers the 18 MW given.**

> **Back-substitution is worth the fifteen seconds on any rearranged formula, because it catches an inverted division immediately — the commonest error of this type.**

> **Dividing the wrong way here would give 18,000 × 801.5, an absurd number, which is easily spotted; but a subtler inversion, such as dividing by η instead of multiplying, gives 16.6 m³/s, which looks entirely plausible.**

> **So the distractor at 16.6 is not a careless error but a reasonable-looking one, and only the back-substitution distinguishes it.**

**A USEFUL CROSS-CHECK USING THE FIELD RULE OF THUMB:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **P ≈ 8.5 Q H for a typical efficiency** | ← |
| **So Q ≈ P ÷ (8.5 H) = 18,000 ÷ (8.5 × 95)** | ← |
| ** ** | **= 18,000 ÷ 807.5 = 22.3 m³/s** ← |
| **Which agrees with 22.46 to within 1 per cent** | **Because 0.86 is close to the 0.866 the rule assumes** ← |

> **THE AGREEMENT CONFIRMS BOTH THE ANSWER AND THE RULE OF THUMB'S USEFULNESS, and it shows why carrying 8.5 is worthwhile: it converts a four-step calculation into a one-step estimate accurate enough for almost any preliminary purpose.**

> **The rule works in either direction — power from flow and head, or flow from power and head — and it is the same relationship rearranged.**

> **Where the actual efficiency differs markedly from 0.87 the rule drifts, so a small hydro scheme at 0.70 overall would need 9.81 × 0.70 ≈ 6.9 rather than 8.5, and using 8.5 there would understate the flow by a fifth.**

> **So the rule carries an assumption and it is worth knowing what that assumption is, rather than applying it universally.**

**AND THE RESULT INVITES A CHECK AGAINST THE RIVER, WHICH IS THE ENGINEERING POINT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **22.5 m³/s is the plant's design discharge** ← | ← |
| **It must be available from the river after the riparian release** ← | ← |
| **At the chosen dependability — Q40 or thereabouts for an ROR scheme** ← | ← |
| **And the intake, gravel trap, settling basin, headrace and penstock must all pass it** ← | ← |
| **Plus the continuous flushing allowance if that system is used** ← | **Which adds 2 to 5 per cent to what the intake must take** ← |

> **The last row is a detail that is easy to omit from a preliminary sizing and it matters: the headworks must divert MORE than the turbines pass, by the flushing allowance.**

> **An intake sized for exactly the turbine discharge leaves nothing for flushing, so either the flushing does not happen or the plant runs below capacity whenever it does.**

> **The same applies to any other continuous abstraction — cooling water, a fish release taken from the headrace, or leakage.**

> **So the intake's design flow is the turbine flow plus every continuous withdrawal downstream of it, and stating those explicitly in the design basis prevents a shortfall that would otherwise appear only in operation.**

examTip.trap: **Back-substitute to check** — dividing by η instead of multiplying gives 16.6, which looks perfectly plausible and is wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **The intake must take MORE than the turbines pass** — add the flushing allowance and every other continuous withdrawal.

questions.stem: COMMISSIONING tests on a new hydro unit include a run-up to RUNAWAY SPEED. This test is performed to:
options: Determine the unit's maximum power output
Calibrate the flow measurement instruments
Establish the turbine's efficiency at full load
Verify that the rotating assembly
questions.solution:
**To VERIFY that the rotating assembly, the bearings and the generator can withstand the speed they would reach on a full load rejection with the closing mechanism failed** — a condition the machine must survive without damage.

**What runaway speed is and why it must be tested:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **RUNAWAY is the speed reached with full flow and NO load, the gates failing to close** ← | ← |
| **It is typically 1.7 to 2.0 times rated speed for a Francis machine** ← | **And can exceed 2.5 times for a Kaplan at an unfavourable blade angle** ← |
| **Centrifugal stress rises with the SQUARE of speed** ← | **So twice the speed is four times the stress** ← |
| **The machine must survive it without damage and without disintegration** ← | ← |
| **So the design must accommodate it, and the test confirms the design** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHY RUNAWAY IS A SERIOUS DESIGN CONDITION RATHER THAN AN INCIDENTAL ONE: at twice rated speed the centrifugal forces on the generator rotor are four times their normal value.**

> **The rotor rim, its retaining wedges and the pole fixings must all be designed for that.**

> **A generator rotor failing at runaway would disintegrate, throwing large pieces of steel through the machine hall, so the requirement is absolute rather than economic.**

> **And because runaway can occur from a simple mechanical failure of the closing mechanism — an event of modest probability rather than a remote one — designing for it is not conservatism but a straightforward response to a credible condition.**

**THE COMMISSIONING TEST PROGRAMME MORE BROADLY IS WORTH KNOWING SINCE IT IS THE PROJECT'S FINAL PROOF:**

| Test | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **Dry tests of all controls, protections and interlocks** ← | **Before water is admitted** ← |
| **First filling of the waterway, staged** ← | **As described earlier** ← |
| **First rotation at low speed, checking bearings and vibration** ← | ← |
| **Speed rise to rated, with vibration and temperature monitoring** ← | ← |
| **RUNAWAY test** ← | **Brief, with careful monitoring** ← |
| **Synchronisation and first connection to the grid** ← | ← |
| **LOAD REJECTION tests at 25, 50, 75 and 100 per cent** ← | **Verifying pressure rise and speed rise against the design predictions** ← |
| **INDEX and efficiency tests** ← | **Verifying the guaranteed performance** ← |
| **A continuous RELIABILITY run before takeover** ← | **Commonly 15 to 30 days** ← |

> **THE LOAD REJECTION SERIES IS THE MOST INFORMATIVE OF THESE AND IT IS THE DIRECT TEST OF THE GOVERNING COMPROMISE DISCUSSED EARLIER: each rejection is instrumented, and the measured penstock pressure rise and speed rise are compared against the values the design predicted.**

> **Agreement confirms the whole chain of assumptions — the wave speed, the conduit lengths, the closure time, the flywheel effect, the surge tank's behaviour.**

> **Disagreement means one of those was wrong, and it is far better to discover that during commissioning than during a real incident.**

> **The tests are done in ascending order for the obvious reason: if the 25 per cent rejection produces a larger pressure rise than predicted, the 100 per cent test is not attempted until the discrepancy is understood.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE CONTRACTUAL MILESTONE THAT MATTERS MOST TO EVERYONE INVOLVED AND ITS PURPOSE IS OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD: the reliability run is not a performance test but an ENDURANCE test.**

> **Many defects — a bearing running slightly hot, a seal weeping, a control that hunts under particular conditions, a cooling system marginal on a hot afternoon — appear only after sustained operation.**

> **A machine can pass every instantaneous test and fail within a fortnight of continuous running.**

> **So the reliability run exists to expose those, and shortening it under commercial pressure to begin earning revenue transfers the risk from the contractor to the owner at precisely the moment the contractor's obligations are being discharged — which is why its duration is written into the contract and should not be traded away.**
tags: centrifugal stress varies as speed squared
load rejection tests verify the design
reliability run is an endurance test

examTip.trick: **Prove the machine survives full flow with no load and the gates failed** — 1.7 to 2.0 times rated speed for a Francis.
examTip.trap: **Stress rises with speed SQUARED** — twice the speed is four times the centrifugal force on the rotor rim and pole fixings.
examTip.mnemonic: **Load rejections in ASCENDING order** — 25, 50, 75, 100% — each checking measured pressure and speed rise against prediction before the next.

questions.stem: For a hydropower plant in a sediment-laden Himalayan river, the most realistic strategy for the turbine runner over the plant's life is to:
options: Specify the hardest available material and expect the runner to last the plant's full design life without attention
Rely on the settling basin to remove all abrasive material
Shut the plant down for the entire monsoon to avoid all sediment exposure

Accept that abrasion will occur, and manage it — by hard coatings, by designing for removal and refurbishment at planned intervals, by holding spare runners or components, and by budgeting the cost from the outset
questions.solution:
**Accept that ABRASION WILL OCCUR, and manage it** — by hard coatings, by designing for removal and refurbishment at planned intervals, by holding spare runners or components, and by budgeting the cost from the outset.

**Why the other strategies fail:**

| Strategy | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| **Hardest material, expect full life** ← | **No material resists Himalayan quartz at Pelton jet velocities for decades. Hardness alone is not the answer** ← |
| **Shut down through the monsoon** ← | **Forgoes the majority of the annual energy — the monsoon is when the water is there** ← |
| **Rely on the settling basin** ← | **A basin economically removes particles down to perhaps 0.15 to 0.2 mm; the finer quartz passes and still abrades** ← |
| **ACCEPT AND MANAGE** ← | **The only strategy that is both technically honest and economically viable** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE KEY TECHNICAL FACT AND IT WAS ESTABLISHED EARLIER IN THE SETTLING BASIN DISCUSSION: removing progressively finer particles costs disproportionately more, because the required basin length grows as the inverse square of the particle diameter.**

> **So there is always a fine fraction that it is uneconomic to remove, and that fraction reaches the turbine.**

> **The design question is therefore not how to eliminate abrasion but where to set the boundary between what the basin removes and what the runner endures — and that boundary is an economic optimum between basin cost and runner life.**

> **Setting it explicitly, with the runner refurbishment cost quantified, is what turns an unavoidable problem into a managed one.**

**WHAT THE MANAGEMENT STRATEGY CONSISTS OF IN PRACTICE:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **HARD COATINGS — tungsten carbide applied by HVOF spraying** ← | **Extends life several times; must be reapplied periodically** ← |
| **Erosion-resistant BASE MATERIAL — high-chromium martensitic stainless steels** ← | ← |
| **Designing the runner for REMOVAL without major dismantling** ← | **Which shortens every outage for its whole life** ← |
| **Holding a SPARE runner, or spare Pelton buckets** ← | **So the exchange is a short outage rather than a months-long repair** ← |
| **Scheduling refurbishment in the DRY season** ← | **When the energy forgone is least** ← |
| **And BUDGETING it as a recurring operating cost, not an unexpected repair** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE WHERE THE MOST VALUE LIES AND THEY ARE PLANNING DECISIONS RATHER THAN TECHNICAL ONES: a spare runner is expensive capital sitting idle, and it converts a three-month repair outage into a two-week exchange.**

> **Scheduling that exchange for February rather than August means the energy forgone is a fraction of what a monsoon outage would cost.**

> **Together they can reduce the annual cost of abrasion by more than any metallurgical improvement available.**

> **So the response to sediment is as much about logistics and scheduling as about materials, and a project that invests heavily in coatings while holding no spares and repairing reactively has optimised the less important half.**

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE FINANCIAL DISCIPLINE THAT MAKES THE WHOLE STRATEGY WORK AND IT CONNECTS BACK TO THE ECONOMIC LIFE DISCUSSION: runner refurbishment on a Himalayan scheme is a predictable, recurring cost occurring every few years.**

> **Treating it as such — a line in the operating budget, with a sinking fund — means the money is there when the outage is due.**

> **Treating it as an unexpected repair means the expenditure competes with everything else at the moment it arises, and the refurbishment is deferred, and the deferred refurbishment costs more because the damage has progressed and the efficiency loss has accumulated.**

> **This is the same pattern seen with flushing, with drainage maintenance and with instrumentation: a predictable recurring cost that is not budgeted becomes a deferred one, and deferral converts a manageable expense into a larger one — which is perhaps the single most useful operational lesson this chapter has to offer.**
tags: schedule refurbishment in the dry season
budget recurring costs or they are deferred

examTip.trick: **Accept and manage** — coatings, planned refurbishment, spares, and a budget line. Elimination is not available.
examTip.trap: **A basin economically reaches about 0.15-0.2 mm** — finer quartz passes and abrades. The boundary is an economic optimum, not a technical limit.
examTip.mnemonic: **A spare runner plus a dry-season exchange beats any metallurgy** — logistics and scheduling save more than materials do.
